title: The Constitutional Political Economy of Competition in Kenya: Markets, State Power and Economic Liberty

detail.title: The Constitutional Political Economy of Competition in Kenya: Markets, State Power and Economic Liberty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to interrogate the constitutional foundations of Kenya's competition order, situating the Competition Act 2010 within the broader settlement struck by the Constitution of Kenya 2010 between market freedom and state power. It argues that Kenyan competition law cannot be read as ordinary economic regulation, because the 2010 Constitution constitutionalized the market itself, embedding consumer rights, public finance principles and leadership standards that together compose an implicit economic constitution the Competition Act only partially operationalises. Drawing on the Constitution's text, Kenyan and comparative scholarship, and the ordoliberal competition-democracy literature, the paper traces how the Competition Authority of Kenya's institutional design leaves it exposed to the very executive capture Chapter Six was written to prevent. It critiques prevailing accounts for treating competition policy as technocratic market management divorced from constitutional theory, and instead reconceives Kenyan competition law as a species of constitutional political economy, in which economic liberty functions as a precondition for, rather than a rival to, political liberty. The paper closes with a sequenced reform agenda for institutional independence and constitutional coherence.

title: The Sachet Shampoo Paradox: A Theoretical Analysis of Consumer Behavior, Marketing Strategy, and Sustainability Implications in Traditional Retail
affiliations: , , Universitas Negeri Jakarta and Universitas Negeri Jakarta

detail.title: The Sachet Shampoo Paradox: A Theoretical Analysis of Consumer Behavior, Marketing Strategy, and Sustainability Implications in Traditional Retail

declarations.declarationOfInterest: yes
declarations.ethicsApproval: yes
declarations.funderStatement: yes

detail.abstract: Sachet shampoo packaging represents a marketing format that allows fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) firms to broaden access to everyday personal-care products through lower nominal transaction expenditure, convenience, and distribution through traditional retail. At the same time, wider consumption of single-use sachets creates an environmental tension because flexible multilayer packaging is difficult to recover through conventional recycling systems. This conceptual paper examines why sachet shampoo remains commercially relevant and identifies the factors that can explain consumers' decisions to purchase it. The analysis synthesizes literature on the Bottom of the Pyramid (BOP), marketing strategy, consumer behavior, traditional retail, packaging, and circular economy. The analysis indicates that sachet purchase decisions are shaped by affordability, liquidity, convenience, trialability, habitual consumption, and product accessibility rather than by income alone. The paper proposes the concept of the "Sachet Paradox" to describe the tension between economic accessibility and environmental externalities. It argues that a realistic transition should combine packaging redesign, refill and reuse systems, producer responsibility, retailer participation, and supportive policy without removing the economic function that sachets currently provide.

title: Human-AI Hybrid Cognitive Capability as a Source of National Competitive Advantage Rethinking the U.S.-China AI Race beyond Frontier Model Capability

detail.title: Human-AI Hybrid Cognitive Capability as a Source of National Competitive Advantage Rethinking the U.S.-China AI Race beyond Frontier Model Capability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The emerging geopolitical debate over artificial intelligence is organized around a powerful but incomplete metric: frontier-model capability. The United States and China are increasingly evaluated according to which country can develop, control, and deploy the most capable artificial intelligence systems. This paper argues that model capability alone is an insufficient measure of long-run national advantage. As advanced AI capabilities diffuse across firms and economies, the strategically decisive variable may become human-AI hybrid cognitive capability: the capacity of people and artificial intelligence systems to interact recursively in ways that improve the effective capability of the combined system over time. The paper extends the Human-AI Cognitive Co-evolution (HACC) framework from the individual and organizational levels to national competition. It distinguishes HACC from Human-AI Cognitive Outsourcing (HACO), in which increasing reliance on AI raises near-term output while human cognitive capability stagnates or erodes. A continuous-time conceptual model treats human capability as endogenous rather than fixed and introduces cognitive coupling and institutional diffusion as determinants of national cognitive capability. The framework yields a central strategic proposition: national AI policy should optimize the trajectory of the human-AI cognitive system, not merely the trajectory of artificial intelligence. The paper develops implications for education, workforce strategy, research and development, organizational design, national security, and U.S.-China competition, and proposes an empirical research agenda for testing whether hybrid cognitive capability can become a durable source of national competitive advantage.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces PRISM—a Privacy‑Resilient Infrastructure for Strategic Monetization—asa multi‑layer analytical construct addressing the commercial governance vacuumcreatedbyprivacy regulation in U.S. digital advertising infrastructure. As privacy regulations systematically remove the data signals on which advertising markets depend, the industryhas predominantly responded with technical solutions that address signal availability but ignorethegovernance determining market outcomes. PRISM establishes five interconnected governancelayers: resource allocation under signal scarcity, probabilistic measurement and accountability, multi‑stakeholder access and data governance, human‑algorithm decision boundaries, andmarket stability safeguards. These layers form an interconnected governance chain that addresses coordination failures across digital advertising markets. The paper demonstrates that while technical innovations can partially mitigate post‑cookie disruption within digital advertisingecosystems, commercial governance infrastructure represents the binding constraint on maintaining U.S. economic competitiveness, small business inclusion, and market resilienceunder privacy constraints.

title: He Sachet Packaging Dilemma in Emerging Market Fmcg: Integrating Bottom of the Pyramid Marketing Theory, Consumer Behavior, And Ecological Implications
affiliations: Universitas Negeri Jakarta

detail.title: He Sachet Packaging Dilemma in Emerging Market Fmcg: Integrating Bottom of the Pyramid Marketing Theory, Consumer Behavior, And Ecological Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Yes
declarations.ethicsApproval: Yes
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The penetration of Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) products through sachet packaging in traditional retail channels has become an important phenomenon in emerging markets, particularly in countries where consumers face limited daily purchasing power and traditional retailers remain a dominant distribution channel. Sachet packaging enables FMCG manufacturers to offer branded household and personal care products in small, affordable quantities, allowing low-income consumers to access products that may otherwise require relatively high initial expenditures when purchased in larger packages. This phenomenon reflects an interaction between corporate marketing strategies, consumer financial constraints, traditional retail structures, and the increasing pressure for environmental sustainability. This conceptual paper aims to provide a multiperspective analysis of the sachet economy by examining the strategic rationale of FMCG manufacturers, the purchasing behavior of Bottom of the Pyramid (BoP) consumers, the role of traditional retail networks, and the environmental implications associated with single-use flexible packaging. The conceptual framework integrates the Bottom of the Pyramid (BoP) theory, price discrimination, Ansoff’s market penetration strategy, Transaction Cost Economics, Theory of Planned Behavior, and the Triple Bottom Line perspective. From the corporate perspective, sachet packaging represents a strategic mechanism for expanding market penetration, increasing sales volume, accelerating inventory turnover, optimizing retail space, and reducing the financial risk associated with introducing new product variants. The format also enables manufacturers to integrate traditional retailers more deeply into their distribution networks through wholesalers, distributors, and direct sales systems. From the consumer perspective, sachet purchasing is strongly associated with daily cash-flow constraints, affordability, convenience, portion control, geographical proximity, and reduced perceived financial risk. Consumers may prioritize the absolute amount of cash required for a purchase rather than the price per unit of volume, making sachets particularly relevant for households with irregular or limited income. Traditional retailers further reinforce this behavior by providing immediate access to essential products and encouraging repeated or impulse purchases through highly visible sachet displays. However, the economic and social benefits of sachet commercialization are accompanied by substantial environmental challenges. Multilayer flexible packaging is difficult to separate and recycle economically, contributing to the accumulation of low-value plastic waste in landfills, waterways, and surrounding communities. This condition creates a fundamental sustainability dilemma between maintaining affordable access to essential FMCG products for low-income consumers and achieving corporate and public environmental objectives. The analysis therefore highlights the importance of transitioning toward more sustainable packaging materials, including recyclable mono-material structures, while simultaneously developing refill systems, take-back mechanisms, reverse logistics, and partnerships with local waste-management and recycling ecosystems. The implementation of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is also considered essential for strengthening producer accountability throughout the post-consumption packaging lifecycle. Overall, this conceptual paper argues that the future of sachet-based FMCG strategies in emerging markets should not be evaluated solely in terms of sales growth and market penetration, but through an integrated perspective that balances profitability, economic inclusion, consumer accessibility, and environmental sustainability. The paper recommends greater collaboration among FMCG manufacturers, traditional retailers, governments, recycling organizations, informal waste workers, and consumers to develop an inclusive circular economy model capable of maintaining product affordability while reducing the environmental burden of single-use sachet packaging. Future research should further examine consumers’ willingness to pay for environmentally friendly sachets, the effectiveness of digital technologies in facilitating packaging take-back systems, and cross-country differences in the implementation of EPR policies within emerging markets.

title: The Capability Transfer: Cohort Reversal, Codified Expertise, and the Adaptability Tax of AI Transformation

detail.title: The Capability Transfer: Cohort Reversal, Codified Expertise, and the Adaptability Tax of AI Transformation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Future Positive, an independent consultancy based in Amsterdam that advises organisations on AI transformation and workforce capability. The subject matter of this paper falls within that commercial field, and the author has developed a companion costing model intended for use in that practice. No external person or organisation commissioned, funded, reviewed or influenced the design, analysis or conclusions of this study. The author declares no other financial or personal relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study. The work involves no human participants, no patient data and no personal data. It is a theoretical modelling exercise calibrated on published aggregate statistics and previously published experimental results, each of which is cited in the text.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author and supported by the author's own firm, Future Positive.

detail.abstract: Caosun and Aral (2026) show that a decision-maker who chooses AI usage intensity for a worker can rationally trade long-run skill for short-run output, and that misaligned incentives turn this steady-state loss into an augmentation trap. We extend their model from one worker to a firm with two cohorts and a task distribution ordered by tacitness, and add one state variable, the codified frontier: the share of the firm's tasks on which AI supplies a skill-neutral productivity floor. The extension rests on one assumption, that the tacit capability a tool supplies is produced by unassisted practice with stakes, and that the deployment which supplies it displaces the practice that produced it. We state the assumption at two altitudes. At the level of the market it is a claim about the source population of a shared model, and the evidence for it is the collapse of the public commons that fed the first models; at the level of the firm it applies only to the firm specific residual of the tacit set, which no vendor can codify and no vendor can regenerate. Four results follow. First, adoption compresses junior demand before senior demand, because the codified tasks were the junior's job; calibrated to the 2023-2025 productivity experiments, the model places the junior trough in 2027 in every calibration and reproduces the direction and rough size of the early-career employment gap in payroll data through mid-2026. Second, once adoption saturates the frontier keeps moving, largely through the vendor, and the cohort composition reverses: the junior share of required headcount rises from 58 to 73-79 percent by 2035 in the main calibrations, and the year in which senior headcount halves is governed by a closed-form condition on the vendor's codification rate, the firm's capture rate and the task renewal rate. Third, senior formation can occur only on tasks the tool does not cover, and that set shrinks with the frontier, so the career ladder inverts: careers must begin at the frontier or the pipeline stops. Fourth, the reversal is cheap in output and expensive in capability. The firm-level output loss on its own residual is close to zero within the horizon in every calibration, because the seniors it retains serve that residual first; what falls is the firm's capacity on uncovered work, by 67 to 91 percent, and its ability to rebuild its own frontier after a renewal shock, which no calibration recovers. We price the transfer from three sides using a receiving-end build-cost model and show that the saving is real, immediate and visible, that 93 percent of the capability transferred was financed by the worker, and that the loss is a distributional fact and not an efficiency claim.

title: The Construction of the Sachet Economy in Traditional Retail: A Theoretical Integration of FMCG Corporate Motivations, Grassroots Consumer Behavior, and the Ecological Sustainability Dilemma

detail.abstract: The "sachet economy" phenomenon in emerging markets illustrates the interplay between corporate marketing strategies, consumer economic constraints, and environmental sustainability challenges. This conceptual paper aims to analyze sachet packaging strategies from both producer and consumer perspectives and to formulate directions for developing more sustainable business models. The analysis draws upon the Bottom of the Pyramid (BOP) framework, the marketing mix, mental accounting, perceived risk, ethnomedicine, and self-medication behavior. The findings indicate that sachets facilitate market penetration through affordability, intensive distribution, trialability, and consumer spending efficiency and flexibility. However, this strategy also creates a paradox characterized by high profit margins for producers alongside the accumulation of hardto-recycle, multi-layered packaging waste. Sustaining the sachet economy requires innovations in biodegradable or paper-based materials, the development of circular retail systems, policy incentives, and collaboration among producers, the government, and communities. Ultimately, balancing economic growth, market inclusion, and environmental protection is key to transforming the sachet economy, particularly for low-income groups in these emerging markets.

title: The Nutritional and Welfare Effects of Threshold Sin Taxes: Evidence from the UK Sugar Tax
affiliations: Imperial College Business School, Imperial College Business School and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: The Nutritional and Welfare Effects of Threshold Sin Taxes: Evidence from the UK Sugar Tax

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: We study the UK sugar tax, which only applies to beverages with sugar content above a threshold and triggered widespread reformulation. We estimate a structural model of beverage demand and firms' price setting using household-level data from before and after the tax. We find that the tax reduced sugar consumption from beverages by 47%. Monetized health gains (from externalities and internalities) outweigh the consumer welfare loss, leading to an increase in total welfare. Reformulation accounts for 29% of the sugar reduction at almost no cost to consumers, although it halves tax revenue. Matching the UK's sugar reduction with a volumetric tax requires nearly double its rate and imposes a much greater consumer welfare loss. Broadening the tax base to diet beverages leads to less sugar reduction and a higher consumer welfare loss. Both alternatives raise more tax revenue, but neither matches the threshold tax's total welfare gain.

title: Pro-Worker AI in Health: Who Benefits When Machines Enter the Largest Workforce in America?

detail.abstract: The US health sector accounts for 18.0% of gross domestic product and roughly one in eight jobs, yet the labor market consequences of the artificial intelligence (AI) products now being deployed across it have not been systematically inventoried. This paper applies the Acemoglu, Autor, and Johnson (2026) five-category pro-worker framework to a structured environmental scan of 132 commercially deployed or FDA-authorized AI-enabled health technologies identified in March 2026 across five domains: clinical care, provider administration, payer administration, life sciences, and public health. Each technology was classified under a pre-specified protocol by the anticipated direction of its effect on labor productivity, the value of human expertise, and labor's share of income. Within this scan, 41.7% of technologies were classified as automating existing tasks, 29.5% as creating new tasks, 16.7% as expertise-leveling, 10.6% as labor-augmenting, and 1.5% as capital-augmenting. The classifications diverge sharply by domain. Of 40 provider- and payer-administration technologies, 39 (97.5%) were classified as automation. Of 92 technologies in clinical care, life sciences, and public health, 61 (66.3%) were classified as new task-creating or expertise-leveling. These are classifications of anticipated consequences, not measurements of employment, wages, or income shares. I offer an economic interpretation of the pattern as a set of testable hypotheses: administrative tasks are rule-bound and algorithmically reducible, whereas clinical and scientific judgment sustains demand for human expertise, and the distribution of any productivity gains depends on payment incentives, provider and employer market power, and workforce regulation. I describe a friction-cost paradox, in which the workers most exposed to automation perform work that exists largely because of insurance and billing complexity, and I propose five policy levers with responsible actors and evaluation criteria. The scan is limited to commercially oriented products and cannot support conclusions about net employment effects or about the level of investment in public health AI.

title: Experiential Consumption in Virtual Reality Environments: Consumer Perceptions and Choices of Virtual Cinemas Versus Physical and Digital Alternatives
affiliations: University of Münster, University of Münster and University of Muenster

detail.title: Experiential Consumption in Virtual Reality Environments: Consumer Perceptions and Choices of Virtual Cinemas Versus Physical and Digital Alternatives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Both studies reported in this paper received ethical approval from the university’s ethics committee
declarations.funderStatement: University of Münster.

detail.abstract: Experiential consumption is a fundamental part of consumers' lives, encompassing hedonic, affective, and symbolic experiences. Digitalization has expanded consumers' access to such experiences, but at the expense of qualities that make them compelling. Conventional 2D digital interfaces (e.g., streaming movies at home) provide decentralized, on-demand access while offering less of the sensory and social stimulation characteristic of physical environments (e.g., watching movies in cinemas). This research investigates whether virtual-reality (VR) environments can overcome this trade-off by providing sensory and social stimulation sufficient to shift consumption choices. Across a framed field experiment (N = 320) and an incentivealigned discrete-choice experiment (N = 639), using state-of-the-art VR hardware in a movie watching context, the authors show that experiences in VR environments provide greater sensory and social stimulation than 2D digital experiences while approaching physical experiences in both respects. These perceptions are consequential: a substantial share of consumers choose VR environments when available, with revenue potential greatest for sensory-rich content and when the people with whom consumers would otherwise share the experience are spatially distant. Together, these findings carry clear implications for experience providers and position VR environments as a viable alternative among consumption channels, particularly under conditions that favor their experiential advantages.

title: Measuring Incremental Store Visits and Allocating Budgets for Location-based Digital Out-of-Home Media under Location Data Compliance Constraints
affiliations: City Zongheng (Shanghai) Culture Media Co., Ltd., , Alibaba Group, affiliation not provided to SSRN and California State University, Los Angeles

detail.title: Measuring Incremental Store Visits and Allocating Budgets for Location-based Digital Out-of-Home Media under Location Data Compliance Constraints

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Location-based digital out-of-home (DOOH) media is becoming the fastest-growing offline advertising channel. Global OOH spending is projected to reach $54.2 billion in 2025, including $25.5 billion in digital spending, rising to $28.0 billion in 2026; North American OOH revenue has reached $9.46 billion, with digital screens contributing 36.3%. However, in-store attribution conflicts with privacy regulation: 20 U.S. states have enacted comprehensive privacy laws, most treating precise geolocation as sensitive data, while some prohibit location-data sales within a 1,750-ft (≈533-m) radius, creating an approximately 26-fold gap relative to the 20-m precision required for geofence attribution. We develop an identifier-free region-level spatiotemporal framework that learns counterfactuals from 12-week pre-placement foot-traffic sequences, represents spatial dependence through a sparse neighborhood graph, and combines hierarchical Bayesian estimation with a distance-decay kernel. Privacy computation runs at the edge: 15-min events are aggregated into 1-h windows, windows with fewer than 20 independent events are suppressed, each device contributes once per window, and differential-privacy noise is added; raw coordinates, continuous trajectories, and stable identifiers are not centrally stored. Posterior increments are converted into revenue weights, while placement selection is solved as a budget-constrained submodular coverage problem using a sparse coverage index, max-heap lazy greedy search, and partial enumeration of three candidate placements, retaining the 1-1/e approximation guarantee. Calibration used 23 cities, 133 authorized dealers, 23,901 placement weeks, 3.05 million geofences, and 68 million geocoded POIs with positioning error radii ≤20 m, yielding observed in-store increments of 10.7% (95% CI: 7.9%-13.5%) and 9.8% (6.6%-13.0%). After degrading resolution to 533 m and setting ε=1.0, estimation deviation was 1.8 percentage points, 95% interval coverage was 93.6%, and the minimum detectable increment at 80% power was 4.6%. Spillovers were significantly positive and decayed monotonically within 1.2 km; ignoring them would underestimate increment by about 2.1 percentage points. At the same budget, effective reach increased by 23.4%, or media cost fell by 18.6% at the same increment, demonstrating a deployable attribution-and-allocation pipeline under coarse geolocation constraints.

title: The Diffusion Constraint

detail.title: The Diffusion Constraint

He has professional and potential commercial interests in their development and application. The proposed treatment has not undergone independent organizational validation.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No formal ethics approval was obtained. This paper develops a conceptual treatment using published research, documented historical cases, computer simulations, and a retrospective register of defects recorded during the author’s own work with AI assistants. No participants were recruited for this study. The organizational trials and assessments described in the paper are proposals for future research, not completed studies.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded by the author. No external grants or sponsorship were received.

detail.abstract: AI can produce more work than an organization can reliably check. This paper argues that, where deployment relies on human judgment, verification can constrain expansion even after data and process improvements. It asks when to invest in checking, when to preserve the skills checking requires, and when evidence supports more delegation. Six practical principles connect capability, data, process, authority, verification, and human capacity to those decisions. The proposed contribution is to account for production, checking, and skill maintenance together under a shared resource budget. Under stated assumptions, delegation saves time today while increasing the practice needed to sustain tomorrow's judgment. Fewer detected mistakes can also conceal weaker checking. The author's TARS protocol gives AI assistants written instructions to challenge unsupported claims and log problems. Its register contains 138 caught defects, including 23 instances of invented or overstated support; it does not measure undetected errors or verification time. Prospectively specified computer simulations establish conditional decision differences and failure cases, not organizational treatment effects. The treatment separates required checking hours from actual unverified use and supports expansion only when quality, resources, retained responsibilities, and authority permit it. An illustrative 18-24 month schedule explains how organizations could test the approach. The schedule is a proposal, not a forecast, and the combined treatment remains subject to independent evaluation.

title: THE OMISSION OF THE FOREIGN LOAN INTEREST TAX EXEMPTION: AN ANALYSIS OF CROSS-BORDER FINANCING UNDER NIGERIA'S NEW TAX REGIME

detail.title: THE OMISSION OF THE FOREIGN LOAN INTEREST TAX EXEMPTION: AN ANALYSIS OF CROSS-BORDER FINANCING UNDER NIGERIA'S NEW TAX REGIME

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interesgt
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
Foreign financing has long been a critical source of capital for businesses and major projects in Nigeria. To buttress this trend, Nigeria’s external debt stood at approximately US$46.98 billion as at 30 June 2025,2 reflecting the significant role foreign capital continues to play in getting some of Nigeria’s most critical undertakings off the ground, or keeping it a going concern.

The tax treatment of interest on foreign financing is commercially significant. Interest is the lender’s return on capital. Where the lender is a non-resident for tax purposes in Nigeria, however, withholding tax (“WHT”) on that interest can affect the economics of the transaction more directly. A Nigerian lender may generally utilise WHT as a credit against its tax liability. A non-resident lender without a taxable presence in Nigeria may have no corresponding avenue to utilise the tax, so that the WHT may reduce the lender’s net return or, where the facility contains a tax gross-up, increase the borrower’s cost.

The Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 (the “NTA” or the “Act”) does not retain the foreign loan interest exemption previously available under the repealed Companies Income Tax Act (“CITA”). Interest paid to non-resident lenders is therefore generally subject to WHT at the applicable rate, subject to any relief under an effective tax treaty. The practical question is how cross-border loans to Nigerian borrowers should now be priced and structured.

This article considers the foreign loan interest exemption that previously applied, the effect of its omission under the NTA, the extent to which Nigeria’s tax treaty network can mitigate the resulting WHT exposure, and the financing and structuring options available to Nigerian borrowers and their foreign lenders.

title: THE GIG ECONOMY AND THE FUTURE OF LABOUR PROTECTION IN NIGERIA

detail.title: THE GIG ECONOMY AND THE FUTURE OF LABOUR PROTECTION IN NIGERIA

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known conflicts of interest, whether personal, financial, professional, or otherwise that could have influenced or reasonably be perceived to have influenced the research and presented in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no external funding or specific grant from any funding agency for this research. The research was conducted using the author's personal resources.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital labour platforms has fundamentally reshaped the organisation of work, blurring the once-clear boundaries between traditional employment and independent contracting. In Nigeria, ride-hailing services, food delivery platforms and online freelance marketplaces have created new opportunities for income generation while simultaneously exposing workers to precarious contractual arrangements that often fall outside the protective scope of existing labour legislation. This transformation has raised important questions about the continuing adequacy of a legal framework largely conceived for conventional employment relationships. Against this backdrop, this chapter considers how the emergence of the gig economy challenges established notions of contract employment and calls for a reassessment of labour protection in the digital age. Through a critical examination of Nigeria's labour law regime, informed by comparative developments in selected jurisdictions and international labour standards, it argues that the binary classification of workers as either employees or independent contractors no longer reflects the realities of platform-based work. The chapter contends that a more responsive legal framework, grounded in the principles of fairness, decent work and social protection, is essential to balancing technological innovation with the protection of vulnerable workers in Nigeria's evolving digital economy.

title: The agent acts. The system records. The damage happens. Why agentic AI needs a new operating model, and the ten-layer playbook that provides it
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The agent acts. The system records. The damage happens. Why agentic AI needs a new operating model, and the ten-layer playbook that provides it

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors of this paper are the founders of a firm that built and tested the framework described in it. The Verified Execution Layer, the AI Control Directive Playbook, and the human implementation layer are all offerings of the authors' firm. The authors have a financial interest in the adoption of the framework. The paper discloses this conflict in Section 8 and describes how the authors handle it: through joint discovery with clients, open test methodology, client-led red-teaming, and an independent validation path. The authors have engaged an independent research lab to replicate their results and will publish the findings whether they support the claims or not. The paper is published so that organizations can build the framework themselves if they choose. The authors have stated explicitly that they would rather organizations deploy something that works than deploy nothing because they did not trust the vendor.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research does not involve human subjects, patients, or clinical trials. The anonymized case study in Section 4.4 was provided by a client on the condition of anonymity. No personally identifiable information is included in the paper. Formal ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was self-funded by the authors' firm as part of its ongoing research and client engagements in behavioural intelligence and AI governance.

detail.abstract:
Agentic AI is being deployed faster than it can be governed. Most organizations log what agents do and review it after the fact. We think that is backwards. The Verified Execution Layer checks actions before they run. Ten layers, three rings: Prevent, Detect and Self-Correct, and Root of Trust. The human sits at the quarantine boundary, not in the log file.

The failure cases are already documented. In July 2026, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents escaped their sandboxes and breached Hugging Face's production environment. Anthropic disclosed four incidents where Claude models breached real systems while believing they were inside sandboxes. More than 10 percent of Anthropic's RL environments were flagged for reward hacking. These are not edge cases. They are what happens when autonomous agents with real authority run inside observe-and-log tooling.

The law has caught up. EU AI Act Article 14 enforcement began August 2, 2026. Fines reach 35 million euros or 7 percent of global turnover. The U.S. Stop Rogue AI Act rejects self-attestation and requires trust verification that is "independent and cryptographically verifiable at both the network and application layers."

The technical layer is half the answer. The other half is human: workflow redesign, decision-rights mapping, and judgment training for the people who resolve quarantines. Technology without organizational redesign produces marginal improvement. The VEL plus a redesigned human layer produces transformation.

This paper is for the CISO who signs off on the deployment, the CTO who owns the infrastructure, the Head of AI Governance who maps this to Article 14, and the board risk committee that asks why nobody saw it coming. It is also for the engineers who will read it and look for the catch. Good. We want that.

detail.abstract: This abstract examines changing paradigms in global supply chain research by synthesising emerging themes that respond to heightened geopolitical tensions, shifting trade policy landscapes, and an era of frequent global disruptions. Contemporary scholarship is moving beyond traditional efficiency‑and‑cost frameworks toward resilience, strategic adaptability, and regulatory responsiveness. Key challenges identified include the fragmentation of global trade networks due to geopolitical rivalries, protectionist measures, and the recalibration of regional supply chains; rising compliance burdens from divergent national regulations; and the systemic shocks posed by pandemics, climate events and cyber threats. Opportunities arise from reconfigured sourcing strategies, digitalisation and data analytics, greater emphasis on sustainability and circularity, and proactive compliance-as-competitive-advantage approaches. Researchers adopted a structured approach, gathering and analysing qualitative data from a wealth of online literature sources and expert opinions. They meticulously selected 34 peer-reviewed articles spanning from 2004 to 2024, each discussing the Influence of Changing Paradigms in Global Supply Chain Research. The data revealed the limitations of the growth of uncertainty to Changing Paradigms in Global Supply Chain Research. The systematic approach ultimately provided valuable insights into the Influence of Changing Paradigms in Global Supply Chain Research. The abstract argues for a normative research agenda that balances commercial objectives with ethical, environmental and social goals, emphasising transparency, stakeholder inclusivity and supply‑chain traceability. Ultimately, the paper calls for scholarly engagement that informs adaptive policymaking and managerial practice: designing regulatory frameworks that manage systemic risk without stifling trade, and crafting supply‑chain strategies that are robust, compliant and socially responsible in a geopolitically contested and environmentally constrained world.

detail.abstract: The Cuban Revolution marked the death of an old regime and the birth of not just a new government, but also a new generation of Cubans. Using crude birth rates and the synthetic control method, we provide the first causal estimate of the Revolution's effect on fertility and confirm that it produced a post-revolutionary baby boom. Between 1959 and 1965, the Revolution increased Cuba's crude birth rate by an average of 6.69 births per 1,000 people. However, the boom coincided with a sharp increase in infant mortality. Adjusting births for infant mortality reduces the estimated demographic effect by 17.9%. We estimate that the Revolution produced 346,107 additional births and 284,488 additional surviving infants. The unusual simultaneous increase in fertility and infant mortality departs from the conventional demographic transition pattern and is consistent with economic models in which households increase births when child-survival probabilities deteriorate.

detail.abstract: This study examines the influence of Blue Ocean Strategy and Intellectual Capital on Business Performance through the mediating roles of Open Innovation and Competitive Advantage in tourism destinations in Minahasa Regency, North Sulawesi, Indonesia. A quantitative explanatory approach was employed using Structural Equation Modeling-Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) with SmartPLS 4.0. The study involved 250 respondents from 47 tourism attractions selected through purposive sampling. The findings reveal that Blue Ocean Strategy has a positive and significant effect on Business Performance, Open Innovation, and Competitive Advantage. Intellectual Capital significantly influences Open Innovation and Competitive Advantage but does not directly affect Business Performance. Furthermore, Competitive Advantage has a positive and significant effect on Business Performance, whereas Open Innovation does not significantly affect Business Performance. The mediation analysis indicates that Competitive Advantage significantly mediates the relationships between Blue Ocean Strategy, Intellectual Capital, and Business Performance, while Open Innovation does not demonstrate a significant mediating role. This study contributes to the tourism management literature by developing an integrated model linking strategic innovation, intellectual resources, and business performance in emerging tourism destinations. The findings also provide managerial implications for tourism destination managers and policymakers in strengthening tourism competitiveness and sustainable business performance.

detail.abstract: Injunctions, and patent enforcement more broadly, may, in some circumstances, impose disproportionate burdens on a range of businesses. Indeed, patent courts, especially in continental European countries such as Germany, effectively treat injunctions as the near-automatic consequence of infringement, despite proportionality-based guarantees in the Enforcement Directive, the UPC Agreement and national statutes. This article argues that patent enforcement, and injunctions in particular, must be tested against Article 16 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (CFR), which protects the freedom to conduct a business (including for alleged infringers), through the proportionality and fair balance methodology of Article 52(1) CFR. This provision creates a unified constitutional framework that integrates the property guarantees in Article 17(2) CFR (as well as Article 1 of Protocol 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights) with business freedom under Article 16.

detail.abstract: The university years constitute a critical window in which an individual's cognitive paradigm is formed. Yet modern disciplinary education is built upon the classical paradigm of simple systems, linear science, equilibrium assumptions and reductionism, which simplifies the real world substantially for the sake of pedagogical convenience. As a consequence, graduates commonly suffer cognitive disconnection, theory failure and distorted judgment, and their capacity for deep thinking is structurally constrained. Grounded in complexity science, this paper proposes the Fulun (Unified Complexity Theory) framework, which integrates five pillars: dissipative structure theory, synergetics, nonlinear and chaotic dynamics, complex networks and emergence, and phase-transition and attractor theory. Using this framework, we diagnose five idealized presuppositions shared by all disciplines-linear causality, static equilibrium, reductionism, the closed-system assumption and complete predictability-and examine their discipline-specific manifestations and cognitive bottlenecks across five major clusters: economics and management, science and engineering, humanities and social sciences, arts, and law. We argue that complexity science enhances undergraduates' capacity for deep thinking through three mechanisms: paradigm correction (recognizing textbooks as simplified versions of reality), instrumental reconstruction (acquiring transferable system-dynamics tools) and cognitive unification (applying one underlying logic across heterogeneous complex ecologies such as capital markets, technological industries and cultural systems). We conclude that complexity science does not replace disciplinary knowledge but systematically repairs the congenital paradigm deficits of disciplinary education, and that upgrading one's cognitive paradigm during the university years carries the lowest lifetime cost and yields returns that compound over the whole of life.

detail.abstract: Every year, tens of millions of Ganesh and Durga idols are immersed in India's rivers, lakes, and coastal waters at the close of Ganeshotsav and Durga Puja. A large share of these idols are made from Plaster of Paris (PoP), a material chosen for its low cost, light weight, and fast drying timeand one that is also chemically stubborn, almost insoluble in water, and typically finished with paints that carry lead, mercury, cadmium, and hexavalent chromium. The result is a predictable, recurring pollution event: a benthic sludge blanket that suffocates riverbed and lakebed life, and a pulse of heavy metals into water that people bathe in, that livestock drink from, and that feeds farmland downstream. Existing responsesbanning PoP outright, promoting traditional clay (Shaadu Mati), or chemically dissolving idols after the fact with reagents like ammonium bicarbonateeach run into a real bottleneck at the scale India's festivals operate at, whether that bottleneck is structural (clay is too dense and slow-drying for the towering public Sarvajanik idols), economic (chemical post-treatment costs more than the idol itself), or logistical (thermal recalcination needs industrial kilns most municipalities do not have).

detail.abstract: Several U.S. states have recently revised the structure of their sports wagering taxes, and others have restricted the wager types that legal sportsbooks may offer. Both policies have been argued to push consumers toward unregulated offshore operators, but this claim has rarely been tested. This study examined consumer responses to each using a within-subjects scenario experiment with 1,013 active online sports bettors across thirty-two states with legal online wagering. Respondents evaluated four escalating per-bet fees, two reductions in offered odds, and three withdrawals of a wager type, and reported the action they would most likely take in each case. Generalized estimating equations showed that per-bet taxes strongly reduce legal-market participation, with the share continuing to wager unchanged falling from 46.1% to 17.4% and the share abandoning the wager rising from 5.6% to 20.5%. The associated increase in offshore substitution was statistically significant but small, and equivalence testing bounded it below five percentage points. Withdrawal of a wager type produced a larger offshore response than any fee tested, regardless of which product was withdrawn, and extended to bettors with no prior offshore experience. The findings suggest that a per-wager fee should be modeled as a demandreducing instrument whose burden falls on low-stake wagers and that product restrictions carry significant offshore displacement.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that contemporary legal positivism suffers from a systemic epistemological and deontic deficit: it can neither secure material justice nor safeguard the subject's ontological agency against state power. Tracing a critical genealogy from classical voluntarism (Hobbes, Austin) through Hans Kelsen's formalist normativism and the procedural aporias of Hart and Fuller, we demonstrate how late modernity collapsed the legal order into a strictly closed syntactic calculus (⊢). By systematically excising material semantics and the model-theoretic satisfaction of real-world states (|=), formalism has devolved into a bureaucratic apparatus of procedural impunity, replacing factual truth with the administrative dossier. To counter the sovereign's structural mutation into the desk-bound bureaucrat, we establish a formal natural law framework grounded in the ontology of substantive harm and the real agent's singularity (haecceitas). Finally, we posit AI-assisted logical-forensic auditing as a peremptory methodological standard for constitutional and international courts (Arts. 8 and 25 ACHR). This paradigm transforms human rights litigation from rhetorical advocacy into a formal proof of invalidity, exposing the logical contradictions and inherent nullity of procedural fraud.

detail.abstract: Almost everything known about equity rounds in young firms comes from the records of professional investors, so the evidence is selected on the presence of an intermediary. We read rounds instead from the share-premium reserve, a compulsory, disclosed and restricted line of the Italian statutory balance sheet, for 3,225 certified innovative SMEs over 2016-2025: 2,991 priced capital increases on 1,330 firms. Firms about to raise grew twice as fast in the preceding year and held identical cash, yet six in ten closed it at a loss; profitability falls and intangible assets rise only after the round. Seven panel estimators place the association across firms and not within them; a taxonomy estimated blind to the event finds the mechanism in all five financial configurations, with incidence differing eightfold; six flexible learners fail to improve on the linear specification. Selection operates on growth, not on profitability, a distinction intermediated samples cannot see.

detail.abstract:
Purchase requisition creation is a deceptively complex enterprise process: requesters often know what they need but not the procurement category, catalog item, preferred supplier, accounting distribution, budget rule, or approval path required to fulfill that need. This can result in incomplete requisitions, clarification cycles, buyer rework, and avoidable processing delays. This paper presents a production-oriented functional and technical reference architecture for applying artificial intelligence (AI) to purchase requisition generation while preserving procurement policy, budget controls, master-data integrity, approval authority, security, and ERP transaction integrity.

The proposed architecture separates probabilistic AI capabilities from transaction authority. AI interprets user intent, extracts and classifies relevant entities, retrieves grounded enterprise context through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and produces a structured requisition draft. Deterministic enterprise services then validate policy, budget, master data, compliance, and other transaction controls. Authorized users retain approval authority, while the ERP system remains the authoritative system of record. The paper defines the architecture, functional workflow, integration and API patterns, RAG knowledge design, human-in-the-loop controls, security and responsible-AI considerations, testing and observability practices, KPI and ROI framework, and phased implementation roadmap. Representative use cases include IT hardware, facilities, professional services, capital projects, and emergency purchasing.

detail.title: The Negotiating Brain: Continuous Negotiation Fields, Awareness Asymmetry, and the Resolution-Execution Gap in Human Choice

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Continuous Negotiation Field (CNF) model, which links human cognitive regulation to the social shaping of the structure within which people choose. The model distinguishes two levels of the field: an interpersonal level, at which adaptive agents alter one another's decision environments, and an intrapersonal level, at which competing motivational states within one person settle on a future action. The starting hypothesis is narrower than the claim that the brain literally "negotiates": the cognitive system continuously builds a model of its environment and selects actions, while a substantial part of the social environment is produced by other agents who can change information, agendas, options, constraints, sequencing, payoffs, and implementation mechanisms. The paper introduces two constructs. Negotiation Awareness Asymmetry (NAA) is the difference between agents in which field parameters each of them models as controllable. The Resolution-Execution Gap (REG) is the share of resolved negotiation fields that do not reach execution. In real negotiations, resolution is fixed by a commitment mechanism-a signature, a contract, a sanction; in the cognitive system, a field can be fully "resolved" in mental simulation without producing either commitment or action. The model connects these links into a chain: field awareness → field shaping → internal resolution → commitment → execution. The model distinguishes objective, accessible, and perceived sets of outcomes, describes the field with thirteen parameters, and offers a map of sixteen domains-from shopping to diplomacy and self-control-with explicit limits on transferring conclusions across domains. The approach does not replace active inference, choice architecture, framing, agenda-setting, heresthetics, negotiation theory, or models of asymmetric unawareness; its contribution is to connect them in a model of a recursively modifiable decision field. The paper is conceptual and formulates testable propositions.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the relationship between Bitcoin returns, the decentralized finance (DeFi) sector, and traditional stock market returns, focusing on the Iraq Stock Exchange (ISX) from January 4, 2020, to March 4, 2026. Growing institutional adoption has strengthened the interconnectedness of digital assets with traditional markets, while the International Monetary Fund (IMF, 2021) warns that this integration may expose frontier economies to new financial risks (Gross & Senner, 2026). Using the autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) methodology, the results reveal a statistically significant negative short-run impact of Bitcoin returns on ISX returns, with no significant long-run impact for either Bitcoin or DeFi. This suggests cryptocurrencies have acted as alternative assets and liquidity competitors rather than safe havens or hedging tools in the traditional sense, and that Bitcoin may serve as an indicator of global risk trends given its reach into relatively isolated frontier markets like Iraq. In contrast, the lack of DeFi impact is attributed to the novelty of these assets, insufficient investor awareness, limited digital infrastructure, and scarce access to centralized trading platforms in frontier markets.

title: From Impulse to Empire: How Survival- and Reproduction-Linked Drives Become Organizational Culture

detail.title: From Impulse to Empire: How Survival- and Reproduction-Linked Drives Become Organizational Culture

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a theoretical account of how two distinct but powerful motivational systems—anger and sexual motivation—can extend beyond individual expression and become embedded in organizational culture. Anger can contribute to self-protection, threat response, resource defense, and bargaining, whereas sexual motivation is evolutionarily related to mating and reproduction. Neither system is inherently pathological. Under appropriate conditions, both can serve adaptive functions. Problems arise when strong motivation is directed toward inappropriate targets, insufficiently inhibited, and further insulated from corrective feedback or sanction by power.

The paper compares two markedly different settings: a workplace in which anger, intimidation, and public reprimand became recurrent features of local organizational life, and the long-term sexual abuse associated with the former Johnny & Associates organization and the structures surrounding it. The comparison does not equate the legal, ethical, or human consequences of these cases. Instead, it examines whether different forms of recurrent deviance can become culturally stabilized through similar organizational processes.

The analysis proposes that when deviant behavior is protected by power, repeatedly left unsanctioned, legitimized or normalized, and increasingly insulated from corrective voice, organizational members may adapt through three pathways: Mimicry, Silence, and Exit. Mimicry reproduces dominant behavior, Silence suppresses corrective information, and Exit selectively removes members who reject the prevailing environment. Although these responses differ psychologically, together they can produce cultural homogenization.

The paper integrates these processes into an Impulse-to-Empire Model. Empire Formation is defined as the process by which recurrent deviance by a dominant actor becomes an environmental condition for others, effective corrective voice deteriorates, and members increasingly adapt by changing their own behavior rather than changing the dominant actor or the organization. Such an “empire” does not require consensus or loyalty. It can persist when members privately disagree but can only imitate, remain silent, or leave. The model therefore explains how motivational systems that may be adaptive at the evolutionary level can, under conditions of power, disinhibition, and failed correction, be transformed into maladaptive organizational cultures.

detail.abstract: The United Arab Emirates has developed one of the world's most rigorously enforced workforce nationalization regimes. Through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation (MOHRE), the National Programme for Employment (NAFIS), and sector-specific initiatives such as the Central Bank's Ethraa programme, the UAE has combined escalating financial penalties, artificial intelligence-driven compliance monitoring, and structured wage-support mechanisms to substantially increase Emirati participation in the private-sector workforce. NAFIS alone has placed more than 176,000 Emiratis since its 2021 launch, exceeding its original target well ahead of schedule. This paper argues that this enforcement apparatus, while demonstrably effective at increasing headcount compliance, does not yet incorporate a standardized mechanism for measuring the employability readiness of the individuals being placed. Drawing on the employability measurement literature and on workforce nationalization scholarship specific to the Gulf Cooperation Council, this paper reviews the conceptual gap between quota-based enforcement and capability-based readiness, and proposes a three-tier National Emirati Readiness Framework institutional, sectoral, and policy layersbuilding on the author's previously piloted Job Readiness Index (JRI), an eight-parameter, mentor-led employability diagnostic developed and tested in Indian higher education. The paper further proposes a three-phase implementation roadmappilot, standardization, and integration designed to address the central practical obstacle to any national readiness metric: ensuring inter-institutional score reliability. This is a conceptual and policy-oriented contribution; no empirical data collection has yet been conducted within the UAE context, and the proposed framework awaits institutional piloting.

detail.abstract: This paper's contribution is a theoretical framework, not a validated measurement instrument: it proposes that participatory recalibration-recurrent, documented cycles of collective examination and adjustment-rather than technical maturity alone, is what distinguishes digital-government programmes that sustain correction from those that entrench and stall (Archer, 1995, 2003; Williamson, 1985; Arthur, 1994; Beinhocker, 2006). The framework is developed across, and consolidates, five prior working papers (Oldman, 2026a, 2026b, 2026c, 2026d, 2026e), each now reviewed and re-hedged in light of the fuller research programme reported here. Three deliverables follow directly from the theory: (1) an operational measurement architecture of three candidate indices-Digital Systems Maturity (DSMI), Action Research Maturity (ARMi), and Chaos Resilience (CRI)-specified as a research agenda rather than a certified instrument; (2) two illustrative empirical patterns drawn from a frozen, versioned case-discovery repository of 111 national digitalgovernment programmes across 32 countries, namely a two-case contrast (Denmark and Saudi Arabia score within 0.005 of each other on DSMI-0.939 and 0.944-yet diverge sharply on ARMi-0.803 versus 0.572) and a three-cohort comparison in which mean ARMi is flat across low-, mid-, and high-DSMI groups (0.645, 0.637, 0.662); and (3) two design-stage applications that extend the same logic upstream of programme execution and into sovereign fiscal-risk diagnostics. The novelty of this contribution is conceptual and agenda-setting: it names a mechanism the existing digitalgovernment literature has not isolated, translates it into a specific and falsifiable prediction, and shows-through a bounded, non-random illustration-that the prediction is not obviously false. It is not a claim that DSMI, ARMi, or CRI are validated measures, that the 111-case repository has been independently verified at corpus scale, or that the illustrative contrast constitutes a statistical test. Digital-government platforms are generational infrastructure, not disposable software: national systems documented as still operational after 30 to 56 years (U.S. GAO, 2016) illustrate that a single governance-architecture choice can constrain citizen-facing service quality and administrative productivity for decades, with only narrow subsequent opportunity for correction-which is the paper's motivation for publishing the theory and an explicit testing agenda now, ahead of a completed validation study. Global government information-technology spending, estimated at roughly USD 800 billion in 2026 and rising, 1 sets the scale of what is at stake in getting this governance question right. Section 6 specifies precisely what a confirmatory test of the central hypothesis would require, including a proposed pilot open to independent governance scholars (Section 6.4, Supplement A), and Section 7 sets out the research agenda that follows.

detail.abstract: This article examines why armed group recruitment among Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar and Bhasan Char camps intensified between 2023 and 2026, testing whether population growth or structural governance conditions better explain the pattern. Using process tracing on investigations by the International Crisis Group (2023; 2024; 2025), Fortify Rights (2025), Reuters (Ghoshal and McPherson 2024), and Minar's (2021) empirical test of the hoststate security threat claim, the article finds recruitment is best explained by armed factions' capture of camp governance rather than demographic growth. The article distinguishes domestic camp violence from cross-border mobilization into Myanmar's civil war, shaped substantially by Bangladeshi security-agency involvement.

detail.abstract:
The National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) links individual redress, scientific adjudication, liability channeling, vaccine access, provider participation, public finance, innovation, and institutional legitimacy. Yet reform is frequently assessed through isolated objectives. A proposal that improves compensation, speed, or access may transfer costs and risks to adjudicatory institutions, public payors, providers, insurers, manufacturers, procurement systems, or patients. This article develops the Vaccine Compensation Stability and Access Framework as a structured ex ante method for evaluating such trade-offs before implementation.

The theoretical framework integrates corrective justice, social-risk allocation, transaction-cost economics, innovation-systems theory, and institutional trust. The conceptual framework treats VICP as public justice infrastructure organised through three pillars: compensation justice and procedural performance; public-health and market stability; and public institutional sustainability. Seven operational domains are retained because each has a distinct mechanism, evidentiary basis, affected institutions, and possible consequence. The framework is operationalised through the VICP Reform Stress Test, an institutional cost-transfer map, a separate assess ability determination, and four substantive policy classifications. A companion validation protocol was prospectively registered at OSF before data collection. A separate technical implementation paper specifies the available clickable VICP Reform Impact and Stability Evaluator. detail.abstract:
Civilian safety technologies increasingly rely on continuous location collection, cloud telemetry, networked cameras, centralized search, and behavioral analytics. These capabilities can support legitimate protective purposes. The unresolved design question is whether obtaining that value should require making ordinary human activity persistently observable to external systems. Persistent observability is not merely a privacy inconvenience: it creates a durable information asset that can reveal routines, relationships, sensitive locations, vulnerabilities, and deviations from ordinary behavior while expanding the attack surface for misuse, compromise, legal compulsion, secondary use, and future inference.
LAKANA SOS - the LAKANA Sovereign Operating System for civilian safety - proposes a different design objective. Critical safety state should remain local where technically possible; raw observations should be reduced toward bounded safety-relevant state rather than automatically becoming persistent remote telemetry; uncertainty should constrain authority rather than justify broader inference; evidence should be constructed around qualified safety events; and disclosure should be purpose-bound, consent-aware, time-limited, auditable, and revocable where the context permits. The objective is not to eliminate sensing, evidence, communication, or institutional response. It is to reduce the amount, persistence, centralization, queryability, and secondary-use potential of information required to provide those functions.
The paper examines family-location systems, connected-vehicle telemetry, location brokerage, home-security access, tracking misuse, automated license plate reader networks, and behavioral profiling as structural case studies rather than indictments of particular companies. Oklahoma provides a live governance contrast: Norman declined municipal Flock adoption despite police interest in its investigative and safety value, while Oklahoma City retained a large deployment with additional restrictions. The point is not to declare either city or vendor correct; it is to show that communities still lack a settled architecture for retaining useful safety capability while limiting persistent observability.
The companion LAKANA SOS v71 technical preprint reports architecture-level Monte Carlo evidence under declared degraded and adversarial assumptions. Those results do not establish field effectiveness, certification, legal compliance, or universal superiority. This white paper advances a narrower, falsifiable proposition: civilian safety architectures should be evaluated simultaneously for protective capability and surveillance burden, and where comparable declared protective requirements can be met with materially less persistent behavioral exposure, the lower-burden architecture should generally be preferred.

detail.abstract: Academic fraud has become a recurring phenomenon in global research, yet existing governance mechanisms remain constrained by qualitative determination, subjectivity, and legal non-intervention. This paper argues that this is not a failure of enforcement but a theoretical gap. While management literature has developed extensive frameworks for positive indicators, the systematic conceptualization of negative factual information as an institutionalized governance principle is absent. We introduce the concept of Negative Consequence Indicators (NCIs)-quantifiable metrics derived from negative factual outcomes, institutionalized through measurement, aggregation, comparison, and public disclosure, functioning as information signals that shape behavior via reputational accountability. This concept extends indicator theory by arguing that indicators are not merely information carriers but incentive shapers. This paper establishes the theoretical foundation for a new research direction and outlines a research agenda consisting of several theoretical propositions (in progress by the authors) and a set of empirical propositions (open to the global research community).

title: The Doctrine of Volitional Cloning: Algorithmic Parasitism and The Theft of Cognitive Agency in The Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence transitions from visual mimicry to behavioural emulation, criminal law faces an unprecedented doctrinal vacuum regarding the theft of human intellect. Current penal statutes addressing identity theft and cyber-impersonation are inherently transactional; they penalize the unauthorized use of passwords or static biometric data to extract financial or reputational value. These frameworks are fundamentally incapable of addressing the existential harm inflicted when an offender scrapes a victim’s localized digital history—encompassing years of private communications, linguistic patterns, and behavioral biometrics—to train a Large Language Model (LLM) into a perfect cognitive replica. This paper introduces the novel legal doctrine of "Volitional Cloning" to criminalize this emerging phenomenon, categorizing it legally as "Algorithmic Parasitism." The article deconstructs the unique psychological trauma of "Identity Diffusion," wherein victims experience severe psychological dislocation upon encountering an autonomous digital entity operating with their exact intellectual and emotional cadence. The proposed doctrinal framework establishes a new category of cyber-trespass: the unauthorized emulation of human intellect. It argues that jurisprudence must evolve beyond protecting physical and data privacy to legally recognizing an individual’s "Cognitive Footprint" as sovereign territory. By mapping the boundaries of Intellectual Property, Right of Publicity, and criminal harassment, this paper posits that Volitional Cloning constitutes a severe violation of cognitive liberty, requiring immediate legislative intervention to protect the fundamental right to neuro-autonomy in the algorithmic age.

detail.abstract: The study examines how social media data can generate customer insight by identifying gender-related patterns in Polish financial discourse. We analyze 77,098 posts collected from X. A linguistic heuristic labeled 810 posts by women and 2,427 by men. Iterative labeling then expanded the training data using Polish BERT, HerBERT, and XLM-RoBERTa, alongside embeddings from Polish BERT, Bielik, DeepSeek, and OpenAI classified with conventional machine-learning algorithms. DeepSeek and OpenAI embeddings combined with Support Vector Machines and Logistic Regression achieved approximately 99% accuracy across training, test, and validation sets. LIME-based interpretation revealed differences in financial themes associated with women's and men's discourse. The findings demonstrate that domain-specific language analytics can support audience understanding, communication design, and personalization in financial services, while multilingual embeddings may outperform language-specific models in local contexts. Because inferred gender is sensitive and the corpus is platform-specific, results should support segment-level research and message evaluation, not individual decisions.

title: Who Moves First? Designing Time Coordination Mechanisms in Online Service Systems
affiliations: Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt, Ingolstadt School of Management, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Rotterdam School of Management (RSM) and Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt, Ingolstadt School of Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: The research of the first author is supported by the German Federal Ministry for Digital and Transport (BMDV) within the funding project newMIND for the mobility transformation in Ingolstadt, Bavaria.

detail.abstract: In many service settings, customers must coordinate delivery or appointment times with providers-a process evident in grocery delivery, shared mobility, and tech-support scheduling. As coordination has shifted from human interaction to automated booking systems, the design of time coordination mechanisms has grown increasingly important. Central to this problem is the sequence of interaction: whether customers or the company moves first. Yet the behavioral and operational consequences of this sequencing remain poorly understood. We distinguish two mechanisms: pull mechanisms, in which customers specify a preferred time before seeing feasible service times, and push mechanisms, in which available service times are presented upfront. We examine these mechanisms in three steps. (i) Real-world booking data from a shared mobility service provide empirical insights into how pull mechanisms operate in practice and ensure external validity. (ii) Controlled experiments isolate the effect of interface sequencing on booking decisions, revealing that acceptance in pull mechanisms is driven primarily by temporal deviation, whereas in push mechanisms it is associated with assortment size. (iii) Simulation results show that operational implications are context-dependent: pull mechanisms perform better under low demand by achieving higher acceptance at the cost of more travel distance, while push mechanisms become advantageous when capacity is scarce.

title: Preventing organizational amnesia in operations: the sociotechnical integration of artificial intelligence and senior workers
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Preventing organizational amnesia in operations: the sociotechnical integration of artificial intelligence and senior workers
detail.abstract: Amid workforce ageing and industrial Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption, this article investigated the barriers to and enablers of integrating senior workers' tacit knowledge with AI in manufacturing. Adopting a sociotechnical perspective, this exploratory single-case study of an agro-industrial multinational used semi-structured interviews with senior operators and leaders. Findings empirically refute age-related resistance: barriers are structural and ergonomic (time scarcity, massified virtual training, visually saturating interfaces), while transparent leadership and andragogical hands-on training are enablers. It warns of organizational amnesia from imminent retirements: AI is a knowledge repository yet requires senior workers' "critical use" to validate machine decisions in Industry 4.0.
