detail.abstract: This study examines whether the internal configuration of hybrid deep learning architectures influences stock price forecasting performance. Six models are evaluated using daily prices of 18 SET50 stocks in Thailand from July 2019 to July 2024: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)-LSTM, and four Conditional Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty (CWGAN-GP) configurations employing different generator and discriminator architectures. Forecasting performance is assessed using price-level error metrics and directional measures. The results show that CNN-LSTM-CWGAN-GP, which employs a CNN generator and LSTM discriminator, provides the strongest price-level forecasting performance, achieving the lowest RMSE, MAE, and MAPE for 14 of the 18 stocks. However, superiority in price-level accuracy does not translate directly into directional forecasting performance. CWGAN-GP achieves the highest directional accuracy for seven stocks, while CWGAN-GP and LSTM-CWGAN-GP each achieve the highest F1score for five stocks. These findings demonstrate that forecasting performance depends on both the allocation of neural components within the adversarial architecture and the forecasting objective. The study provides evidence that hybrid adversarial configurations differ substantially in their relative forecasting performance, while highlighting the importance of evaluating price-level accuracy and directional performance separately.

title: Employer-Led Approaches to Recruit, Retain and Support Workers Aged 50 and Over: A Scoping Review with Implications for Wales
affiliations: , Government of the United Kingdom - Public Health Wales and Government of the United Kingdom - Public Health Wales

detail.title: Employer-Led Approaches to Recruit, Retain and Support Workers Aged 50 and Over: A Scoping Review with Implications for Wales

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was undertaken within Healthy Working Wales, a national programme funded by Welsh Government and delivered by Public Health Wales. There was no separate external research grant for this review.

detail.abstract:
Background: Population ageing and longer working lives increase the importance of workplaces that enable people to enter, remain in and progress through employment in later life. In Wales, 31.9% of people aged 50-64 were economically inactive in the year ending 31 March 2026. Evidence relevant to older workers is dispersed across occupational health, human resources, rehabilitation, job design, recruitment, skills and organisational research. This review mapped recent employer-led and workplace-based evidence and considered its transferability to Wales. 

Methods: A scoping review was conducted using Arksey and O'Malley, Levac and colleagues, updated Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting principles. MEDLINE and Embase were searched, supplemented by Google Scholar, targeted grey-literature searches and reference checking. Eligible evidence was published from January 2020 to April 2026 and examined workers or jobseekers aged 50 and over, or populations in which older-worker relevance was central, together with an employer-led, workplace-based or otherwise employer-actionable practice. 

Results: The search identified 2,327 records; 55 studies and reports were included. Ten connected evidence themes were identified, spanning health and work-ability, retention and job design, return to work and adjustments, recruitment, skills, management and culture, caring, menopause and gendered experience, physically demanding work, and implementation, costs and the business case. Across themes, work-ability reflected the fit between worker circumstances and job demands rather than age alone. Flexible and predictable work, manageable demands, early and individualised adjustments, continued access to learning, age-inclusive recruitment and supportive management were recurring employer-actionable mechanisms. Implementation depended on manager capability, leadership, worker trust, access to human resources or occupational health support, and adaptation to sector and employer size. 

Conclusions: No single intervention is effective for every older worker or employer. Evidence supports a whole-employment-pathway approach integrating age-inclusive recruitment, sustainable job design, health and work-ability support, reasonable adjustments and return to work, continued development and supportive management. Evidence is stronger for identifying what employers can act on than for estimating comparative effectiveness, productivity gains or return on investment. Welsh implementation, small and medium-sized employers, equity groups and cost outcomes remain priorities for prospective evaluation.

detail.abstract: AI is moving from tools that help people write, search and summarise towards systems that recommend, influence decisions, make decisions within defined limits and, increasingly, take actions across digital systems. Established frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the OECD AI Principles and the EU AI Act already provide strong foundations for responsible AI. The practical challenge is deciding how governance should change as organisations give AI more authority. This paper proposes a simple decision lens built around three connected factors: authority, autonomy and consequence. It also uses an Assist - Recommend - Influence - Decide - Act continuum to show how controls can become stronger as AI moves closer to consequential decisions and actions. EdTech is used as the main applied example because AI can move quickly from helping a teacher to shaping a learner's experience. The paper does not propose another large compliance checklist. It offers a practical way for leaders to decide what AI may see, recommend, decide and do, and what should happen when it is wrong.

detail.abstract: This study tests whether digital connectivity strengthens the association between logistics capability and real-export resilience in the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA). The dataset combines World Bank Logistics Performance Index dimensions, internet use, macroeconomic indicators, and constant-price exports. It contains 69 export-growth intervals across 15 economies between 2007 and 2022. Logistics capability is constructed from customs, infrastructure, and logistics competence scores measured at the beginning of each interval. The primary year-fixed-effects model yields positive coefficients for logistics capability and internet use, but neither is statistically precise; the interaction coefficient is near zero (beta=0.36, p=0.904). Country-and-year fixed effects and winsorized outcomes produce the same conclusion. The severe-contraction model suggests that stronger logistics capability and the interaction may reduce downside risk, but estimates remain imprecise. Configuration summaries show no severe contractions among high-logistics/high-digital intervals, yet the lower-logistics/high-digital configuration exhibits the greatest volatility. The evidence does not support a universal complementarity claim. Digital connectivity appears insufficient when logistics institutions and physical capabilities are weak. AI disclosure. detail.abstract: This article examines the mandatory pre-trial claims procedure governing disputes with railway carriers under Russian law as it stood on December 31, 2022. It explains the procedural function of the claim, the evidentiary record that should accompany it, the persons entitled to proceed, acceptable methods of service, and the relationship between shortened claim periods and the one-year limitation period. Particular attention is given to commercial acts, general-form acts, electronic transport records, proof of losses, assignment of claims, insurer subrogation, and contractual claim clauses in international railway carriage. The article argues that a claimant should treat the pre-trial stage as the first phase of the merits record rather than as a formal letter preceding litigation. The six-month and forty-five-day claim periods organize prompt investigation but do not extinguish the right where the statutory procedure is ultimately completed and the action is filed within the applicable limitation period.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether maritime connectivity and container throughput are associated with manufacturing resilience in nine Mediterranean gateway economies. The observed panel combines the UNCTAD Liner Shipping Connectivity Index, container throughput, constant-price manufacturing value added, and exports for 2010-2021. Growth models contain 99 country-year observations and use country fixed effects with country-clustered standard errors. Lagged container throughput is positively associated with manufacturing growth (beta=9.50, p=0.017), while lagged liner connectivity is not statistically distinguishable from zero (beta=-4.96, p=0.329). The 2020 shock is associated with a 9.0-percentage-point reduction in manufacturing growth, followed by a 5.3-point 2021 recovery. Interaction models do not show that pre-shock connectivity or throughput significantly moderated the 2020 contraction. A level fixed-effects model finds a positive association between connectivity and manufacturing scale. The results distinguish long-run gateway integration from short-run shock absorption: maritime capability supports the productive base, but it does not eliminate economy-wide disruption. detail.abstract: The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) represents India's principal national policy effort to create an interoperable, citizen-centered digital health ecosystem connecting patients, healthcare professionals, and medical facilities [1, 4, 11]. This study evaluates the policy trajectory, systemic government implementation, hospital-level adoption, and remaining functional implementation gaps under ABDM using qualitative policy analysis and secondary data from official Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) releases, National Health Authority (NHA) dashboards, parliamentary disclosures, and peer-reviewed literature [2, 6, 7, 10]. By September 2026, the mission achieved massive macro scale, recording over 97.54 crore Ayushman Bharat Health Accounts (ABHA), 119.45 crore linked digital health records, 5.76 lakh registered health facilities on the Health Facility Registry (HFR), and 10.96 lakh verified healthcare professionals on the Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR) [2, 6]. However, granular analysis reveals a stark divergence between registration scale and functional utilization [10, 15]. Despite high account creation, ABHA integration within operational national health programs remains severely constrained, with major programs such as Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) and Sickle Cell disease exhibiting linkage rates of approximately 0.3% [10, 15]. Furthermore, facility adoption is structurally skewed toward public institutions (~86% public vs. 14% private), and functional module depth is uneven, with front-office QR-based OPD registration vastly outstripping transaction-level modules such as digital payments [10]. The paper concludes that evaluating ABDM solely through aggregate registration metrics masks critical operational friction. Long-term success necessitates shifting performance management from registration KPIs to functional outcome indicators, expanding private-sector integration, enhancing workflow interoperability, addressing digital literacy barriers, and enforcing robust data governance under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 [8, 10, 13].

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming a source of engineering speed, manufacturing efficiency, and product differentiation in defense. It is also a new channel through which classified information, design knowledge, operational data, and bargaining power can leave the firm. The strategic problem is therefore not whether a defense company should use AI, but which capabilities it should build internally, buy from vendors, or develop with partners-and under what technical and contractual controls. This paper develops a three-layer framework that separates sourcing, deployment, and decision authority. At the sourcing layer, Build, Buy, and Partner are evaluated through strategic differentiation, data sensitivity, capability maturity, urgency, and reversibility. At the deployment layer, the same capability can be placed in an external enterprise service, private cloud, on-premises environment, or airgapped edge system. At the authority layer, AI may recommend, prepare an action, execute within bounded limits, or operate autonomously inside a validated envelope, while humans retain final control over consequential military decisions. The framework is applied to Hanwha Aerospace as the principal case and compared with publicly announced initiatives at LIG Nex1 (now LIG Defense & Aerospace), Korea Aerospace Industries, and Hyundai Rotem. The analysis finds that proprietary engineering models, mission-specific autonomy, security controls, and evaluation capability are candidates for internal ownership; commodity productivity tools are candidates for purchase; and frontier physical AI, on-device semiconductors, and complementary autonomy stacks often justify partnership. Secure commercialization depends less on owning every model than on retaining control of sensitive data, interfaces, derived intellectual property, update rights, and vendor exit. The paper concludes with a phased roadmap and a contract-oriented scorecard for Korean defense firms. Because most recent corporate evidence consists of announcements, memoranda, and development milestones, the paper distinguishes planned capability from verified operational performance and avoids causal claims about financial outcomes.

detail.abstract: Agricultural biologicals-including biopesticides, biofertilizers, biostimulants, microbial consortia and emerging biological technologies-are increasingly important to debates on sustainable intensification, climate resilience, soil health and reduced dependence on hazardous chemical inputs. Yet their regulation remains fragmented and is often poorly aligned with the biological characteristics and heterogeneous risk profiles of these products. This paper examines the policy rationale for a dedicated, risk-proportionate regulatory framework for agricultural biologicals in India. Drawing on an analysis of India's existing regulatory architecture, a proposed Agricultural Biologicals (Regulation, Quality Assurance and Farmer Protection) Bill, 2026, and recent international regulatory developments, particularly European Union reforms intended to accelerate access to biological control products, the paper develops a lifecycle governance framework. The framework differentiates regulatory requirements according to biological and ecological risk; combines proportionate pre-market assessment with biology-specific quality standards; introduces digital and time-bound registration; strengthens traceability and claims governance; provides limited safeguards for farmer-and Farmer Producer Organisation-produced inputs; and shifts part of regulatory effort from extensive pre-market documentation towards post-market surveillance, adverse-event reporting and rapid recall. The paper argues that the policy challenge is not whether agricultural biologicals should be regulated, but how regulation can simultaneously protect farmers, consumers and ecosystems while avoiding unnecessary barriers to innovation. The proposed framework provides a policy model potentially relevant to other developing countries seeking to govern rapidly evolving agricultural technologies under conditions of institutional fragmentation and limited regulatory capacity.

title: Tax Administration and Technology: from Enhanced to No-Cooperation?

detail.title: Tax Administration and Technology: from Enhanced to No-Cooperation?
detail.abstract:
In recent years, technology has induced many reforms within tax administration and improved the relations between taxpayers and tax authorities. There is a growing consensus that increasing the relationship between those parties leads to increased levels of voluntary compliance, and that technology-driven reforms are the best way to implement that goal.

However, increasing the relations between the Parties does not always improve the trust relationship or voluntary compliance levels. Moreover, the continuous implementation of technology-driven reforms on tax systems that were not conceived to operate in a technological environment has led to several downfalls.

In the author’s view, this situation may be overcome by a paradigm shift which is focused on the long-term and on the optimisation of tax administration against the backdrop of an increasing digitalised economy. This would allow moving from the current “enhanced cooperation” model to the “no-cooperation” model which would be beneficial for both tax authorities and taxpayers.

In this paper, the author puts forward the principles that should guide policy-makers in the design of this new model and its main structural elements.

This paper was drafted in the framework of the research project "Digitalization of tax administrations in the EU" ( 612029-EPP-1-2019-1-ES-EPPJMO-PROJECT).

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a conceptual architecture and specification paper; the worked example and counterexamples are synthetic and do not involve human participants, patients, or real personal or company data.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. Self-funded by the author / Clobal Industries.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Reference version: Zenodo, Version 1.0, published 11 September 2026, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22708881 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22708881). This SSRN posting is a secondary distribution of the same Version 1.0; Zenodo is the primary repository and reference identifier.

detail.abstract:
Carbon information is increasingly used across reporting, customer, financing and supply-chain contexts, while the underlying calculations, evidence and recipient-specific statements may evolve over time. This paper develops a conceptual architecture for treating carbon information as an auditable information state rather than solely as a calculated value.

The proposed architecture connects version-bound CarbonEntries, calculation recipes and emission factors with closed ReportingStates, assessed EvidenceObjects, qualitative Assertions and recipient-specific ResponsePackages. Three design propositions and eight invariants specify requirements for historical reconstruction, controlled release and impact assessment following subsequent changes.

The architecture is examined through a synthetic worked example in which a supplier correction changes a customer-selected result from 450 to 490 kg CO2e per batch while a bank-selected Scope 1 and Scope 2 sum remains unchanged at 1,450 kg CO2e. Additional counterexamples demonstrate how changes in evidence or permitted use can require reassessment without changing the underlying numerical result.

The paper contributes an explicit connection between carbon-accounting states and the evidence, authorization and external communications that depend on them. It does not report an implemented system, empirical organizational benefits or assurance. Prototype testing and comparison with well-controlled existing workflows are proposed as the next validation steps.

title: Hidden Vulnerabilities: Where Complex Systems Actually Fail

detail.title: Hidden Vulnerabilities: Where Complex Systems Actually Fail

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am fully independent with over 3 decades of experience.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the concept of Hidden Vulnerabilities which are unintended weaknesses introduced when systems are designed, upgraded, connected, optimized, or expanded without fully understanding their interdependencies. Hidden vulnerabilities are not defective components waiting to fail. They are timing mismatches, latency gaps, misaligned assumptions, and fragile interfaces that operate invisibly within normal parameters — until a disturbance removes the margin that was silently protecting the system.

The concept presented here is not theoretical in origin. The author's career spans three distinct operational contexts that shaped its development: systems vulnerability analysis supporting combat operations during a decade at the Department of Defense; the evaluation of emerging technologies to ensure they did not introduce new failure pathways into existing R&D programs at the Department of Energy; and the application of this lens to grid resilience and critical infrastructure architecture. The term Hidden Vulnerabilities was coined during that latter work and is formalized here for the first time as a named analytical framework.

Drawing on forensic analysis of major infrastructure failures including the 1977 New York City blackout, the 1996 Western Interconnection blackout, and the 2003 Northeast blackout, the paper establishes a critical distinction between system failure — localized and containable — and systemic failure, where linkages between systems amplify an initial disturbance until consequences extend far beyond the original event.

The paper then applies this framework to contemporary challenges: the rapid expansion of AI data centers as high-speed systemic actors embedded in physical infrastructure designed for slower decision cycles, and the role of latency as an emerging vulnerability in systems where human operators can no longer respond faster than cascade dynamics propagate.

While this paper focuses primarily on physical infrastructure systems, the concept of Hidden Vulnerabilities is not bounded by the physical layer. Over three decades of operational experience revealed that humans, institutions, policies, and regulatory frameworks can themselves become hidden vulnerabilities when the systems they govern accelerate beyond the assumptions embedded in their design. A regulatory framework built for a slower era, a decision authority that introduces latency into a millisecond-speed system, or a governance architecture mismatched to the complexity it oversees — these are hidden vulnerabilities of a different kind but the same structural character. The latency analysis presented in this paper touches on this dimension explicitly. Future work will address the institutional and human decision architecture layer more directly.

The author proposes that future resilience requires moving beyond monitoring toward adaptive response where systems are capable of detecting weak signals, understanding complex interactions, and acting before failures cascade. This transition is formalized through the Cedres Integral of Autonomy, a framework describing the structural shift from human-in-the-loop control toward architectures that integrate Adaptive Intelligence with Autonomous Dynamic Machines. This paper is a companion to the author's earlier work, Sovereign Compute: Why Nations That Miss the AI × ADM Window Will Become the Third World of the 21st Century (SSRN, 2026), which addresses the sovereign infrastructure implications of this transition at the national scale.

The trigger is never the vulnerability. The architecture is.

title: The Architectural Entrapment, Sexual Politics, and Gendered Cartography of Spaces: A Hermeneutical Understanding of Surveillance and Politics of Space in Tennyson's 'Lady of Shalott'
affiliations: Cachar College Silchar

detail.title: The Architectural Entrapment, Sexual Politics, and Gendered Cartography of Spaces: A Hermeneutical Understanding of Surveillance and Politics of Space in Tennyson's 'Lady of Shalott'

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The short article journal is my personal work based on my developed interest and admiration for the ballad and it's Artistic association and appreciation.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The research is purely based on self understanding and through academic interests and pursuit and i consent to its publication in the said website.
declarations.funderStatement: The work was self funded.

detail.abstract: The Lady of Shalott (Tennyson, 1833) is recognized as a poem that centrally concerns itself on the relations and conditions between 'art' and 'life', respectively, producing an understanding that 'life' is inherently antipathetic to the possibility of an ongoing artistic production-a perspective that was subsequently taken in turn to be enacted by the demise which befalls the Lady. The following paradigmatic formulation of this canonical approach represents the dilemma of the introspective artist who is condemned to a life of confinement in the shadows. The following article attempts to interrogate the ideological boundaries of Victorian genders, offering a descriptive hermeneutical analysis of the sexual politics and spatial dichotomy that lay between the imprisoned-feminine chambers of the Lady and the masculine, public space of Sir Lancelot. Using the theoretical frameworks of Laura Mulvey's male gaze and female spectacle and Michel Foucault's panopticons, the article argues that Tennyson's poem covertly suggests its heroine's failure to identify herself within a patriarchal ideology that positions space and enforced passivity as integral to women's destinies in Victorian society. This study articulates how her feminine psyche is rendered both invisible and surveilled, manifesting the politically self-divided stance towards the values of patriarchal ideology-colluding with and critiquing them at once-by means of what might be called a discourse of the gaze. Tennyson's ballad, whilst it ostensibly stands as a medieval romance but encodes a profound disjuncture between the female subject and the construction or interpellation of the subject as 'feminine' by patriarchal ideology, disclosing the rationale that governs the supererogatory strategies of resistance to the transition from Shalott to Camelot.

title: The Level of Innovation of European Capitals and Cities: The Innovation Cities Index in EU and Non-EU Countries
affiliations: Ustka City Hall, Polish-Japanese Academy of Information Technology, Warsaw University of Technology and Warsaw Agricultural University (SGGW)

detail.title: The Level of Innovation of European Capitals and Cities: The Innovation Cities Index in EU and Non-EU Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Authors state no conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: Authors state no funding involved.

detail.abstract: The study aims to assess innovation levels of European cities and capitals using both hard data and soft indicators that shape an innovation-friendly climate. Innovation Cities Index 2023 data (2ThinkNow) covering 139 European cities, including 34 capitals, were analyzed. Capitals were compared with other national cities, and countries were grouped by innovation gaps between capitals and second-ranked cities. EU capitals outperform other European capitals, while non-EU capitals with close EU cooperation also achieve higher scores. Capitals generally exceed other cities in innovation, with exceptions. Two structural patterns emerge: countries with large capital-city innovation gaps versus those with balanced urban development. Results provide guidance for policymakers and urban planners seeking to foster balanced and sustainable innovation across national urban systems. The study uniquely integrates hard and soft innovation data to reveal how EU integration influences comparative urban innovation patterns across Europe.

title: Organizational Inheritance and Conditional Centralization: Regional Party Leadership in Taiwan
affiliations: and Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers University

detail.title: Organizational Inheritance and Conditional Centralization: Regional Party Leadership in Taiwan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research relied exclusively on publicly available records and did not involve human participants or the collection of personal data. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by Taiwan National Science and Technology Council Grant # NSTC 113-2410-H-004-002-MY2.

detail.abstract: Why do national party leaders rely on locally rooted officials in some regions but install personnel who depend more directly on the center in others? We argue that regional leadership selection reflects the interaction of organizational inheritance and oligarchic strategy. Parties built through territorial penetration inherit routines and legitimacy for vertical control, aligning their founding structure with leaders' later incentives to coordinate and monitor the organization. Parties assembled through territorial diffusion inherit autonomous local networks and participatory commitments, making centralization more contested and conditional on political stakes. Taiwan offers a controlled comparison between the penetration-based Kuomintang (KMT) and the diffusion-based Democratic Progressive Party (DPP). We analyze 349 regional party-leader spells from 1978 to 2025 and classify each leader's highest prior electoral experience as none, local, regional, or national. KMT leaders are substantially more likely than DPP leaders to enter office without prior electoral experience, whereas DPP leaders are more often rooted in regional electoral careers. Regional experience is most common where a party dominates national legislative seats but not regional legislative seats, combining a valuable national base with territorial vulnerability. Multinomial logit models retain the KMT difference and this cross-tier pattern, while several higher-order interactions remain imprecise. The findings show that democratization does not homogenize party organization: common incentives to centralize operate through inherited center-periphery relationships that shape the personnel instruments, legitimacy costs, and regional resources available to party leaders.

title: Innovation and Politics: How the Revolution Affected the Cuban Patent Network, 1947‒1976
affiliations: University San Pablo CEU, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid and Universidad Autónoma de Madrid

detail.title: Innovation and Politics: How the Revolution Affected the Cuban Patent Network, 1947‒1976

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declared in the article
declarations.funderStatement: Declared in the article

detail.abstract: This study investigates how the Cuban Revolution of 1959-a shock that marked the country's transition from a capitalist to a socialist economy-reshaped the structure and dynamics of Cuba's innovation system between 1947 and 1976, with effects that still endure today. Drawing on historical patent data and social network analysis, the paper examines shifts in innovators' connectivity, clustering, and centrality, offering new insights into the long-term effects of institutional and geopolitical changes on innovation and economic trajectories, particularly in developing economies. The analysis reveals i) the dominant role of U.S. companies, especially in the pharmaceutical and chemical sectors during the 1950s; ii) the impact of the revolution's structural changes on the decline of patent activities and the attrition of the collaborative network; and iii) the subsequent emergence of innovation paths fostered by state-led initiatives and new international collaborations. The results underscore the key and evolving role of both Cuban public institutions and U.S. foreign policy, the resilience of central actors in the patent network-including several U.S. corporations that continued protecting their inventions despite the trade embargo-and the relative success of domestic initiatives in healthcare and pharmaceuticals. However, the findings also demonstrate how innovation ties became geographically concentrated after the revolution, as the international relationships of the island shifted. Overall, this research contextualizes contemporary debates on structural change and innovation dynamics regarding the role of public/private institutions, the implications of intellectual property rights, the importance of collaboration and absorptive capacities, or the influence of geopolitical realignments.

title: A CRITICAL COMMENTARY ON THE TRUST ADMINISTRATION ACT, 2026

detail.title: A CRITICAL COMMENTARY ON THE TRUST ADMINISTRATION ACT, 2026

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
On 8th September 2026, the President assented to the Trust Administration Act, 2026, a consolidating statute that, upon its commencement on 25 September 2026, repeals two of the oldest surviving pieces of received colonial legislation still governing Kenyan private law and, in the same stroke, amends the Registration of Documents Act and the Business Registration Service Act. This commentary offers a close, section-by-section reading of the Act, situated against the near-century arc of Kenyan trust regulation and the contemporaneous pressure of international anti-money-laundering conditionality.

It argues that the Act is, at once, a genuine and overdue modernization of an inherited body of law that had scarcely been touched since the interwar period, and an instrument whose transparency architecture was drafted less for the ordinary Kenyan family settling land for its grandchildren than for the anonymous global holder of capital whom the Financial Action Task Force has asked Nairobi to unmask. The two audiences are not the same, and the Act does not always trouble itself to say which one it is addressing at any given moment. That ambivalence, more than any single clause, is the analytical thread this commentary pulls.

title:
The AI Failure Ladder
 Autonomy, Intentional Misuse, Control Lag, and the Migration of Artificial Intelligence into the Real World
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title:
The AI Failure Ladder
 Autonomy, Intentional Misuse, Control Lag, and the Migration of Artificial Intelligence into the Real World

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract: Advanced artificial intelligence presents two different but increasingly interconnected control problems. The first is intentional: humans may use increasingly capable AI systems to conduct harmful activities more effectively, cheaply, rapidly, or at greater scale. The second is unintentional: increasingly autonomous systems may produce consequential actions beyond what their human operators intended, understood, or retained sufficient time to prevent. This paper examines both pathways through a systems-engineering and control-theory framework. Autonomy itself is not new. Earlier systems such as Longbow and the Brilliant Antiarmor Submunition delegated sensing, classification, guidance, and in some cases individual target selection to algorithms operating within bounded mission and engagement envelopes. What is changing is the potential breadth of the delegated decision envelope: the decisions a machine may make after the last meaningful human intervention. Risk increases when capability is combined with autonomy, access to consequential real-world actuators, and machine-speed decision cycles. Historical and contemporary examples - including bounded weapon autonomy, the 2010 Flash Crash, military decision support, and recent autonomous-agent incidents - illustrate distinct mechanisms by which effective control can erode. Safety-critical aviation provides a mature precedent for development assurance, diverse redundancy, common-mode analysis, airworthiness security, configuration control, and certification of high-consequence software-controlled systems. A five-year AI Failure Ladder is used as a prospective engineering risk register to display relative risk categories rather than statistically precise forecasts. Finally, the paper considers AI-assisted AI development as a potential accelerator that may shorten capability-development cycles relative to safety validation and governance. The central engineering objective is preservation of sufficient intervention margin as AI capability, autonomy, authority, and real-world access expand.

title: Personal Data Protection and Digital Persuasion: The Potential and Limits of Brazil's LGPD in the Face of Informational Power

detail.title: Personal Data Protection and Digital Persuasion: The Potential and Limits of Brazil's LGPD in the Face of Informational Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial, personal, professional, or institutional conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it is based exclusively on a narrative literature review, doctrinal legal analysis, and publicly available documents. The research did not involve human participants, interviews, experiments, or the collection of personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Personal data processing helps shape the information, classifications, and opportunities offered to individuals in digital environments. This article examines how Brazil's General Data Protection Law (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais, or LGPD) can constrain profiling and persuasion without requiring proof of their effects on aggregate electoral outcomes. It combines a narrative literature review, documentary analysis, and doctrinal legal interpretation, with a selective international comparison and a documentary cutoff date of September 14, 2026. The documentaries The Great Hack and The Social Dilemma are treated as public framings of the issue and contrasted with investigations into Cambridge Analytica and Brexit, as well as research on inference, recommendation, and AI persuasion. The analysis distinguishes unlawful processing, predictive capacity, persuasive effects, and electoral causation. It identifies heterogeneous findings, methodological disputes, and limitations that preclude both universal claims of technological efficacy and assumptions of harmlessness. It argues that uncertainty about aggregate effects does not remove the duty to justify data provenance, processing purposes, and the use of inferences. An analytical framework for legal practice is proposed without claiming empirical validation. The study concludes that the LGPD provides relevant preventive tools whose effectiveness depends on oversight, verifiable transparency, and coordination with other fields of law. 
This article is an expanded and substantially revised development of Oliveira, Filipe Fonseca de, and Cléber Vicente Gonçalves, “A Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados como Garantia da Inviolabilidade da Privacidade da Pessoa Natural,” Simpósio de Práticas Pedagógicas do UGB, no. 10, 2022.

The author independently reviewed the cited materials, evaluated the legal arguments, directed the scope and revisions of the article, and approved the final text. The author assumes full responsibility for the accuracy, analysis, interpretations, conclusions, and integrity of the work.

title: Investor Complaints and Earnings Management: Evidence on Managerial Reporting Behavior from India
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Management (IIM), Indore

detail.title: Investor Complaints and Earnings Management: Evidence on Managerial Reporting Behavior from India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants or animals. It uses publicly available, firm-level secondary data obtained from company regulatory filings, the National Stock Exchange of India, and the Prowess IQ database. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether investor complaints, an under-researched external governance mechanism, influence managerial financial reporting behavior, and whether internal board structure conditions influence. Using 6,288 firm-year observations of Indian listed companies and exploiting the mandatory quarterly complaint disclosure regime introduced under SEBI's SCORES platform and Regulation 13 of the LODR Regulations, we find that firms receiving investor complaints report lower signed discretionary accruals than firms receiving none, consistent with complaints raising the expected cost of income-increasing discretion. This disciplining association is strongly contingent on the on-board structure. Under CEO duality, the relationship reverses in sign: the interaction is economically large and statistically significant, and the constraining effect of complaint intensity declines monotonically with board size, turning positive beyond approximately fourteen directors. Neither CEO duality nor board size is independently associated with discretionary accruals, indicating that these attributes function as transmission conditions rather than direct determinants of reporting quality. Estimates absorb firmand industry-by-year fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the firm level, and are robust to kernel propensity score matching and a two-stage Heckman correction for self-selection. The findings position investor complaints as a governance signal rather than an administrative one, and show that external monitoring translates into reporting discipline only where internal governance is structured to transmit that signal.

title: An autonomous decomposition strategy for fairness-aware edge control of multi-area EV charging loads under feeder constraints
affiliations: Sichuan University, Sichuan University, Sichuan University, Sichuan University and Sichuan University - College of Electrical Engineering

detail.title: An autonomous decomposition strategy for fairness-aware edge control of multi-area EV charging loads under feeder constraints
detail.abstract: Increasing electric vehicle (EV) penetration provides distribution networks with operational flexibility, but real-time coordination of dispersed charging areas remains constrained by feeder limits, local information requirements, and unequal regulation burdens. This paper proposes an autonomous decomposition strategy based on hierarchical learning and optimization. A deep reinforcement learning (DRL) leader determines a scalar aggregate adjustment relative to rolling charging baselines. Deterministic followers allocate this adjustment through a capacity-constrained optimization with direction-dependent weights derived from charging urgency, historical burden, and available flexibility. The follower allocation has a unique solution and, for fixed capacities, weights, and direction, varies continuously with the aggregate request. A lexicographic correction first maximizes the feasible aggregate response and then minimizes deviation from the follower allocation, preserving the requested response whenever a feasible spatial redistribution exists. In the 33-bus benchmark comparison, the proposed method reduces the learned action dimension from six to one relative to multi-action DRL. Upward and downward Jain indices achieve 0.819/0.944, with no observed feeder violations and 100% departure-energy satisfaction. A correction stress test illustrates constraint recovery through spatial redistribution without reducing the selected aggregate request. Tests on the 123-node feeder topology further support applicability at larger coordination scales.

title: From Predator Swamping to Cognitive Swamping: An Applied Learning Framework for Human Resilience in AI-Mediated Cyberbiosecurity

detail.title: From Predator Swamping to Cognitive Swamping: An Applied Learning Framework for Human Resilience in AI-Mediated Cyberbiosecurity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and owner of AI Governance Federal, LLC, a consulting practice whose services relate to the subject matter discussed in this paper. The author may have a financial interest in the future development or commercialization of related frameworks, training, or consulting services. This paper represents the author’s independent scholarly analysis.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is conceptual and does not report original research involving human participants, identifiable private information, or animal subjects. Therefore, institutional ethics approval was not required. Any future empirical research involving human participants will undergo the appropriate institutional review and approval or exemption process before data collection begins.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for the research or preparation of this paper.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is changing the scale, speed, and complexity at which information can be generated, classified, and acted upon. In cybersecurity and cyberbiosecurity, this creates a problem that is not reducible to technical detection capacity: human and organizational systems must still determine which signals deserve attention, which require verification, and which warrant action. This conceptual paper proposes the term cognitive swamping to describe a potential capacity mismatch in which the volume, velocity, complexity, ambiguity, or strategic coordination of information exceeds the human or organizational capacity required for reliable sensemaking and decision-making. The concept is developed through an ecological analogy to predator swamping, in which synchronized prey emergence can temporarily exceed a predator's handling capacity. The analogy is not proposed as biological equivalence. Rather, it is used as a generative model for examining capacity limits in human-centered security systems.

The paper situates cognitive swamping at the intersection of applied learning sciences, cybersecurity, cyberbiosecurity, AI governance, and operational risk. Recent research demonstrates that artificial intelligence is increasingly being applied to invasive-species risk assessment, biological surveillance, marine biosecurity, and AI-enabled life sciences. At the same time, recent cybersecurity research documents alert overload, automation bias, automation complacency, trust calibration problems, and the continuing importance of human-centered security. These literatures suggest a research opportunity: studying how people can learn to maintain decision quality when AI-mediated information environments become too large, fast, uncertain, or contradictory for ordinary human sensemaking.

The paper proposes a learning-centered research agenda and an experimental simulation in which participants respond to an evolving cyberbiosecurity incident under varying information-load and AI-assistance conditions. The proposed contribution is a testable framework rather than a claim that artificial general intelligence or artificial superintelligence currently possesses unlimited processing capacity. The practical objective is to move from teaching people to process more information toward teaching people to recognize what information deserves processing.

title: From Psychosocial Explanation to Behavioral Prediction: Anticipating Donation Frequency and Resource Type in Post-Disaster Humanitarian Logistics
affiliations: Universidad Andres Bello, University of Chile, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Psychosocial Explanation to Behavioral Prediction: Anticipating Donation Frequency and Resource Type in Post-Disaster Humanitarian Logistics
detail.abstract: ​Post-disaster humanitarian logistics faces major challenges related to uncertainty, volatile aid flows, and material convergence. Although donation prediction has advanced at aggregate and organizational levels, individual-level behavioral and psychosocial determinants remain insufficiently integrated into predictive frameworks. This study proposes a predictive extension of a previously validated socio-technical framework, integrating outcome-free SEM-derived latent constructs, donor profiles, and questionnaire variables into a machine learning layer to anticipate donation frequency and resource type.The empirical analysis uses 362 valid observations from adults in rural municipalities of the Maule Region, Chile. Several predictor configurations and model families were evaluated, including multinomial logistic regression, ensemble models, and benchmark classifiers, complemented by SHAP-based interpretability analysis. Results show that psychosocial variables contain meaningful predictive signal. For donation frequency, the best-performing models achieve Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) values close to 0.30. For donation type, Random Forest models using classifier chains obtain the strongest performance, with a macro-averaged F1 score close to 0.59. SHAP results indicate that frequency is mainly discriminated by granular resilience and motivation items, whereas perceived constraints and donation-type dependencies help predict resource composition.These findings provide behavioral inputs for anticipating donation intensity, resource composition, and aid-flow congestion in post-disaster contexts.

title: Defaults, Present Bias, and Household Financial Decisions in India

detail.title: Defaults, Present Bias, and Household Financial Decisions in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, professional, or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved adult participants in a survey based behavioral experiment. No formal institutional ethics approval was obtained. Participation was voluntary, and the study procedures were designed to minimize risk to participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The research was independently conducted without external financial support.

detail.abstract: Indian households now hold bank accounts almost universally and use them for saving far less often: in the most recent Global Findex wave, 89.0% of adults report an account while 27.0% report having saved at a financial institution, a gap of 62 percentage points. Between 2014 and 2024, gaps in account ownership by sex, income and education closed by 15.4 points on average while gaps in institutional saving did not close on either standard measure. That asymmetry-access converging, use notis the setting for this paper. It asks how default choice architecture and present-biased preferences jointly shape household saving and borrowing decisions, and in particular whether defaults help most the households whose own preferences hurt them most. The paper has two deliberately separate parts. The first is a pre-registered randomised design, not yet fielded, in which participants allocate part of a monthly budget to saving under one of four choice architectures-no default, a |500 default, a |1,000 default, or an active-choice requirement-with present bias, attention, numeracy, financial literacy and liquidity constraint all elicited before randomisation. The design is powered on the default × present-bias interaction rather than on the main effect, and is built to separate present bias from three competing mechanisms: inattention, endorsement and anchoring. The second is a descriptive account of the Indian household financial decision environment from public official statistics. The two are complements with a visible seam between them; they are never pooled. No experimental results are reported, because the experiment has not been run. What is reported is the design, its power properties, a complete and tested analysis pipeline, and descriptive evidence on the environment in which the mechanism would operate. The contribution at this stage is a specified, powered, pre-registered test of a stated gap-the interaction between default response and present bias in a setting where formal payroll deduction is unavailable to most households while digital financial infrastructure is dense-together with the honest statement that a design is not a finding.

title: One Force: Diversification as the Unifying Principle Behind the Drivers of Human Infidelity
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: One Force: Diversification as the Unifying Principle Behind the Drivers of Human Infidelity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests, other than being the author of related trade books on marriage and relationships — Not Tonight and It Just Happened, part of the series The Two Mortal Threats to Every Marriage — which develop at book length some of the concepts discussed in this paper. The author received no compensation from any party in connection with this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Human infidelity is currently explained by a scattered set of mechanisms, each with its own literature: the Coolidge effect and novelty-seeking, extrapair copulation and dual mating, concealed or cryptic ovulation, sperm competition, female multiple mating, and a loose financial "portfolio" analogy. I argue that these are not distinct drivers but a single one, read at the level of the gene: diversification of the gene's reproductive bet. The components are individually well established; the contribution here is their unification under one principle. The unification survives the objection that most threatens it-that spreading copies across more partners raises offspring number (mean expansion) while classic bet-hedging lowers the variance of reproductive success, seemingly the opposite-by showing that both are faces of the same pressure, expressed differently in the two sexes because their reproductive constraints differ. This sex-dependent expression is not an embarrassment for the unification but a prediction of it, one that connects directly to the observed human asymmetry in who ends a marriage (developed in a companion paper; Maymin, 2026b). The framework is parsimonious, predictive, and it identifies the single structural defense against the force: non-diversifiability.

title: De-Financializing Gold: China's Retail Paper Gold Shutdown and The Eastward Shift in Bullion Settlement
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: De-Financializing Gold: China's Retail Paper Gold Shutdown and The Eastward Shift in Bullion Settlement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare that this research was conducted independently as a student research project and has no financial, personal, or institutional conflicts of interest. The authors have no financial interests, commercial affiliations, or personal relationships with any organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced the design, analysis, or conclusions presented in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animal subjects, or clinical data. Consequently, formal ethical approval was not required for the conduct of this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or non-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: On June 24, 2026, major Chinese state banks announced the termination of retail paper gold and silver trading linked to the Shanghai Gold Exchange, effective July 24, 2026, following a historic gold price correction and elevated margin distress among leveraged retail accounts. This paper argues that the shutdown is best understood not as an isolated risk-management measure, but as one element of a broader structural shift toward the de-financialization of gold, a transition of global price discovery away from Western paper-derivative venues (COMEX/LBMA), where synthetic claims routinely exceed available physical metal, toward physically-settled Eastern hubs (SGE/Hong Kong). Drawing on the market microstructure and price-discovery literature (Garbade & Silber, 1983; Hasbrouck, 1995; Hauptfleisch et al., 2016), the paper first examines how COMEX's leveraged futures market dominates short-term gold price discovery despite low physical delivery rates, and revisits the March 2020 COMEX-LBMA dislocation as a real-world demonstration of the Limits to Arbitrage (Shleifer & Vishny, 1997) when physical logistics break down. It then situates China's retail shutdown within a wider sovereign pivot, record central bank gold accumulation, China's sustained divestment from US Treasuries in favor of physical bullion, and the expansion of non-USD settlement infrastructure (CIPS, mBridge) following the 2022 freezing of Russian reserves. Finally, the paper examines Western policy responses under consideration, including proposals to revalue the US Treasury's statutorily frozen 1973 gold price and gold-redeemable debt instruments, neither of which has yet been enacted. The paper concludes that the international monetary system is undergoing a gradual, multipolar reallocation of reserve functions rather than an abrupt displacement of the dollar.

title: The Company You No Longer Control: Shadow AI, Shadow Agents, and the Governance Gap

detail.abstract:
Shadow AI creates a practical crisis of corporate control. Employees can introduce systems that handle company information before management understands their use. Agents deepen the problem by turning informal assistance into delegated action. This conceptual paper examines that transition through public incident disclosures, industry statements, identity-security research, and practitioner discussions. It distinguishes observed incidents from controlled evaluations and unverified anecdotes. Its central argument is that technology, corporate oversight, and public regulation move on different timescales.

When operational capability expands before effective controls are in place, a period of exposure opens. The paper calls this interval control delay. During it, management can remain formally accountable while losing the ability to establish what happened or to intervene. The proposed response is to govern specific delegations, preserve evidence of consequential actions, and test containment and recovery. Agent identities need clear owners and a managed lifecycle.

The immediate danger is an organization that appears productive and compliant while its real decision process becomes increasingly difficult to reconstruct.

title: Gated Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Inverse Local Volatility Calibration with Learned Regime Structure
affiliations: Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore Institute of Technology and Vellore Institute of Technology

detail.title: Gated Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Inverse Local Volatility Calibration with Learned Regime Structure
detail.abstract: Local volatility calibration from discrete option prices is inherently ill-posed, and the classical Dupire formula fails catastrophically under realistic market conditions of noise and sparsity. Physics-Informed Neural Networks offer a principled alternative through PDE-constrained learning, but standard joint optimisation of price and volatility networks encounters a fourth- order gradient pathology that limits convergence quality. We propose a decoupled PINN architecture in which the call-price surface is learned under Black-Scholes constraints whilst volatility is recovered via independent regression. A stop-gradient operation eliminates the gradient pathology by breaking the computational dependency of PDE residuals on volatility parameters. This architectural choice yields a structural invariance: volatility error becomes independent of the PDE loss weight λPDE , removing what is typically the most consequential hyperparameter in such frameworks. Additionally, we represent volatility as a gated mixture of two expert networks, enabling regime structure to emerge naturally during training. The method is validated on synthetic two-regime surfaces and real equity options, demonstrating substantial improvements in reconstruction stability under data sparsity compared to Dupire- based methods. No-arbitrage constraints are satisfied consistently throughout the calibrated domain.

title: No Single Best Model: Zone- and Horizon-Dependent Performance of MachineLearning Approaches for PM2.5 Forecasting in Kathmandu Valley
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: No Single Best Model: Zone- and Horizon-Dependent Performance of MachineLearning Approaches for PM2.5 Forecasting in Kathmandu Valley
detail.abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure is a leading contributor to cardiovascular, respiratory, and metabolic disease burden worldwide, making accurate short-term forecasting essential for timely public health warnings. However, most machine learning studies of PM2.5 forecasting report results for a single forecast horizon, a single train/testsplitting protocol, and a single monitoring location, leaving it unclear whether a reported ”best” model would still win under a different horizon, evaluation design, or location. This study evaluated five forecasting approaches — persistence, Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM, and Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) — across three geographically distinct zones of the Kathmandu Valley, at forecast horizons of 1, 3, and 6 hours, under both a strict chronological(future-only) evaluation protocol and a season-balanced block-stratified protocol, with SHAP-based explainability and a dedicated precipitation-feature ablation test. Persistence proved to be a strong baseline at 1 hour ahead but declined sharply with horizon, collapsing to negative R2 by 6 hours in every zone once the dataset was extended to include the monsoon season, confirming that naive forecasts become actively misleading beyond short lead times in that setting; machine learning models degraded far more gracefully, but which architecture performed best reversed depending on zone, with tree-based models dominating in two zones and Bi-LSTM dominating in the third; and adding reanalysis-derived precipitation as a predictor produced a similarly zone-dependent effect, meaningfully improving one zone’s accuracy while showing no benefit elsewhere. These findings indicate that robustPM2.5 forecasting system design requires horizon-aware and zone-aware model selection rather than reliance on a single universally ”best” architecture.

detail.abstract: Reliable unemployment statistics are essential for assessing labour-market conditions, identifying vulnerable populations, and designing targeted employment policies. However, unemploymentrate estimation at regional and local levels is often constrained by small survey samples, high sampling variability, and limited statistical infrastructure. These challenges are particularly pronounced in data-scarce regions where conventional direct survey estimates may be unstable or unavailable for smaller geographic domains. This study develops a multilevel Bayesian small area estimation framework for improving unemployment-rate estimates in regions with limited survey information. The proposed approach combines direct labour-force survey estimates with demographic, socioeconomic, and geographic auxiliary information while allowing information to be shared across related geographic areas. A hierarchical structure accounts for differences between regions and provides partial pooling, reducing excessive variability in areas with limited observations while preserving meaningful local differences. The framework is evaluated against direct survey estimation and alternative small area approaches using estimation precision, predictive accuracy, uncertainty coverage, and robustness across domains. The findings indicate that multilevel Bayesian estimation can provide more stable unemployment-rate estimates, particularly for regions with small samples. The approach also produces posterior uncertainty measures that allow users to distinguish relatively precise estimates from those requiring cautious interpretation. The study demonstrates the potential of multilevel Bayesian small area models to strengthen subnational unemployment statistics and support more geographically targeted labourmarket analysis in data-scarce settings.

detail.abstract: Between 2008 and 2022, near-zero rates fuelled a venture capital boom, pushing VC funding from $50 billion to $671 billion and helping create Tesla, Spotify, and Airbnb. The same conditions produced WeWork, a $47 billion valuation built on narrative, not fundamentals. This article argues cheap money is neither good nor bad for innovation; low rates make patient and speculative capital indistinguishable in real time. declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author holds and has traded funded accounts with providers of the type analyzed here and has received payouts from them during the sample period. The author also produces educational material and commercial trading indicators for retail traders. No provider is named, no provider funded or reviewed this research, and the analysis reflects only the author's independent work.

detail.abstract: Proprietary-trading "evaluation challenges" — paid tests that, once passed, grant a simulated "funded" account paying a share of simulated profits — have become a large retail product, yet their economics have not been analyzed rigorously. We model a challenge as a barrier-crossing problem. For a driftless participant facing a fixed loss limit, optional stopping gives a pass probability of L/(T+L), the ratio of the loss limit to the sum of loss limit and profit target, independent of volatility. We show that this is a ceiling rather than a value: the loss limit trails the account's high-water mark, positions are flattened daily, and frictions are charged per trade, so the attainable rate falls below it. On six years of one-minute index-futures data we decompose the gap — 44.4% under the bare geometry, 40.4% once the daily bracket and its truncation are imposed, 34.7% once the floor trails — and we show the ceiling is unattainable from either direction, since larger positions break the continuity the theorem assumes while smaller ones pay a fixed cost per trade. We then price the full life cycle — evaluation, funded lock, qualification and withdrawals — on realized paths. Expected value per evaluation is +0.052 L at the fee actually paid and -0.018 L at list price. The consistency rule that operators present as a hurdle is met with exact equality by a repeated fixed bracket and costs nothing, but the design sits precisely on that boundary. We derive the population pass rate at which the seller breaks even — 20% at the fee paid, 40% at list price, against 34.7% for the mechanical participant we model — and show the two are consistent. The economics assume no directional edge and are therefore a lower bound for the buyer.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how cash pressure relates to the adjustment of defined benefit (DB) plan portfolios, using monthly data from 78 Brazilian plans between 2015 and 2025. Cash pressure is measured by the relationship between pension deductions and additions, and its temporal stability is assessed by structural change tests that allow changes in level and trend. We examine characteristics associated with the main changes in investment allocations and, above all, we compare the observed flows with a pro-rata benchmark based on the pre-existing portfolio composition. The results show broad instability in the box dynamics, and changes occur both in the direction of increasing and reducing pressure, not characterizing a uniform deterioration process. In the analysis of investments, there is no robust evidence that Fixed Income functions as a disproportionate source of liquidity, although Fixed Income presents marginal evidence of adjustment above pro-rata in the symmetric specification. The decomposition between inflows and outflows, however, reveals that Participant Operations adjust significantly less than prorata during months of net outflow, consistent with their limited ability to function as a discretionary source of liquidity. The results show that adjustment volume and settlement preference are distinct concepts and suggest that liquidity management of DB plans must consider not only the asset composition, but also the effective mobilization capacity of each component of the portfolio.

detail.abstract: This contribution, based on a presentation at the GlobTaxGov Roundtable of 10 June 2026 on the Inclusive Framework Side-by-Side (SBS) package of 5 January 2026, argues that Pillar Two has a "Janus-faced" character. Rather than imposing a floor on tax competition, Pillar Two restructures it through mechanisms such as QRTCs and QTIs and the recalibration of the effective tax rate calculation, enabling continued, system-aligned competition while producing global asymmetries. At the same time, the incorporation of the SBS package via Article 32 of the EU Pillar Two Directive creates a constitutional Catch-22, raising concerns under EU law regarding delegation, State aid, and the autonomy of EU law. Pillar Two accordingly emerges as a functional but legally and politically fragile framework.

detail.abstract: Movements in stock prices are hard to forecast, and hard to explain even in hindsight. We show that OIRet, an option-implied measure of expected returns with no free parameters, outperforms predictions based on analysts' expectations, in and out of sample, at horizons from one to 12 months. OIRet and shocks to OIRet also play a major role in explaining stock returns ex post: relative to explanations based on shocks to analysts' cash-flow expectations alone, they raise the explained share of realized returns from 17% to 33% at the 12-month horizon, and from 1.1% to 22% at the 1-month horizon.

title: Financial Representation and Closed-Loop Bank Balance-Sheet Management: A Dynamic Model of Financial-State Evolution, Reverse Optimization, and Governance
affiliations: and Hanyang University

detail.title: Financial Representation and Closed-Loop Bank Balance-Sheet Management: A Dynamic Model of Financial-State Evolution, Reverse Optimization, and Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: self funded

detail.abstract:
Bank balance-sheet management is supported by increasingly sophisticated models for valuation, asset-liability management, capital, liquidity, interest-rate risk, and optimization. Yet these models generally begin with a particular decision problem and construct the state variables and constraints required for that problem. This paper addresses a logically prior question: how should the financial condition of a bank be represented so that different management decisions can operate on a common, economically coherent financial state?

We develop Financial Representation, a dynamic framework that maps balance-sheet positions, market and customer conditions, and a coherent enterprise assumption structure into a Canonical Financial State. Risk Attribution provides economically interpretable coordinates that reconcile changes in Economic Value of Equity and Net Interest Income to their underlying financial drivers. Successive states form a financial-state trajectory reflecting both exogenous market and customer developments and endogenous management actions.

The framework then introduces Reverse Optimization. Rather than beginning with a proposed balance-sheet transaction and determining its consequences, management begins with a target vector of Key Performance and Regulatory Indicators and identifies balance-sheet actions capable of moving the institution toward those targets. Governance is incorporated directly into the feasible action set, so candidate strategies are constrained by Board policies, regulatory requirements, risk appetite, capital, liquidity, and other institutional limits.

These elements form a recursive closed-loop model of bank balance-sheet choice: represent the current financial state, identify governance-feasible actions toward target outcomes, observe the resulting state transition, and repeat. The framework provides a common theoretical foundation for studying financial-state dynamics, managerial behavior, balance-sheet optimization, governance, and intelligent decision systems.

detail.abstract: Management-friendly governance arrangements are often viewed as manifestations of weak governance that enable rent extraction. We show that such arrangements may arise endogenously as an efficient response to a commitment problem induced by transferable ownership. When shareholders can sell their claims before the long-run outcomes of managerial actions are realized, anticipated resale weakens commitment to long-term investment. In response, shareholders optimally cede bargaining power over compensation design to managers, despite the higher managerial rents this may entail. Nevertheless, severe shareholder short-termism limits the extent to which relinquishing bargaining power restores commitment to long-term investment. The optimal transfer of power is therefore non-monotonic, peaking at an intermediate degree of ownership instability. Consequently, governance constraints on managerial bargaining power may have a perverse effect on investment efficiency, and limited compensation disclosure can further exacerbate underinvestment relative to contract opacity.

title: The Algorithmic Caste System: Gig Work, Informality & Caste Formations in Urban India

detail.title: The Algorithmic Caste System: Gig Work, Informality & Caste Formations in Urban India

detail.abstract:
This research project examines the intersection of caste, informality, and platform capitalism, asking how digital labour platforms reshape, conceal, and at times reinforce social inequality. According to the India Employment Report 2024, published by the Institute for Human Development and the International Labour Organisation, nearly ninety per cent of India's workforce remains informally employed, and this informality has never been caste-neutral. As platforms increasingly mediate everyday work, they risk reproducing rather than dismantling longstanding hierarchies, now through algorithmic management, consumer-driven ratings, and opaque systems of evaluation. Yet how these hierarchies are enacted at the point of interaction remains underexamined. This study therefore investigates the perceptions and everyday encounters of middle-class urban consumers with gig workers, tracing how such encounters reproduce deeper caste-class relations beneath the veneer of technological neutrality. Drawing on primary survey data, semi-structured interviews, and secondary literature, it develops a Social Distance Index, adapted from the Bogardus Social Distance Scale and calibrated to the conditions of the platform economy, to measure these relations empirically.  


The findings are striking: nearly two-thirds of respondents (64.7%) scored above the lowest band of social distance, with almost 40% falling into the highest band  and even on the more guarded measure of active discrimination, one in five admitted bias-consistent behaviour despite strong social pressure to deny it. Social boundaries once drawn along caste and class lines persist, largely intact, within ostensibly neutral digital transactions.


On this basis, the paper contends that India's existing legal framework is insufficient to address discrimination embedded within data-driven systems of work organisation. Bringing together labour law, political economy, science and technology studies, it proposes a discrimination-conscious regulatory framework built on algorithmic accountability, transparency, and stronger protections for platform workers. In doing so, the study contributes to the emerging scholarship on platform labour while offering a distinctly Indian account of how historical structures of inequality continue to shape the digital economy.

title: De-Risking the Blue Horizon: A Legal and Financial Architecture for Unlocking Private Capital in African and SIDS Ocean Economy Projects

detail.abstract: Despite the multi-trillion-dollar valuation of the global blue economy, private capital deployment across African littoral states and Small Island Developing States (SIDS) remains constrained. While institutional rhetoric attributes this investment gap to generic risk aversion, this article argues that the primary impediment lies in structural bankability deficits embedded within early-stage project preparation. Specifically, unmitigated foreign exchange (FX) mismatches, ambiguous marine concession enforceability, unproven revenue and off-take models, weak public counterparty creditworthiness, undefined operations-and-maintenance and climate risk, and fragmented multi-ministerial governance collectively render ocean infrastructure uninvestable for international debt and equity. By evaluating legal frameworks across African maritime jurisdictions and SIDS alongside comparative project finance mechanisms from Latin America, SouthEast Asia, and Europe, this paper formulates a regulatory and financial architecture to bridge the bankability divide across all six risk dimensions. It advocates for standardized Marine Public-Private Partnership (MP3) concession frameworks, a proposed sovereign-backed local currency hedging facility, ringfenced escrow mechanisms, minimum revenue guarantees, parametric climate insurance, a single-window governance authority, and regional investor-facing preparation templates.

title: Why Europe should strategise on the U.S. DBCFT debate, and fast
