detail.abstract: Financial fraud is now among the most serious threats to global financial systems. Reported losses in the United States alone exceeded $12.5 billion in 2024 [1]. Rule-based detection, long the industry default, is steadily losing ground to fraud schemes that adapt faster than the rules meant to catch them [4, 8]. This paper surveys how Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are currently applied to financial fraud detection, with attention to the resources and skills that matter for Data Analyst and Financial Analyst roles. We review seven publicly available datasets [9, 10] and set out six research gaps supported by 2025-2026 literature. We also draw on work from adjacent fields: AI-driven cybersecurity threat detection [13], hybrid phishing detection [14], AI-powered software defect prediction [15], structural bias auditing in security systems [16], deep learning for malware classification and threat intelligence in hospital environments [28], and explainable AI for trust and transparency in financial security systems [27]. Read together, these domains share a recurring set of problems: class imbalance, limited model explainability, concept drift, and regulatory compliance, all of which apply squarely to fraud detection [17, 18, 22]. We link these themes to what analysts actually do day to day, and close with a career-oriented roadmap.

detail.abstract: This paper values the unpaid labor of enslaved Black people in the United States, 1776–1860. It re-parameterizes the wage model of Craemer et al. (2020), first reproducing their published accumulation within a few dollars from their stated inputs, with three disclosed departures: actual billed hours, not a 24-hour day; an age-graded effective labor share; and a skill-weighted free-market wage basis, compounded at a disclosed real rate. Central estimate: approximately $30.7 trillion in 2026 purchasing-power dollars at a 2% real rate. The estimate is scope-conservative, pricing stolen labor-time only and excluding atrocity, opportunity loss, pain and suffering, but rate-central: the paper publishes the full rate menu (1% real to $4.6T; 4% real to $1.46Q), every rate's nominal equivalent, a complete sensitivity table, and the paper's totals at the literature's own 3% and 6% nominal rates. The peer-reviewed high-rate wage scenarios are carried as context, not as this paper's claim: Darity, Mullen, and Slaughter (2022) print "$7 quadrillion" for the 24-hour scenario at 6% nominal (2021 dollars), and this paper replicates it at $7.386561 quadrillion. Post-emancipation expropriation, national enrichment, and atrocity sit in separate ledgers under an explicit non-additivity discipline. The paper designs a perpetual remedy instrument at an unspecified parameter, $30.7 trillion as a labeled worked illustration, and answers the three strongest method objections at full strength. It values the ledger, illustrates the instrument, issues no demand.

detail.abstract: Does a widening gap between company revenue and staff expense per employee provide evidence of declining rent-sharing? We examine how reporting selection and sector composition affect that inference, as a follow-up to Acemoglu, He, and le Maire's Eclipse of Rent-Sharing. We assemble 7,000 company-years for 695 firms over 2015-2025. In a fixed sample of 75 staffexpense reporters, nominal revenue per employee rises 83.6%, while staff expense per employee rises 51.0%. The pooled expense-to-revenue ratio falls, but the pattern is concentrated in financial firms; among the other 25 reporters, aggregate staff expense per employee grows slightly faster than aggregate revenue per employee. These accounting measures identify neither real productivity nor the allocation of its gains between labor and capital. A separate audit of the original paper's reported estimates finds that some US output effects remain imprecisely estimated, while several Danish estimates support tighter bounds. The fitted reporting-probability model exhibits concentrated weights, substantial two-group imbalance and sectors without reporters; it does not justify generalizing payroll results. We extend the original study's measurement discussion to public-company accounts and qualify a blanket interpretation of no output effects: precision varies across its estimates. Our sector-dependent accounting results neither confirm nor overturn its causal wage and labor-share findings.

detail.abstract: AI agents operate through software, but the computing infrastructure behind them occupies physical space. Data centers turn that need into investment in buildings, power infrastructure and capacity leased to businesses. This paper examines one economic risk in that investment: how much capacity still needs tenants as construction expands? We add vacant operating capacity to unleased construction, using CBRE aggregates covering eight primary U.S. markets. The data cover commercial data centers broadly and do not isolate AI demand. Between H1 2025 and H1 2026, construction rose from 64.3% to 68.6% of operating stock, while this uncommitted-capacity indicator fell from 18.1% to 14.8%. Absolute uncommitted capacity nevertheless increased from approximately 1,478 to 1,619 MW. If commitments covering approximately 5.9% of preleased capacity were lost, the exposure ratio would return to its H1 2025 level. This calculation holds the H1 2026 pipeline and vacancy fixed and assumes no replacement leases. The contribution is a transparent measure of contractual exposure and its retention threshold. The indicator combines capacity available at different dates and does not forecast vacancy or estimate cancellation probabilities.

title: Plymouth Rock Landed on US The American Dream

detail.abstract: This paper develops a forensic accounting of Foundational Black America. It uses Foundational Black Americans (FBA) as a manuscript-defined hemispheric lineage category: Black peoples formed in the Americas through Atlantic-world racial hereditary chattel slavery and the post-emancipation orders that followed it. Under this usage, descendants of U.S. slavery are one national branch of a larger foundational population that also includes distinct Haitian, Jamaican and wider Caribbean, Afro-Cuban, Afro-Brazilian, Afro-Colombian, Afro-Mexican, Black Seminole/Mascogo, and other chattel-descended American branches. The term does not claim that those peoples are one culture, one nationality, one political community, or holders of one identical legal claim. It identifies a shared historical formation produced by the Atlantic chattel system and then divided by imperial and national borders. The paper's central accounting proposition is structural: Black freedom repeatedly arrived with the bill still attached. Different governments ended slavery differently. None of those endings restored the balance sheet to the people slavery had dispossessed. In the United States, formerly enslaved people generally received no compensation for generations of stolen labor. In the British Caribbean, the state compensated slaveowners while the formerly enslaved received no equivalent payment. Haiti defeated slavery and colonial rule and then spent generations carrying an independence indemnity that transferred wealth outward. Brazil abolished slavery without the abolition law redistributing the accumulated property of the slave economy to the people whose labor had produced it. Black Seminoles could cross into Mexico to escape the danger of re-enslavement, but escape from ownership was not compensation for what had already been taken. The mechanisms differ. The unsettled account is the common inheritance. The manuscript therefore does not begin as a reparations debtor directory. Creditor and debtor identity matter when a specific injury is assigned to a specific state, institution, firm, legal successor, or beneficiary, but that inquiry comes after the larger structure is visible: labor taken; people converted to property; freedom eventually recognized; accumulated value left elsewhere; descendants inheriting the remainder. The paper's deepest legal and family archive remains the United States, where the analysis follows racial violence, emancipation, Reconstruction, Jim Crow, labor, culture, invention, civil-rights architecture, and contemporary institutional conflict. The four distinctions used throughout are not merely methodological cautions. They are a recurrence map for changing mechanisms: legal status is not lived condition; continuity is not identity; access is not power; and injury and repair operate on different clocks. Bounded histories from the author's Spinks/Burford, Dickerson/Bucktrout, and Jackson/Bowden/Webster lines appear as one U.S. family ledger inside that hemispheric account. The manuscript distinguishes repair from settlement. Institutions can correct a record, compensate an injury, reopen access, recognize a person, restore property, or create a reparative program; those actions may be real repairs. They do not, merely by occurring, prove that the accumulated account has been settled. Keywords: Foundational Black Americans (FBA); Foundational Black America; Black peoples of the Americas; racial hereditary chattel slavery; Atlantic-world racial chattel slavery; hemispheric unsettled ledger; Caribbean slavery; Haitian independence indemnity; Black Seminoles; Mascogos; Reconstruction; sharecropping; Jim Crow; civil rights; reparations; capital memory; intergenerational injury; window of repair; repair and settlement.

detail.abstract: How robust is the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT)-the most widely used instrument for evaluating creativity in experimental research-to external factors that may bias raters' judgments? We address this question through a laboratory experiment in which 134 subjects evaluate the creativity of drawings produced by children, under three experimental manipulations: order of presentation, dominant drawing style norm, and communication between raters. Our results confirm the robustness of the CAT at the aggregate level: none of the three factors significantly alters overall creativity scores. However, we identify two sources of bias at the individual level: drawings presented in first positions tend to be overrated, and communication leads to underrating drawings that are already below average in creativity. Given the widespread use of CAT-like procedures in contexts ranging from academic research to the evaluation of public funding proposals, understanding and controlling these sources of bias has direct practical implications.

detail.abstract: Supercritical water liquefaction (SCWL) is a promising route for converting polyolefin waste into oil refinery-range hydrocarbon products, but process-scale evaluation remains limited. This study developed an Aspen Plus model for the continuous SCWL of polypropylene (PP) using a staged CSTR-PFR configuration based on a semi-continuous experimental rig. The product oil was represented using TBP-derived oil refinery pseudo-components, and PP degradation was described using a cascade kinetic degradation model. The Aspen Plus model was validated against two semi-continuous experimental runs. The combined validation gave a mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.21 wt.%, root mean square error (RMSE) of 3.14 wt.%, and R 2 of 0.9585 across 12 lump-condition pairs, demonstrating good agreement between experimental and simulated product distributions. Sensitivity analysis showed that the PFR is the main product-shaping unit, with temperature, residence time, water feed rate, and reactor geometry controlling the redistribution of heavy oil fractions towards kerosene-and naphtharange compounds. Energy analysis showed that reactor-effluent heat recovery reduced the external utility target from 24.5 to 4.31 kW, corresponding to an 82.4% reduction in external utility demand. On a product basis, the external thermal requirement decreased from 10.4 MJ kg-1 to 1.8 MJ kg-1 for refinery-range oil. Preliminary economic analysis at a 10,000 tpa PP basis gave a total capital estimate of £26.8M, with the high-pressure reaction section dominating the capital structure. Overall, the results show that continuous PP SCWL is technically promising, but scale-up depends strongly on controlled reactor severity, heat integration, high-pressure equipment design, and downstream product recovery.

detail.abstract: Seafarer Recruitment and Placement Services (SRPS) play a key role in the global shipping industry by linking seafarers with shipowners and ensuring compliance with employment standards. In labor-supplying countries such as Myanmar and China, SRPS agencies are essential for facilitating overseas employment, verifying seafarer qualifications, and protecting seafarers' rights. However, differences in legal design, administrative capacity, enforcement mechanisms, and dispute-resolution procedures affect the practical effectiveness of SRPS governance. Therefore, this study provides a comparative analysis of SRPS systems in China and Myanmar, focusing on legal frameworks, administrative control, civil obligations, and compliance with the Maritime Labor Convention (MLC), 2006, particularly Regulation 1.4 and Standard A1.4. The study examines two core dimensions of an effective SRPS system: administrative supervision and civil protection of seafarers' rights. Based on these comparative findings, the study recommends targeted legal and institutional reforms, especially for Myanmar, while also highlighting the need for greater consistency and clarity in China's SRPS regulatory framework. The study contributes to strengthening SRPS governance, improving MLC 2006 compliance, and enhancing the protection of seafarers' rights in the international maritime labor market.

detail.abstract: This chapter focuses on legal but illegitimate aggressive tax planning as the most controversial component of tax advisory work. Aggressive tax-planning arrangements comply with the letter but not with the spirit of the law. They reduce governments' capacities to provide goods and services to sustain society at the expense of distributive justice and public trust. Tax advisers are often involved in these tax minimization arrangements. However, tax advisers are gatekeepers of the integrity of the tax system. They may also be lawyers, gatekeepers of the rule of law, and as such be regulated by law. Three kinds of obligations will be distinguished: legal obligations, such as reporting obligations, professional ethical obligations, laid down in tax advisers' codes of conduct, and societal or moral expectations, voiced by civil society, politicians and institutional investors, concerning the payment of a fair share of tax. Professional ethical codes have recently internalized some of these expectations although they do not contain any strict requirements in this regard.

detail.abstract: Agricultural-residue burning in northwestern India is a recurring environmental and resource-management problem, particularly during the post-monsoon rice-harvesting period. The contribution of crop-residue burning (CRB) to Delhi-NCR particulate pollution is not, however, a fixed percentage; it varies with meteorology, emission timing, source region, and attribution methodology, and recent studies report substantially different estimates. At the same time, agricultural residue should not be treated exclusively as an environmental liability: paddy straw is a lignocellulosic feedstock for biomass pellets, briquettes, bioenergy, compressed biogas, biochar, pyrolysis, and other industrial applications, and Indian policy has increasingly attempted to build markets for agricultural residue, including supply-chain support and mandatory biomass utilisation in coal-based thermal power generation. This paper reframes stubble burning as a resource-market and supply-chain coordination problem rather than solely as a pollution problem, examining why a large, seasonal, and spatially dispersed residue resource does not automatically become a reliable industrial commodity. The analysis combines peer-reviewed literature and policy evidence with illustrative, non-attributable observations drawn from the author's general professional exposure to agricultural-residue feasibility work in Punjab; no project-specific, client-identifiable, or confidential figures are used or reproduced. The paper argues that the binding constraint is not physical biomass availability alone but the conversion of seasonal, dispersed residue into continuously available, quality-controlled, commercially deliverable feedstock. A five-layer availability framework-gross, surplus, collectible, economically deliverable, and market-compatible residue-is developed, together with a proposed Feedstock Diversion Efficiency (FDE) metric. The study concludes that aggregation, storage, logistics, quality assurance, and offtake contracting deserve treatment as investable infrastructure rather than secondary operational functions.

detail.abstract: Economics has developed rich but partly separate literatures on how information is generated, transmitted, interpreted, and incorporated into market outcomes. This paper organizes these literatures around the life cycle of an economic signal-production, transmission, processing and use, and allocation-and introduces informational distance as a compact representation of the downstream coordination environment. Informational distance is defined as D = B/K, where B is coordination burden and K is coordination capacity. Holding a surviving signal and informational domain fixed, greater informational distance increases the divergence of decentralized allocation from the competitive benchmark. The framework therefore separates signal informativeness from signal coordination sufficiency: a price or other scalar can remain observable and informative while becoming less able to coordinate action near the benchmark. A scalar-coordination corollary shows that, for a fixed tolerance, the informational domain over which a scalar remains coordination-sufficient contracts as D rises. The framework provides a common downstream criterion for comparing heterogeneous informational frictions without treating them as equivalent and highlights the roles of institutions, screening, verification, and other forms of coordination capacity.

detail.abstract:
AI-enabled and digitally coordinated litigation can improve legal research, evidence organisation, claimant communication, medical-record review, collective redress, and access to justice. It can also make unreliable factual narratives, opaque referral relationships, questionable medical or billing patterns, automated demand practices, and settlement pressure faster, more scalable, and more difficult to examine. Civil justice institutions therefore require a structured method for distinguishing legitimate coordination from arrangements that require enhanced scrutiny or may present serious integrity concerns, without treating technology use, claimant organisation, litigation funding, or collective representation as inherently improper.

Building on the author’s earlier proposal, The Civil Justice Integrity Screening Framework for Litigation Abuse and Institutional Accountability, this article develops the AI-Adapted Civil Justice Integrity Screening Framework for AI-enabled and digitally coordinated litigation environments. The related article, Algorithmic Litigation Finance and Civil Justice Market Integrity, addresses the distinct financial and market-integrity issues associated with AI-enabled litigation funding, valuation, portfolio strategy, settlement prediction, and funder influence. The present article focuses on evidentiary integrity, medical necessity and independence, referral-network transparency, funding and control risk, litigation purpose, settlement distortion, claimant voice, and access-to-justice protection.

The article applies qualitative legal-institutional framework development, integrating doctrinal legal analysis, comparative policy analysis, institutional integrity theory, procedural justice, responsive regulation, sociotechnical AI governance, and access-to-justice balancing. It proposes the AI Civil Justice Integrity Screening Test and the AI-Adapted Litigation Integrity Matrix, which organise assessment into three provisional classifications: legitimate coordination, high-risk coordination, and potentially abusive coordination. These classifications are reviewer-assigned screening judgments rather than findings of fraud, abuse, liability, sanctions, professional misconduct, illegality, or civil RICO liability.

The prospectively registered companion protocol, Validation Protocol for the AI-Adapted Civil Justice Integrity Screening Framework, specifies the methodology for evaluating framework clarity, content validity, feasibility, reviewer agreement, proportionality, international adaptability, access-to-justice protection, and implementation readiness. A complete clickable working prototype of the Civil Justice Integrity Screening System (CJISS) and a confidential technical implementation specification for the Human-Supervised Litigation Integrity Screening Model have already been developed as integral components of the same research programme. The framework, screening test, and matrix will first undergo stakeholder validation. The resulting evidence will confirm or refine the concepts, indicators, classifications, safeguards, and review pathways already represented in the prototype. The refined prototype will then undergo controlled model testing, initially with synthetic, public, anonymised, or permission-based materials and later with real documents only where lawful access, applicable ethics approval or exemption, confidentiality and privilege protections, privacy and security requirements, and appropriate data-governance arrangements are in place.

detail.abstract:
This research paper is written by Douglas W. Arner (University of Hong Kong/University of Cambridge/Queen Mary University of London) and Christine Menglu Wang (National University of Singapore).

The rapid development and increasing accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are transforming finance. In many respects, the financial sector has led AI use (in some cases, for over two decades), not least in the context of trading and risk-management activities. Financial institutions are accelerating AI adoption to increase operational efficiency, improve risk management, and enhance their business activities. In terms of risk management, regulatory compliance, and supervisory monitoring, AI is already being widely used by both industry and regulators, improving the soundness and safety of financial markets. However, the increasing use of AI exposes the financial sector to a range of challenges and risks.

In this paper, we analyse approaches to AI governance in finance. Following an analysis of the use of AI in finance, we first present a new taxonomy of governance and regulatory approaches based on a framework of five main elements: strategy, approach, scope, framework, and technology, derived from analysis of evolving practices across the world. Second, we develop a new analytical framework and taxonomy for the major categories of AI risk and governance across five main risk areas: macro risks, micro or sectoral risks, infrastructure risks, malicious actor and behaviour risks, and culture and human capital risks. We conclude the paper by framing the core elements of strategic approaches in terms of the development and governance of AI in finance, based on these twin taxonomies, focusing on strategy, infrastructure, regulatory approaches, the use of technology for regulatory and supervisory purposes, and the importance of developing the wider ecosystem.

detail.abstract: There is an unexplored dimension of media pluralism in the digital platform economy, namely the coexistence of multiple governance modes across the socio-technical arrangements through which news and content are produced and circulate. This dimension of pluralism is at risk when a single, top-down, centralized governance logic prevails, as is the case with the few big tech companies that control the framing operations that prepare and format transactions and content circulation in social media and the media sector. After demonstrating that new EU regulations are limited by a supply-demand market epistemology that fails to address this dimension of pluralism, the paper proposes-drawing on open and federated protocol initiatives-a policy approach in which interoperability obligations and targeted industrial policy are grounded in a pluralism-throughgovernance framework. Lastly, the paper proposes a resourceegalitarian distribution of governance power that enables the contestability of the hegemonic framings currently shaping the digital public space.

publicationDetails.detailsText: NHH Dept. of Economics Discussion Paper No. 12/2026

detail.abstract: When decision-makers allocate resources between anonymous others, with their own payoffs held constant, own-payoff utility maximization places no restriction on behavior; consistent structure in choices therefore reveals a normative principle. We employ a graphical budget line design to elicit allocations of real money between two anonymous others across many budget sets that vary the relative prices of redistribution. Choices overwhelmingly satisfy the axioms of rational choice, revealing individual normative principles. Subjects reveal a widely shared principle of impartiality (symmetric treatment of the two recipients) but hold heterogeneous views about the best symmetric allocation, ranging from Rawlsian equality to utilitarian efficiency.

detail.abstract:
This research paper is written by Wenqian Huang (Bank for International Settlements), Natalia Rostova (EDHEC Business School) and Zhaogang Song (Johns Hopkins University).

The paper examines decentralized exchanges (DEXs) like Curve that specialize in stablecoin trading, which co-exist with centralized exchanges (CEXs) like Binance. We develop a simple model of stablecoin trading in which a DEX uses a low-convexity bonding curve to determine trading prices, liquidity traders choose between the DEX and CEX conditional on trade size, and an arbitrageur trades to profit from price staleness when the stablecoin experiences a depeg shock. Using trade-level data of stablecoins, we empirically confirm the implications of the model’s main economic mechanism—the price impact is lower on the DEX than on the CEX—for liquidity traders’ venue choice, arbitrage trading volume, and deviations from the peg. Our analyses inform the market design of stablecoin trading with respect to maintaining its price peg.

title: Regression Discontinuity and the Price Effects of Stock Market Indexing
affiliations: National Taiwan University - Department of Finance, Columbia University, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Department of Economics and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance

detail.title: Regression Discontinuity and the Price Effects of Stock Market Indexing
detail.abstract: Studies find price increases for additions to the S&P 500 index but no decreases for deletions. Additions come with good earnings news, suggesting these studies are not just measuring an indexing effect. We develop a regression discontinuity design using Russell Indices for cleaner identification. Stocks are assigned to indices based on their end-of-May market capitalizations. Stocks ranked just below 1000 are in the Russell 2000. The indices are value-weighted so these stocks receive index buying whereas those just above 1000 have close to none. Using this random assignment, we find price effects for both additions and deletions.

title: U.S. Investment in Global Bonds: As the Fed Pushes, Some EMEs Pull
affiliations: Loyola University Maryland - Department of Economics, Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research (IGIDR), University of Virginia - Darden Business School and Darden Business School

detail.title: U.S. Investment in Global Bonds: As the Fed Pushes, Some EMEs Pull
detail.abstract: We analyze reallocations within the international bond portfolios of US investors. The most striking empirical observation is a steady increase in US investors' allocations toward emerging market local currency bonds, unabated by the global financial crisis and accelerating in the post-crisis period. Part of the increase in EME allocations is associated with global "push" factors such as low US long-term interest rates and unconventional monetary policy as well as subdued risk aversion/expected volatility. But also evident is investor differentiation among EMEs, with the largest reallocations going to those EMEs with strong macroeconomic fundamentals such as more positive current account balances, less volatile inflation, and stronger economic growth. We also provide a descriptive analysis of global bond markets' structure and returns.

title: Is It Harder for Older Workers to Find Jobs? New and Improved Evidence from a Field Experiment
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics, Stockholm University - Swedish Institute for Social Research (SOFI) and Tulane University, Department of Economics

detail.title: Is It Harder for Older Workers to Find Jobs? New and Improved Evidence from a Field Experiment
detail.abstract: We design and implement a large-scale field experiment – a resume correspondence study – to address a number of potential limitations of existing field experiments testing for age discrimination, which may bias their results.  One limitation that may bias these studies towards finding discrimination is the practice of giving older and younger applicants similar experience in the job to which they are applying, making them “otherwise comparable.”  The second limitation arises because greater unobserved differences in human capital investment of older applicants may bias existing field experiments against finding age discrimination.  We also study ages closer to retirement than in past studies, and use a richer set of job profiles for older workers to test for differences associated with transitions to less demanding jobs (“bridge jobs”) at older ages.  Based on evidence from over 40,000 job applications, we find robust evidence of age discrimination in hiring against older women, especially those near retirement age.  But we find that there is considerably less evidence of age discrimination against men after correcting for the potential biases this study addresses.

detail.abstract:
This research paper is written by Keith Jin Deng Chan The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Yizhou Huang The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) and Wilson Tsz Shing Wan (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology).

This paper investigated how issuer-level greenwashing risks affect the pricing of carbon risks for publicly listed green bond issuers in the Asian region—the world’s largest source of greenhouse gas emissions. Based on a novel panel dataset of 144 green bond issuers and 2005–2023 GHG emissions and environmental expenditure data, the analysis confirmed a positive, albeit modest, carbon risk premium: firms with high GHG emissions intensities tend to have greater expected stock returns because investors incorporate carbon risks into their valuations. Crucially, this premium is more pronounced among firms that make few green efforts, highlighting the significant role of greenwashing risks in the accumulation of carbon risks. The study further showed that institutional investors play a critical role in the pricing of carbon risks, whereas banks appear to incorporate greenwashing considerations into their lending decisions. These results have direct implications for policymakers and investors, highlighting the importance of continuous incentives and disclosure requirements to promote environmental expenditures and support low-carbon transitions in Asian financial markets. This study expands the literature by offering new insights into carbon risk pricing and the role of environmental expenditures in this underexplored region.

title: The Effect of State Taxes on the Geographical Location of Top Earners: Evidence from Star Scientists
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco

detail.title: The Effect of State Taxes on the Geographical Location of Top Earners: Evidence from Star Scientists
detail.abstract: Using data on the universe of U.S. patents filed between 1976 and 2010, we quantify how sensitive is migration by star scientist to changes in personal and business tax differentials across states. We uncover large, stable, and precisely estimated effects of personal and corporate taxes on star scientists’ migration patterns. The long run elasticity of mobility relative to taxes is 1.6 for personal income taxes, 2.3 for state corporate income tax and -2.6 for the investment tax credit. The effect on mobility is small in the short run, and tends to grow over time. We find no evidence of pre-trends: Changes in mobility follow changes in taxes and do not to precede them. Consistent with their high income, star scientists migratory flows are sensitive to changes in the 99th percentile marginal tax rate, but are insensitive to changes in taxes for the median income. As expected, the effect of corporate income taxes is concentrated among private sector inventors: no effect is found on academic and government researchers. Moreover, corporate taxes only matter in states where the wage bill enters the state’s formula for apportioning multi-state income. No effect is found in states that apportion income based only on sales (in which case labor’s location has little or no effect on the tax bill). We also find no evidence that changes in state taxes are correlated with changes in the fortunes of local firms in the innovation sector in the years leading up to the tax change. Overall, we conclude that state taxes have significant effect of the geographical location of star scientists and possibly other highly skilled workers. While there are many other factors that drive when innovative individual and innovative companies decide to locate, there are enough firms and workers on the margin that relative taxes matter.

detail.abstract: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), enacted in 2005 and implemented from February 2006, is one of India's largest rights-based social protection programmes. This paper presents a quantitative review of MGNREGA's performance across its enforcement architecture, coverage, wage delivery, and asset creation, drawing on primary data from the Ministry of Rural Development's public dashboard, the Economic Survey 2022-23, Ministry of Labour and Employment wage notifications, and Press Information Bureau releases. The paper documents the Act's three-tier implementation structure, its conformity with international right-to-work instruments including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, and its uptake trajectory since 2013-14, including the rising share of women in person-days worked (from 52.8 percent in 2013-14 to 59 percent in 2023-24). It identifies three principal implementation gaps: the shortfall between the 100-day guarantee and the 43 average person-days delivered per household in 2023-24, the widening gap between MGNREGA wages and the statutory agricultural minimum wage, and the accumulation of Rs 6,572 crore in delayed wages in 2023-24. The paper closes with suggestions on wage revision, coverage expansion, and financing options. The analysis reflects data available as of December 2023 and does not incorporate subsequent developments including revised budget allocations or the ongoing debate on Aadhaar-linked payment reforms.

detail.abstract: Historic numismatic items are one of the oldest collectible asset classes, yet unlike art, stamps, wine, and violins they lack a transaction-based academic price index. Existing coin price series are, at least partially, dealer-quoted, methodologically proprietary, or limited in geographical coverage. We introduce the Global Numismatic Academic Index (GNAI), a purely transaction-based price index for a defined universe of internationally traded historic numismatic items, estimated by hedonic timedummy regression on the pooled panel of auction records. It is estimated from several thousand auction transactions in 77 catalogue-defined coin types, each with a defined grade band, across 163 auction houses over exactly twenty years, from 2006 through 2025. Each quarterly value is identified by that quarter's transactions alone, given type price levels estimated from the full panel, and carries a bootstrap standard error. Over the sample the index compounds at 5.1% per year, with measured annualised volatility of 19.9% and model-implied volatility of 8.2% after correcting for sampling noise. At the quarterly horizon, measured correlations place coins and gold jointly as the least correlated assets in the benchmark set. Whether this correlation structure yields diversification benefits once this market's substantial transaction costs are accounted for is examined in a companion paper. The index is offered as a citable reference object for research on alternative assets.

title: The Global Rise of Corporate Saving
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Global Rise of Corporate Saving
detail.abstract: The sectoral composition of global saving changed dramatically during the last three decades. Whereas in the early 1980s most of global investment was funded by household saving, nowadays nearly two-thirds of global investment is funded by corporate saving. This shift in the sectoral composition of saving was not accompanied by changes in the sectoral composition of investment, implying an improvement in the corporate net lending position. We characterize the behavior of corporate saving using both national income accounts and firm-level data and clarify its relationship with the global decline in labor share, the accumulation of corporate cash stocks, and the greater propensity for equity buybacks. We develop a general equilibrium model with product and capital market imperfections to explore quantitatively the determination of the flow of funds across sectors. Changes including declines in the real interest rate, the price of investment, and corporate income taxes generate increases in corporate profits and shifts in the supply of sectoral saving that are of similar magnitude to those observed in the data.

title: Federated Transfer Learning for SME Credit Risk using BayesShield and Paillier Encryption

detail.title: Federated Transfer Learning for SME Credit Risk using BayesShield and Paillier Encryption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: The assessment of credit risk for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) presents a significant challenge in the financial sector, primarily due to these entities' characteristic lack of extensive credit histories and reliance on non-standardized, alternative data. Traditional machine learning models are often ineffective in this sparse data environment, and the fragmented nature of SME data across various financial institutions prevents the development of robust, centralized models due to stringent data privacy regulations. This research proposes a novel framework that synergistically combines Federated Transfer Learning (FTL), a privacy-preserving Bayesian neural network (BayesShield), and Paillier homomorphic encryption to address these dual challenges of data scarcity and privacy. The FTL architecture enables collaborative model training across multiple institutions without the need for raw data exchange, leveraging knowledge from a data-rich source domain (e.g., large corporate credit data) to enhance learning in a data-scarce target domain (SME credit risk). To manage the inherent uncertainty in SME financials and provide well-calibrated risk probabilities, the framework integrates BayesShield, a Bayesian neural network that offers robust uncertainty quantification and is resilient to adversarial attacks. Crucially, the security of the entire collaborative learning process is fortified by the integration of Paillier encryption, a fully homomorphic encryption scheme that allows for mathematical operations on ciphertexts. This ensures that all intermediate model updates, gradients, and parameters exchanged during the federated process remain encrypted, preventing any potential information leakage to malicious adversaries or even the central server. By integrating these advanced techniques, our proposed framework not only enhances the predictive accuracy and reliability of SME credit scoring but also establishes a new standard for secure, privacy-preserving collaborative finance, enabling financial inclusion while rigorously complying with data protection regulations such as GDPR and CCPA.

title: Pension Reform and Return to Work Policies
affiliations: Cornell University

detail.title: Pension Reform and Return to Work Policies
detail.abstract: For many people, working after beginning retirement benefit collection is a way to enhance financial security by increasing income.  Existing research has shown that retirees are sensitive to the Social Security earnings test, which restricts the amount of earnings some beneficiaries can receive.  However, little is known about the effects of other types of policies on post-retirement employment.  Instead of restricting earnings, many public pension plans restrict the number of hours beneficiaries can work.  I use return-to-work rules limiting the number of hours of employment in a state’s public pension plan and administrative data on employment and retirement to determine the rules’ effects on retirement decisions and post-retirement labor supply.  I find that the increases in the maximum number of hours of post-retirement employment lead to no change in retirement benefit collection and to increases in part-time work among retirees.  As such, these policies appear to be binding on the labor supply decisions of some employees.  Policymakers should take this into account when designing policies aimed at extending work-lives or improving the health of pension systems.

detail.abstract: The Jakarta Composite Index (IHSG) is a capitalization-weighted benchmark whose largest single block of weight sits in a domestic banking cluster, and whose broader direction has historically been sensitive to foreign portfolio flow and to Indonesia's commodity-export cycle. Generic price-only technical oscillators (Wilder, 1978; Lane, 1984) are agnostic to this structure, using only the index level itself rather than the sub-components that drive it. This paper develops SHIELD (Sulistyardi Hedging Indicator for Equity-Loss Defense), a composite regime-detection oscillator built from momentum measures of three structurally motivated proxies -- the Infobank15 index (domestic banking flow), Telkom Indonesia / TLKM (a foreign-ownership-heavy liquidity proxy for foreign fund flow), and Indo Tambangraya Megah / ITMG (a coal-sector proxy for the commodity cycle) -- and documents a research process, consistent with the backtest-overfitting literature (Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, & Zhu, 2014; Lopez de Prado, 2018), in which an initial specification that jointly optimizes factor weights, a normalization window, and regime thresholds on the full historical sample is shown to be fragile out-of-sample, while fixing factor weights at structurally motivated values and adapting only the regime threshold on a rolling walk-forward schedule (Pardo, 2008) yields a materially more robust specification (out-of-sample Calmar ratio of 3.53 versus -0.12 for buy-and-hold; maximum drawdown of -8.1% versus -41.5%). The paper further reframes SHIELD's intended use from a precision entry-timing signal to a binary risk-off regime filter, and applies the calibrated framework as an exploratory case illustration to the IHSG decline associated with a temporary 2026 suspension of Indonesia's MSCI market-classification status, and to conditions prevailing as of September 2026. An agenda for further controlled validation against a time-series-momentum benchmark (Moskowitz, Ooi, & Pedersen, 2012) and a longer historical sample is proposed.

title: Monetary Policy and Global Banking
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston and Harvard University

detail.title: Monetary Policy and Global Banking
detail.abstract: When central banks adjust interest rates, the opportunity cost of lending in local currency changes, but—in absence of frictions—there is no spillover effect to lending in other currencies. However, when equity capital is limited, global banks must benchmark domestic and foreign lending opportunities. We show that, in equilibrium, the marginal return on foreign lending is affected by the interest rate differential, with lower domestic rates leading to an increase in local lending, at the expense of a reduction in foreign lending. We test our prediction in the context of changes in interest rates in six major currency areas.

title: GDP-B: Accounting for the Value of New and Free Goods in the Digital Economy
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), Carnegie Mellon University, University of British Columbia (UBC), Copenhagen Business School - Department of Marketing and UNSW Australia Business School, School of Economics

detail.title: GDP-B: Accounting for the Value of New and Free Goods in the Digital Economy
detail.abstract: The welfare contributions of the digital economy, characterized by the proliferation of new and free goods, are not well-measured in our current national accounts. We derive explicit terms for the welfare contributions of these goods and introduce a new metric, GDP-B which quantifies their benefits, rather than costs. We apply this framework to several empirical examples including Facebook and smartphone cameras and estimate their valuations through incentive compatible choice experiments. For example, including the welfare gains from Facebook would have added between 0.05 and 0.11 percentage points to GDP-B growth per year in the US.

detail.abstract: Since 2025, the AI-economy sectors of the Chinese A-share market have held elevated valuations while traditional sectors stayed depressed. The two sides have diverged in valuation position and stayed diverged. This paper names that state persistent structural tearing and asks three questions: whether it can be measured, whether it is a persistent state rather than a passing dislocation, and whether it leads deep drawdowns. Using the Bit-Watt industry framework we isolate 525 core names (set P) and split 110 self-constructed industries into 35 technology and 75 traditional ones. Over the 642 trading days from 2024-01-01 to 2026-08-26 we measure each side against its own historical valuation ceiling and take the difference, written gap. Three findings follow. First, tearing is measurable, and it is a state that formed in 2025 rather than a gradual drift: the share of days on which technology is the richer side jumps from 34.3% to 86.4%. Second, tearing precedes drawdowns instead of propagating through industry tiers: gap forecasts at AUC 0.7440 while it detects at only 0.3912, and core and periphery drawdowns peak at zero lag. Third, detection and forecasting need the same quantities with opposite signs, so a single combined score cancels itself. We therefore split the system into detection, severity and lead-warning layers. On the 6 severe episodes it detects 6/6, classifies 6/6 as critical with no false criticals, and the lead-warning layer reaches AUC 0.8749. Every threshold is calibrated by leave-one-episode-out cross-validation. Data and code are released with the paper.

title: Infrared and Visible Image Fusion Method Based on Frequency-Domain Feature Interaction Network

detail.title: Infrared and Visible Image Fusion Method Based on Frequency-Domain Feature Interaction Network
detail.abstract: Infrared–visible image fusion (IVIF) aims to integrate salient thermal targets from infrared images with rich structural and textural details from visible images. However, many existing deep learning-based methods mainly operate in the spatial domain and lack explicit mechanisms to model cross-modal frequency characteristics, which may lead to structural smoothing or artifact amplification during feature aggregation. To address the above limitations, this paper presents a structured frequency-decoupled fusion framework, termed Cross-Modal Frequency-Decoupled Interaction Network (CFDI-Net), which integrates explicit frequency decomposition, staged representation learning, and bandspecific cross-modal interaction into a unified design. The proposed framework adopts a twostage training strategy. In the first stage, a DWT-based frequency-decoupled reconstruction framework decomposes features into low-frequency structural components and high-frequency detail components, enabling stable band-specific representation learning. In the second stage, a frequency-decoupled cross-modal interaction module (FDCI) performs selective interaction in the decoupled frequency space. The low-frequency branch employs an infrared-guided crossmodal attention mechanism with gated relation fusion to enhance structural alignment and thermal target saliency, while the high-frequency branch preserves modality-specific details through preference-aware aggregation and reduces cross-modal interference. Experiments on the TNO and RoadScene datasets demonstrate that CFDI-Net achieves more balanced performance in cross-modal consistency, structural fidelity, and thermal target saliency compared with several state-of-the-art methods. The source code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open. science/r/CFDI-Net-13FF/.

detail.abstract: Recommender Systems (RSs) have become increasingly important across multiple domains by assisting people in navigating the growing burden of excessive information. Recently, driven by the remarkable competences of Large Language Models (LLMs) to understand and generate natural language, LLM-based RSs (LLMRSs) have developed into a new paradigm. However, the inherent limitations of LLMs, like unfairness, have also surfaced and may even be further amplified in LLMRSs, exposing LLMRSs to various trustworthiness-related threats. Although Trustworthy LLM-based RSs (TLLMRSs) have attracted growing attention, there remains no comprehensive review of this realm. There is a lack of a general problem formulation and an in-depth understanding of the challenges confronted by TLLMRSs. It's still not fully clear how these challenges have been solved, and what the major application scenarios and future research directions of TLLMRSs are. To fill these gaps, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of TLLMRSs. Specifically, we first summarize its core trustworthiness aspects and present a general problem formulation for TLLMRSs, examine the unique challenges of each trustworthiness aspect, and then propose a taxonomy of representative approaches for addressing these challenges. Finally, we discuss typical application domains and outline promising research chances in this active area.

detail.abstract: A reported t-statistic's evidential denominator turns on whether disclosed fields determine a target within tolerance. The identification diameter of a package is the spread of the target across worlds sharing its public record. A package is sufficient exactly when it meets the separating vector of every conflicting pair of worlds, so sufficient packages are the hitting sets of a conflict hypergraph, with the minimal and minimum-cardinality families identified the same way. The raw material for the whole table is one pass over pairs sharing a base record. An empty separating vector certifies in one line that no package suffices at that tolerance. The midpoint rule attains worst-case error half the diameter and is minimax among rules reading the public record.

detail.abstract: Gender equality being a fundamental human right, is deprived for women. Though India is a country which considers women as goddesses, it still restricts them to have a voice of their own. Globalisation expanding and stretching its wings farther and wider in India rarely considers working women as a means of economic growth. Women are limited to domestic chores; few have means to financial independence. The idea of working women is a rare phenomenon. The imbalances of this deprived class in our economy is numerous. In classical economics, full employment of resources give rise to optimum levels of output and profits. Ignoring the potential of 8 million unemployed women according to CMIE Dec 2021, will create a huge opportunity cost. If women are to fully utilize their potential, then it is important to give them the opportunity to do so. Kerala's State Poverty Eradication Mission-Kudumbashree has cogitated to make women arise from the traditional gender inequality, re-emphasize and find a way to live life independently and to take care of their family whilst being economically productive. This research focuses on finding the success rate of this mission in empowering women involved in it. To empirically prove the above, statistical measures have been used to analyze data, collected mainly through survey forms. The results of our study shows that Kudumbashree has certainly led to women empowerment in the society by providing training in enterprise development, microfinance credit, raising awareness on rights, health and nutrition requirements, and so on. This intervention strategy used by the Kerala Government is a universal strategy which could be followed in other states and countries and thereby reflect a ray of hope for a society to be built on the foundations of gender equality.

title: Is There a Universal Prognostic Transition to Persistent Critical Illness? A Multicenter Landmark Study With Independent Health-System Replication

detail.title: Is There a Universal Prognostic Transition to Persistent Critical Illness? A Multicenter Landmark Study With Independent Health-System Replication
detail.abstract: ObjectiveTo determine whether a prognostic transition to persistent critical illness remains identifiable when physiologic and organ-support state is updated before each ICU landmark rather than fixed at episode entry.DesignRetrospective daily landmark study with multicenter discovery, independent single-health-system concept replication, and cluster-resampled simultaneous inference; updated-state analyses were post-primary and non-rescue.SettingTwo deidentified United States critical care databases: eICU Collaborative Research Database v2.0 and Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV v3.1.PatientsAdults alive, hospitalized, and continuously in a core ICU episode at completed ICU days 3-14.InterventionsNone.Measurements and Main ResultsAntecedent predisposition was compared with the same clinical-state concepts measured during episode hours 0-24 and then fixed, or during the 24 hours preceding each landmark. The outcome was in-hospital death within 14 days after the landmark and before live discharge. Paired out-of-fold log-loss differences used hospital-cluster inference in eICU and patient-cluster inference in MIMIC-IV. Day-3 risk sets included 46,182 eICU episodes from 203 hospitals and 24,185 MIMIC-IV episodes. At day 10, predisposition-minus-fixed-state differences were 0.0060 (simultaneous 95% CI, -0.0010 to 0.0130) and 0.0126 (0.0033 to 0.0220), respectively; predisposition-minus-updated-state differences were -0.0360 (-0.0471 to -0.0249) and -0.0387 (-0.0543 to -0.0230). Every updated-state interval was below zero through day 14. eICU nominated no fixed-state transition; MIMIC-IV showed an aggregate fixed-state run beginning on day 5, but settings and predictor definitions disagreed. The updated-state pattern persisted after removing Glasgow Coma Scale and/or missingness indicators, using gradient boosting, and excluding documented treatment limitation at episode entry.ConclusionsThe apparent prognostic crossover depended on comparing predisposition with an aging admission snapshot. Within the studied predictor representations, the data did not support a universal onset through ICU day 14.

detail.abstract: Background: Bank transaction descriptions, the short strings that appear on bank feeds and statements, lack the grammatical structure that named entity recognition (NER) systems are normally built and benchmarked on. Standard architectures trained on news-style corpora such as CoNLL-2003 or OntoNotes lean heavily on syntactic and capitalization cues, and most of that signal is absent from strings composed of merchant codes, truncated payee names, and payment processor identifiers. Objective: We examine why general-purpose NER underperforms on financial transaction text and develop a practitioner-oriented framework for choosing among three architecture classes under realistic labeled-data constraints: a general-purpose transformer fine-tuned on a small domain sample, a transformer continually pretrained on financial text, and a lightweight, structurally aware span-matching architecture in the GLiNER family. Methods: The framework grew out of applied implementation experience with an entity resolution component for transaction text categorization. We compare the three architecture classes along four axes (robustness to non-grammatical input, labeledsample efficiency, entity boundary determinism, and computational cost), together with an explicit boundary annotation protocol, rather than reducing the comparison to a single benchmark score. Results: Structurally aware architectures that exploit positional regularities in transaction strings showed a qualitative advantage on boundary disambiguation and labeled-sample efficiency, while general-purpose fine-tuning remained competitive only when labeled data was relatively abundant. A complementary human-preference evaluation comparing rule-based and learned extraction on a related payee string selection task (195 decisive comparisons) found a numerical but not statistically significant overall preference for the learned approach (53.8% versus 46.2%, exact sign test, p = 0.32), alongside a statistically significant reduction in retained process-language boilerplate and in output length (p < 0.0001 for both). Conclusion: Architecture selection for non-grammatical financial text should prioritize structural fit over benchmark leaderboard rank, and entity boundary annotation conventions deserve as much methodological attention as the choice of model.

title: Biomass and Mineral Nutrient Accumulation in Hydroponic Cress under Varying Levels of Magnesium Fertilization

detail.title: Biomass and Mineral Nutrient Accumulation in Hydroponic Cress under Varying Levels of Magnesium Fertilization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: ### Declaration of Interest Statement The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Cresses are nutrient-dense brassicas. Despite recent studies on their phytonutrient and mineral content, the influence of magnesium fertilization on their mineral and biomass accumulation remains understudied. In this study, five magnesium fertilization rates: 24.3 (control treatment), 100, 150, 200, and 250 mg•L 21 were applied to watercress (Nasturtium officinale) and upland cress (Barbarea verna) in a controlled greenhouse hydroponic environment. A nutrient film technique hydroponic system was used under a split-plot design. The study aimed to examine the effects of magnesium treatments on mineral nutrient accumulation. Inductively coupled plasma emission spectrometry was used to quantify the mineral nutrients. Results indicate that cress variety significantly influenced nutrient accumulation, whereas magnesium fertilization selectively increased potassium (K) (P 5 0.031) and silicon (Si) (P 5 0.016) at 200 mg•L 21 rate, and copper (Cu) (P 5 0.014) at 24.3 mg•L 21. The K and Si concentrations were 1.26 and 2.56 times the control value, respectively, while Cu concentration was 1.27 times the lowest treatment value (at 150 mg•L 21 rate). Upland cress had higher nutrient levels than watercress except for sodium (Na) (P < 0.001), which was 6.3 times higher in watercress. On the other hand, watercress biomass was 2.5 times that of upland cress. These results reveal the importance of optimizing magnesium nutrition and selecting cress varieties for mineral nutrient accumulation in leafy greens.

detail.abstract: This journal examines the pivotal event of August 15, 1971, when U.S. President Richard Nixon closed the "gold window," effectively ending the Bretton Woods system and transitioning the world's money from a gold-backed standard to a fiat currency system— where value rests solely on trust in government. However, this paper goes beyond the standard historical narrative to ask a critical operational question: If gold no longer backs money, what does? Through a personal analytical framework, the author argues that collateral—the assets pledged against bank credit—has become the de facto backing for modern fiat money. Money is not created by government decree alone; it is born through the banking system's credit multiplication, and every unit of credit requires collateral (property, machinery, government bonds, future income). When this collateral base is destabilized, the monetary system itself becomes vulnerable. This thesis is tested against three case studies: 1. Zimbabwe (2008) — where destruction of agricultural collateral through failed land reform triggered hyperinflation 2. Salomon Brothers (1991) — where manipulation of the U.S. Treasury market threatened the primary collateral base of global finance 3. Iran (2025–2026) — where war and sanctions eroded collateral values, accelerating currency collapse The paper concludes that the Nixon Shock did not eliminate the need for monetary backing; it merely transferred that backing from physical gold to the entire productive asset base of the nation—with all its hidden fragilities. This has profound implications for public understanding of money, savings, and systemic risk.

detail.abstract: This study reexamines the effect of adopting a Semi-Autonomous Revenue Authority (SARA) on tax pressure in Sub-Saharan Africa, using a panel of 47 countries (1980-2023, including 19 adopters) that extends the reference window of Dom (2019) by eleven years. A triangulation of three identification strategies-a dynamic GMM replication, three staggered-adoption difference-indifferences estimators (Callaway-Sant'Anna, Sun-Abraham, Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess), and a Bayesian hierarchical event-study model with partial pooling-shows that the null average effect reported in the prior literature reflects a lack of statistical power rather than a genuine absence of effect. All four frequentist methods converge on a positive but nonsignificant effect (p ∈ [0.13, 0.38]), whereas the Bayesian model identifies a credibly positive pooled effect of 0.58 percentage points of GDP (95% CI [0.21, 0.95], P (effect > 0) = 0.999) across treated countries. An analytical and Monte Carlo power analysis confirms this diagnosis. Crosscountry heterogeneity, although theoretically expected, proves contained rather than dominant, and the effect transits mainly through indirect rather than direct revenues. These results are robust to alternative adoption dates, to the exclusion of Zimbabwe, to the addition of time-varying controls (including VAT), to an alternative outcome, and to the sensitivity of Bayesian priors.

detail.abstract: Energy security has traditionally been understood as the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at affordable prices. While this definition remains influential, contemporary energy challenges increasingly demonstrate that energy insecurity is experienced primarily through its effects on people rather than on energy systems alone. Energy disruptions compromise healthcare, water systems, communications, transportation, food security, education, public safety, and economic activity. Consequently, energy security cannot be fully understood solely through supply-side or infrastructure-centered perspectives. This paper advances a normative proposition, referred to here as the proposed framework: "Energy Security is Human Security, and Human Security is Energy Security." Drawing upon traditional energy security literature, the United Nations human security framework, and capability theory as developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum, the paper argues that energy systems should ultimately be evaluated according to their contribution to human well-being, societal resilience, and the preservation of essential human capabilities. The paper builds directly on an existing and closely related body of capability-based energy poverty and vulnerability scholarship-particularly the work of Day, Walker, and Simcock (2016) and Bouzarovski and Petrova (2015)-and seeks to extend the capability lens from householdlevel energy poverty toward system-level energy security, infrastructure planning, and resilience governance. The paper demonstrates that energy security and human security are mutually reinforcing and, in important respects, inseparable dimensions of sustainable development. It further argues that future energy policies, resilience frameworks, and energy transition strategies should place human outcomes more explicitly at the centre of energy security analysis. The framework is offered as a normative, agenda-setting contribution rather than an empirically validated model; its operationalization, including a proposed Global Energy Security Index (GESI), is identified as a direction for future research rather than a settled result.

detail.abstract: We develop limit order book imbalance volatility (LOBIV), which measures high-frequency instability in bid-ask depth imbalance, and document a depth-specific volatility anomaly. Using 10-level LOB data for CSI 300 constituents from 2014 to 2025, we estimate a multivariate log-ACD model. Shallow-book LOBIV shocks reduce contemporaneous realized volatility but predict higher subsequent volatility, whereas deep-book shocks exhibit the reverse pattern. These effects are widespread, robust to alternative recursive orderings and crisis regimes, and evolve smoothly across book levels. Market-wide tests further show that shallow-book LOBIV positively predicts future weekly returns, while deep-book LOBIV predicts them negatively after standard controls.

detail.abstract: Electoral institutions pose two different questions. Which proposals should be under consideration? asks voters to supply direction. Among those under consideration, which should be avoided? asks them to evaluate what has been supplied. Two-round systems pose these in sequence, as a qualification contest followed by an election. This paper develops a rule that poses both on one ballot. In the Fair Voting System, FVS(0.20, 2), each voter may authorize at most one candidate and actively reject at most two. Affirmative marks construct a qualified set from the share of issued authorizations, 𝑆 𝑗 = 𝐴 𝑗 / V > 0.20; active rejections then order the qualified candidates, and the candidate with the lowest rejection rate 𝑅 𝑗 = 𝐷 𝑗 / T wins. The signals are never netted. We prove that within a bounded three-state ballot whose unmarked state carries no imputed content, no qualification function satisfying two weak requirements can be a function of the rejection vector alone; the result is conditional on that design class and is not a general impossibility claim. The paper's principal negative finding concerns the meaning of the negative mark, which an adopting polity must fix in its ballot instructions. Under an aversion reading-mark the candidates you most oppose-a candidate entered solely to absorb rejection capacity, holding two per cent of authorizations and incapable of qualifying, can change the winner; Appendix C gives a closed-form instance. Under an avoidance reading-mark the candidates you most want to prevent from winning-that manipulation is inert, but the rule reduces to plurality within the qualified set whenever four or fewer candidates qualify and voters authorize inside it (Proposition 8), so the negative channel does no independent work in the configurations that recent large-field elections actually produce. Neither reading dominates. The choice is constitutional, not editorial, and the paper states the dilemma rather than resolving it. The French presidential election of 2002 is used as a running case. Applying the gate to that year's official firstpreference distribution returns no qualifier, symmetrically against an incumbent President, an incumbent Prime Minister and a far-right challenger. The paper reports structural results, counterexamples to majority, Condorcet, Condorcet-loser, participation and reinforcement criteria under both readings of the negative mark, and an explicit account of what the rule does not secure.

detail.abstract: Output growth across the advanced economies has slowed and diverged since the mid-1990s. Using the growth-accounting identity Y = H × (Y/H), we adjudicate the leading explanations jointly for twenty OECD economies over 1995–2019 by sorting each onto the margin on which it can act: hours worked or output per hour. Taxation and aging, usually treated as competitors, occupy different margins: the labour tax lowers the level of hours, in the tradition of Prescott, while aging is the most robust correlate of slower output-per-hour growth. The reversed assignment is empirically rejected. The tax-productivity correlation is absorbed once technology is controlled, whereas the aging gradient survives. Because the two margins are orthogonal across countries, the cross-country dispersion partitions cleanly: about a third demographic, a fifth technological, a fifth workforce-and-fiscal, a quarter unexplained. The relationships are cross-sectional; neither aging nor taxation is cleanly causal.

detail.abstract: This study examines how fiscal autonomy affects local government tax choices. I focus on a 2012 Italian reform that replaced national transfers with expected local property tax revenue and expanded municipal discretion over property tax rates. Using a difference-indifferences approach that exploits cross-municipality variation in exposure to the reform, I document three main findings. First, municipalities more affected by the reform increased property tax rates. Second, they also adjusted the broader composition of local taxation by raising personal income tax rates, even though these rates were not directly targeted by the reform. Third, municipalities raised income tax rates more strongly for higher-income individuals while leaving rates for lower-income individuals unchanged, thereby increasing the progressivity of local personal income taxation. Mechanism exercises suggest that these responses are more closely associated with the reform-induced increase in revenue responsibility than with the relaxation of pre-reform property-tax rate constraints.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether corporate insiders' trades that run counter to their political predispositions contain more information. I link corporate insider transactions to individual voter-registration records around six U.S. presidential elections from 2004 through 2024. I find that after elections in which the presidency changes party, opportunistic sales by insiders affiliated with the winning party predict more negative future stock returns than similar sales by insiders affiliated with the losing party. This differential predictability is absent in elections where the incumbent party is reelected, and it survives controls for firm characteristics, lagged returns, firm-level political risk, and trading-day fixed effects. The results suggest that when insiders sell despite receiving a favorable partisan shock, these "trade-against-tribe" sales are less likely to reflect partisan pessimism or other noise and more likely to reveal negative private information.

detail.abstract:
The current electoral college system in the United States is critical to the outcome of the U.S. Presidential System. While there are widely acknowledged flaws in the system, it has been hard to change because alternative systems seem to benefit one party over the other, thus finding resistance from the party that stands to lose from a new system. We propose an alternative path for allocating electoral college votes. Under this system, states adopt an allocation proportional to popular vote, in groups or mini-compacts, ensuring electoral votes gained and lost across compact members offset each other, leaving neither party worse off overall.


Using federal election data from 2000 to 2020, we construct all possible 3-, 4-, and 5-state combinations and assess neutrality on two criteria; balance-change, a measure of how neutral each compact is, and proportional stability, a measure of the impact of the proposed system on overall presidential election outcomes. Our results show a high number of combinations with consistently low balance-change across election cycles. We further find that a majority of combinations are proportional-stable over 2000-2020.


We validate these findings out-of-sample in the 2024 election. Balance-change remained low and persistent and nearly 100% of all combinations were proportional-stable. This suggests proportional allocation within mini-compacts may be a potentially feasible and party-neutral path that preserves historical outcomes while potentially broadening electoral participation. We emphasize that the historical analysis serves as an essential first step for evaluation, but may not necessarily predict future outcomes.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has reopened the socialist calculation debate by weakening constraints once treated as fixed. This paper uses Iain M. Banks's Culture as an institutional thought experiment to ask what follows when prediction can substitute for some transfers of local knowledge. The argument turns on configuration. Prediction matters little for goods that can simply be supplied on request, but more where capacity or shared environments must be set in advance. In those cases, acting on predicted demand can help shape the preferences later observed. Realised demand may then fit more than one account of how those preferences formed, and durable configuration may make some comparisons difficult to recover. The Culture holds together powerful but fallible machine prediction, protected interiority, marginal abundance, configurational constraints, polycentric agency and exit. It therefore clarifies both what AI may weaken in the knowledge problem and what remains difficult on the demand side of planning.

detail.abstract: This study examines how the fragmentation of regulatory authority across federal agencies affects workplace safety in U.S. public firms. Using firm-level measures of regulatory fragmentation and establishment-level Violation Tracker data aggregated to the firm-year level from 2000 to 2024, I find that greater fragmentation is associated with more frequent and severe workplace safety violations. A one-standard-deviation increase in fragmentation corresponds to increases of 10.36% in violations and 8.70% in penalties relative to their respective sample means. To address endogeneity, I exploit the 2016 US presidential election and the ensuing deregulation as a plausibly exogenous shock to regulatory fragmentation. Difference-in-differences estimates show that firms more exposed to fragmentation before the election experienced larger subsequent declines in violations and penalties following the reduction in fragmentation post-election. Channel analyses suggest that weaker organizational safety culture and lower investment in safety are potential mechanisms underlying these effects. The association is stronger for firms operating in higher safety-risk industries, more competitive product markets, lower union representation, and greater workforce adjustment. These findings identify the architecture of regulatory oversight as an important institutional determinant of workplace safety, and inform ongoing policy debates by indicating that streamlining regulatory oversight could meaningfully improve employee wellbeing.
