detail.abstract: This study measured the eco-efficiency of Chinese provinces using the Super-RSBM model based on Chinese provincial panel data from 2005 to 2021. On this basis, this study examines the multifactor linkage effects of government, market and society in the role of improving eco-efficiency using the dynamic fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). In addition, the study analyses the eco-efficiency improvement paths in the eastern, central and western regions separately. The results show that there are regional differences in eco-efficiency among Chinese provinces; the realisation of high eco-efficiency requires the synergistic effect of multiple factors, and no single factor can play an absolute role in the process of realising high ecoefficiency; government regulation is a necessary factor for the realisation of high eco-efficiency in the east-central region, but the situation is reversed in the western region, and market incentives at the national level play an important role in the overall eco-efficiency enhancement; public participation Substitute relationship with government incentives; as the level of economic development increases, the effect of increased urbanisation and market or social integration on eco-efficiency decreases at the margin.

title: The Reach of Institutional Segregation: Evidence from Racially Designated Public Housing
affiliations: Rutgers University and

detail.title: The Reach of Institutional Segregation: Evidence from Racially Designated Public Housing
detail.abstract: Racial segregation in U.S. cities has been partly attributed to institutions that organized housing along racial lines. Focusing on the first racially segregated public housing projects in the U.S., built by the Public Works Administration in the 1930s, we study the effects of such an institution on places and the extent to which those effects persist through the later residential choices of the people it reached. Using full-count Census data and a new set of planned-but-not-built projects as a comparison group, we first show that the projects tilted the racial composition of their sites toward the race of their designation, with little impact beyond its boundaries. We find that the racial exposure created by this shock persisted in households' later residential outcomes. A decade later, after most tenants had returned to the private market, a third of the racial exposure gap the program created for Black tenants remained in the neighborhoods they lived in. Suggestive evidence indicates that nearby residents who moved away also relocated toward the racial composition the project imposed rather than away from it. Our findings provide evidence that a place-based institution can affect segregation beyond the places where it was imposed by shaping the residential trajectories of the households it reaches.

detail.abstract: Randomness in choice can be attributed to many potential mechanisms, including shocks to utility and attention. In a gaze-contingent lottery experiment, we observe attention and choice jointly and provide reduced-form facts that discriminate between these mechanisms. We measure choice reversals and first-order stochastic dominance violations, as well as two margins of attention-extensive (whether an option is seen) and intensive (how long it is examined). Choice 'randomness' is a nearly deterministic function of attention: from the gaze record alone we predict the chosen option in 93% of within-person choice reversals (against a benchmark of 50%), and classify dominated from dominating choices in 95% of repetitions (against a benchmark of 85%). We further show that the extensive margin of attention accounts for well under half of each behavior; behaviors around choice reversals (but not around dominance violations) change at certain gaze thresholds (0.3 seconds, and 0.5 seconds); and attention does not reliably screen out dominated options Moreover, the relationships between attention and both reversals and dominance violations change depending on menu size, but controlling for extensive attention eliminates menu-size effects in reversals while only slightly attenuating them for FOSD violations.

detail.abstract: Third-party monitoring that curbs data falsification can increase the supply of public goods. I show how it can nevertheless distort their allocation. I study China's 2016 transfer of air-quality monitoring to third-party operators, using a multitask Tullock model to examine its effects on urban parks' allocation. Difference-indifferences estimates show that parks' share of supplied land area rises by 1.83 percentage points within 5 kilometers of monitors relative to 20-50 kilometers, accompanied by a relative decline of 0.703 micrograms per cubic meter in satellite-derived PM 2.5. Effects are larger where pre-reform reports suggest more underreporting, among younger officials, and in cities with pollution-reduction targets. Counterfactual analysis shows that reallocating each year's parkland, without changing its total area, raises residents' average benefits from urban parks. Thus, even when third-party monitoring increases the supply of public goods, it may distort their allocation.

detail.abstract: Access to early stage stands as a significant challenge for innovators and inventors in frontier economies such as Ghana. The study examines the role that financial technological platforms play in facilitating inclusive capital formation within the fintech ecosystem of Ghana, through the lens of the Pool prototype. Using a qualitative, exploratory research design, data was collected through semi-structured interviews with innovators, investors and institutional actors involved in digital finance regulation and infrastructure. In order to examine stakeholder perceptions of access to finance, digital trust, regulatory feasibility and platform viability, the study employed thematic analysis. The findings show that while fintech platforms present opportunities for broadening capital access, their effectiveness is shaped by factors such as trust mechanisms, regulatory clarity and stakeholder participation. The study contributes to understanding how fintech-enabled models can support inclusive capital formation and offers insights to policymakers, platform developers and innovation stakeholders in frontier economies, like Ghana.

title: Legal and Ethical Challenges of AI-Driven Insurance Fraud Detection in the United States

detail.title: Legal and Ethical Challenges of AI-Driven Insurance Fraud Detection in the United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: American insurers now screen a large share of first notices of loss through machine learning models that assign each claim a probability of fraud. The technology answers a real problem: fraud is estimated to drain more than $300 billion from the United States economy each year, and generative image tools have made fabricated evidence cheap enough for ordinary claimants to produce. But the architecture that makes these systems efficient also makes them legally exposed and ethically fraught. A fraud score is an accusation rendered in probability, generated from correlations the insurer often cannot fully explain, applied to a population in which genuine fraud is rare, and enforced through delay and demands for documentation rather than formal denial. This paper examines that tension across four fraud archetypes false injury claims, inflated medical bills, staged accidents and identity fraud and maps the governing legal terrain: state insurance regulation under the McCarran-Ferguson framework, the NAIC Model Bulletin and its state analogues, unfair claims settlement practices statutes and bad faith doctrine, antidiscrimination law, privacy and biometric statutes, and the Fair Credit Reporting Act. It then addresses questions law has not resolved: the base rate problem, proxy discrimination, automation bias in nominal human review, surveillance creep, and the structural conflict between fraud control and cost containment. Drawing on pending litigation in Huskey v State Farm and Estate of Lokken v UnitedHealth Group, the paper argues that the decisive question is not whether insurers may use AI to detect fraud they plainly may, and arguably must but whether the claimant burdened by an algorithmic suspicion retains a meaningful capacity to contest it.

title: Digital Public Infrastructure for State-Building in Low-Income Africa: Evidence From E-Immigration System in Burundi
affiliations: University of Science and Technology Beijing, Excelia Business School, Université du Lac Tanganyika, University of Burundi, Seoul National Univesity and University of Burundi

detail.title: Digital Public Infrastructure for State-Building in Low-Income Africa: Evidence From E-Immigration System in Burundi

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Across low-income Africa, weak institutional capacity undermines governance effectiveness, service delivery, and citizen trust. Digital public infrastructure (DPI) is increasingly promoted as a solution, yet empirical evidence from fragile, post-conflict settings remains scarce. This paper investigates whether and how the design of a digital immigration system in Burundi, a post-conflict, low-income African country with only 7% national ICT access (a context that shapes who can be studied) functions as a state-building policy instrument. We analyze survey data from 251 digitally connected Burundians (internet users and diaspora members) using PLS-SEM, integrating the IS Success Model and UTAUT to model causal pathways from DPI design to citizen adoption. Adoption is driven primarily by performance expectancy and effort expectancy. Information quality and service quality exert strong indirect effects through these expectancy beliefs, whereas system quality has no significant effect. Internet experience moderates pathways: performance expectancy matters more for less experienced users, effort expectancy for more experienced users. Contrary to findings from high-income contexts, social influence and facilitating conditions are not significant. We theorize DPI design as a mechanism for fostering citizen adoption, a necessary condition for building state capacity in post-conflict settings. The findings reveal a strategic policy tension between designing for immediate user adoption (ease of use) and long-term institutional capacity (performance reliability). We provide a diagnostic framework for policymakers, shifting focus from technology-centric investments to service-oriented, user-informed DPI design. The study offers lessons for other low-income African countries facing similar digital transformation challenges.

detail.abstract: We propose a continuous-time framework to estimate time-invariant information shares. For this purpose, we employ a cointegrated CAR(k) process which accounts for the degree of temporal aggregation in the observable time series and avoids the many lags needed to specify discrete-time models for high-frequency data. We estimate the parameters by maximizing the Gaussian likelihood and investigate the statistical properties of the continuous-time information shares under mixed infill and long span asymptotics. We use simulations and an empirical application to show the benefits of continuous-time modeling for the analysis of price discovery in fragmented markets.

title: The Multi-Issuance Issue
affiliations: , , Circle Internet Financial and

detail.title: The Multi-Issuance Issue

detail.abstract: Multi-issuance arrangements, under which a single fungible stablecoin is issued and redeemed by legally separate entities inside and outside the EU, each backing only the tokens it has itself issued, have become the practical accommodation between MiCA's requirement of an EU-located issuance and reserve and the need for global fungibility of leading global stablecoins. Whether such arrangements should be permitted is still being debated. This paper makes three contributions to this debate. First, we develop a financial accounts framework covering the two issuing entities, their custodian banks, holders, and an arbitrageur that traces how par arbitrage on a fungible token could redirect redemption pressure toward the accessible issuer. Second, we argue that reserve localisation is either redundant, if foreign reserve rules are sound, or ineffective, if they are not, and that it obliges dollar-denominated tokens to be backed by offshore dollar assets that are inferior to onshore reserves. Third, we assess mitigants and alternatives: technical separation of EU-issued tokens through distinct smart contracts, and direct EU distribution of well-regulated foreign stablecoins under an equivalence regime. We conclude that the latter would not only be more efficient but would also protect EU holders better than the current approach.

title: Categorical Inequality, Social Closure and the Architecture of the Stratified Firm

detail.title: Categorical Inequality, Social Closure and the Architecture of the Stratified Firm

detail.abstract: Modern organisations routinely contain internal hierarchies that their participants experience as natural and that their compliance systems record as lawful. This article argues that a subset of these hierarchies possesses the structural properties of caste rather than of class, that the distinction is analytically tractable rather than merely rhetorical, and that it carries legal consequences which existing compliance practice does not capture. Part II develops a working definition of organisational caste from Weber, Ambedkar and the comparative caste literature, yielding six falsifiable indicia. Part III surveys the historical repertoire of stratification-varna, the estates of the realm, sumptuary law, livery, guild closure, chattel slavery, indenture, colonial labour control and apartheid job reservation-and identifies a recurring architecture together with a recurring migration of legal form from status to contract as status becomes indefensible. Part IV sets out the causal mechanisms, principally Charles Tilly's account of durable inequality, Weberian social closure, and labour market segmentation theory, and argues that categorical stratification recurs because it is organisationally cheap rather than because it is believed. Part V maps these mechanisms onto contemporary employment forms-outsourcing, agency work, franchising, misclassification, serial fixed-term contracting, two-tier structures and export processing regimes-using David Weil's concept of workplace fissuring. Part VI examines the legal architecture in comparative perspective, distinguishing the doctrines that enable categorical boundaries from the growing body of doctrine that polices them, with particular attention to Kenya, South Africa, the United Kingdom, India, the European Union and the United States. Part VII tests the caste characterisation against its strongest objections and concedes its limits. Part VIII proposes a diagnostic framework.

title: Compressing the Settlement Cycle: Cross-Sectional Frictions and Settlement Fails Under the SEC's T+1 Mandate

detail.abstract: On May 28, 2024, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) compressed the standard settlement cycle for U.S. equities from T+2 to T+1 to mitigate counterparty credit risk and lower clearing fund margin requirements. However, accelerating post-trade processing also reduced the available window for trade allocation, affirmation, securities borrowing, and cross-border currency settlement. Moving the automated trade affirmation cutoff to 9:00 PM Eastern on trade date compressed the operational timeframe for market participants. To examine the cross-sectional impact of this transition, I analyze daily Continuous Net Settlement (CNS) records from the SEC, comprising 647,080 security-day observations across 16,242 unique CUSIPs from March through August 2024. Across the post-mandate window, aggregate daily failed shares averaged 31,887 compared to 27,586 pre-mandate. While these aggregate figures provide descriptive context, the dynamic Difference-in-Differences estimates show that illiquid securities experienced a significantly larger relative surge in settlement failures. Over the following eight weeks, fail numbers gradually declined toward pre-reform levels. This trajectory is consistent with temporary implementation frictions and subsequent operational adaptation by market participants, illustrating the operational trade-offs associated with compressed settlement cycles.

title: The Essentiality Contest: How the AI Race Is Reshaping Competition Policy
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Essentiality Contest: How the AI Race Is Reshaping Competition Policy

detail.abstract: In this article, we introduce what we call the ‘essentiality contest’. This is a framework to explain how power over the artificial intelligence (AI) stack is unevenly distributed, and its consequences for competition policy. Traditionally, competition policy has focused on competition at the firm level, but this approach breaks down when applied to the AI stack.  Firm-level market analysis is no longer the correct lens for understanding AI competition. The AI race is re-organising the global political economy into a pattern previously documented in the trade literature – hubs and spokes. Two hub countries, the US and China, anchor their respective AI ecosystems, with the EU remaining an indeterminate third, perhaps large enough to try to achieve hub status. Most other economies feed into these ecosystems in one of two forms – as essential spokes, supplying an indispensable input into the AI stack (e.g., the Netherlands with ASML), or as non-essential spokes, supplying commoditised goods or services that the hub can also get elsewhere. Essentiality can be contested at the state level with weapons that competition experts would readily recognise, such as foreclosure and substitution, as well as some that might be invisible to the antitrust toolkit, such as commoditisation – which antitrust might mistake for vigorous competition. The framework explains why ‘technological sovereignty’ and ‘decoupling’ have become political economy buzzwords, as well as what these terms actually imply when analysed through different positions of essentiality on the AI stack.  Using this framework, we argue that traditional firm-level analysis fails to grasp the dynamics of the AI ecosystems in which competition now operates. Drawing on the enforcement record against digital platforms – where jurisdictions with diverging enforcement schools of thought converged on the same concentrated markets – and on the emerging structure of AI markets, we show that a jurisdiction’s competitiveness is tied to its essentiality position. The question being asked of the field is no longer ‘how should the consumer welfare toolkit adapt?’ but rather ‘how can my jurisdiction survive the essentiality contest?’

Key points:
- Domestic violence is a foreseeable workplace risk, affecting survivors’ safety, health, equality and labour market participation. It undermines women’s economic independence and reinforces labour market inequality, trapping survivors in cycles of dependency and insecure work.
- In accordance with occupational safety and health regulations, employers are required to identify and mitigate these risks as part of workplace safety systems.

title: The Making of the Global Economy: International Law and the Global South

detail.title: The Making of the Global Economy: International Law and the Global South

detail.abstract: Across a fractured geopolitical landscape, the Global South faces renewed constraints on its capacity to pursue sovereign development. Rather than treating these pressures as symptoms of a 'new Cold War', this article returns to the original Cold War as a decisive moment in the consolidation of the legal and epistemic foundations of today's global economy. It argues that the Cold War was a pivotal phase in a longer history of disembedding, through which economic governance was separated from social and political life and reorganized through juridical, financial, and metrological techniques. While the Soviet project often advanced more solidaristic visions of development, both socialist and Western frameworks ultimately relied on technocratic and growth-centred models that narrowed the space for postcolonial demands for redistribution and structural reform. Through a longue durée analysis of the colonial, Cold War and post-Cold War periods, the article traces how international law and development co-evolved as interlocking techniques that rearticulated imperial hierarchies into global economic norms and institutions. Revisiting this history reveals the juridical infrastructures that continue to reproduce global inequality and the legal imaginations and material sites through which the Global South continues to contest its fate.

detail.abstract: This paper provides theoretical foundations and empirical evidence for the directional transmission of inflationary shocks across countries. In a multi-country open economy model with heterogeneous price-setting and incomplete exchange rate passthrough, inflation spillovers propagate across countries through bilateral exports and, because trade itself obeys the gravity equation, inherit its gravity structure: spillovers decrease with geographic distance and increase with economic size. We measure pairwise, directional spillovers with the Diebold-Yilmaz framework applied to commodity-price-adjusted monthly inflation for up to 98 countries over 1978-2023. The system-wide index has risen substantially alongside global trade integration, with the increase strongest among developed economies and in the net transmission from developed to developing countries. Gravity regressions over five-year windows confirm the model's predictions, with the role of proximity strengthening after 2008. Bilateral exports fully absorb the source-country size elasticity: size matters for transmission because larger economies trade more, and the developed economies stand out as the net originators of inflation to the developing world.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how Kenya's Affordable Housing Programme (AHP) affects low-income households in Mukuru Kwa Njenga, a high-density informal settlement in Nairobi. Using a crosssectional comparison of 74 treated households (already allocated AHP units) and 66 pipeline households (eligible but not yet housed), the study combines regression analysis of housing costs, payments, commuting, and satisfaction with semi-structured interviews and document review. The findings show that AHP access is associated with modest but statistically uncertain reductions in housing cost burden, alongside significant improvements in sanitation, safety, service reliability, and residential stability, reflected in higher housing satisfaction. Commuting costs remain unresolved, and irregular incomes continue to strain payment obligations. Distributional analysis shows that satisfaction gains are somewhat smaller for vulnerable households. At the same time, access itself is shaped less by demographic need than by households' capacity to navigate digital registration and documentation requirements. The paper concludes that AHP's core benefits lie in non-monetary welfare gains rather than cost relief, and situates AHP alongside Kenya's Informal Settlements Improvement Programme (KISIP) as a complementary rather than competing policy instrument.

detail.abstract: Who bears the health burden of extreme heat when a universal public system operates alongside a large private insurance sector? We estimate the mortality, hospital-use and fiscal response to heat across Brazil's two tiers and ask whether private coverage absorbs it. We link daily municipality temperature to the universe of death certificates, public hospital admissions and private-insurance claims, together with the regulator's beneficiary registry, the contract terms on each claim, and records identifying insured patients treated in the public system; effects are identified from day-today variation within municipality-months. A day above 34 • C raises same-day mortality by 7.1 percent and public admissions by 3.1 percent. Distributed lags show cardiovascular admissions are displaced within three weeks, whereas all-cause and elderly mortality remain elevated cumulatively, indicating additional deaths; authorized public billed value rises 2.1 percent, though its persistence is sensitive to the exposure measure. In monthly private claims, all-cause and renal responses are near zero and dehydration is positive but borderline: no stable private-sector response. Nothing we observe attenuates the mortality effect. Interacting it with municipal coverage, income and primary-care coverage bounds any attenuation below about 3 percent; the insured do not shift onto the public system on hot days; and the interactions between contract terms and temperature carry no heat-specific pattern across causes, which is what protection would require. Per capita, heat-attributable mortality in the least-covered municipalities is about twice that in the most-covered, so the burden concentrates on the public system serving Brazil's most exposed population.

title: Remedial Closure" of the Strait of Hormuz; Dialectic of Legality and Legitimacy

detail.title: Remedial Closure" of the Strait of Hormuz; Dialectic of Legality and Legitimacy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: nothing

detail.abstract: This research develops an innovative framework for legal assessment of the closure or restriction of the Strait of Hormuz during the situation that threatens a coastal state's survival. The central analysis is structured around four dualistic 2 questions which ask how "internationally legal", how "internationally legitimate", how "legally legitimate" and how "legitimately legal" such a closure would be. The hypothesis of this article is that in the exceptional circumstance of self-defense where state survival is at stake, legitimacy may, under strict conditions, justify a departure from strict positivist legality, giving rise to a new conceptual framework rather than a rule-based exception. Methodologically, the article employs a dialectical approach that moves from the positivist prohibition as the thesis through a legitimacy-based critique as the antithesis to a synthetic resolution. This dialectical movement is complemented by reasoning by analogy in particular from the International Court of Justice's Nuclear Weapons and Kosovo advisory opinions. The central finding is that a strict positivist reading of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and customary international law provides no explicit authorization for closure and leaves the victim state helpless. The article's main hypothesis is that in appearing an existential threat, legitimacy may override mere legality, giving rise to a new legal institution. To operationalize this hypothesis, the article proposes the doctrine of remedial closure as an emergency mechanism grounded in the inherent right of self-defense and strictly conditioned on legal tests. The theoretical results demonstrate that legality and legitimacy are not binary opposites but dialectical partners within a living legal order. The article concludes that even though the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has very little support for legal acceptance under a purely positivist reading, legitimately it can be considered authorized under a reasoned and dialectical interpretation of international law, provided all cumulative conditions are satisfied.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impacts of AI-driven productivity increases on global patterns of trade, income, and wages, using an implementation of CGE modeling that disaggregates the U.S. labor force into 22 occupations and leveraging recent research into the adoption of AI by workers and its labor market impacts. AI exposure and its associated productivity impacts tend to be concentrated in high-skill, high-wage occupations, most notably computer science and mathematics, business and finance, and architecture and engineering. These occupations are used most intensively in the production of services and certain knowledge-intensive goods like computer, electronic, and optical products. While AI increases real GDP in all regions of the world, gains are highest in the United States and other high-income countries that have high exposure to AI. AI reshapes the U.S. pattern of comparative advantage in favor of business services. Increased import demand in high-income countries induces an increase in China's manufacturing output and exports. Skill premiums decrease universally across all countries and regions. The results for GDP, output, and exports are highly robust to whether capital-skill (K-S) complementarity is included in the model. However, wages are sensitive to the model specifications. While all wages increase in the traditional GTAP model, wages for skilled labor often decrease in the model with K-S complementarity, with declines concentrated in the most AI-exposed occupations.

detail.abstract: Mountain states that generate the water other countries consume rarely capture value from that position. The standard explanations are external: asymmetric bargaining power, weak treaty regimes, downstream economic weight. This paper argues that a decisive part of the explanation is internal. In every mountain state examined here, water is administratively subordinated to a sector that treats it as an input rather than an asset-agriculture, energy, public works or environmental protection-while the cryosphere that produces it is held by scientific or emergency bodies with no fiscal or negotiating mandate. The two halves of what should be one sovereignty over water are never held by the same authority. Comparing ten mountain states, with the Kyrgyz Republic as the lead case, the paper identifies four subordination logics and five convergent institutional failures, and derives a model design: a narrow ministry of water and glaciers built on five functions-industrial water rights, tariff methodology and rent capture, a legally binding cryospheric cadastre, the transboundary negotiating mandate, and national water accounting-with operational infrastructure excluded by statute. The principle is separation of the resource owner from the infrastructure operator. The paper also states the conditions under which the model produces nothing.

detail.abstract: Puerto Rico faces the long‑standing challenge of having the lowest labor participation rate in the United States, driven by structural poverty, limited economic opportunities, and widespread reliance on federal assistance programs. As noted in the report, “more than 38% of households depend on the NAP for food and nutrition support” and approximately “250,000 able-bodied individuals…are absent from the formal workforce.” Inspiring Work builds on Centro CRECE’s 2025 policy brief, The Impact of the Welfare State on Puerto Rico’s Labor Participation Rate, to deepen understanding of the socio‑economic, regulatory, and psychological factors that perpetuate long‑term dependency. The study combines quantitative data from 500 able-bodied NAP recipients with qualitative interviews to identify barriers to employment, perceptions of welfare, and the conditions that would motivate beneficiaries to pursue formal work. By combining robust quantitative data with deep qualitative personal accounts, this report moves beyond generalizations to provide a nuanced, evidence-based foundation for policy reform.

detail.abstract: Emergency work requires professionals to convert knowledge into coordinated action under uncertainty, time pressure, emotional intensity, and fatigue. This narrative review examines psychological readiness through four linked components: knowledge, enacted competence, team integration, and sustainable readiness. Drawing on research in disaster training, psychological first aid, simulation, teamwork, occupational mental health, fatigue, and post-incident support, it proposes a diagnostic framework for distinguishing failures that may appear operationally similar but arise at different levels. Knowledge deficits may require instruction; failures to enact known skills may require rehearsal or task redesign; coordination failures may require changes in team processes; and declining performance under cumulative demand may require organizational responses involving workload, recovery, or supervision. Five testable propositions translate the framework into research questions. Psychological readiness is presented not as a personality trait, diagnosis, or fitness score, but as an organizing framework for training, team performance, and system design.

detail.abstract: Despite its limited competences in the social field, the EU is shaping Digital Welfare State(s) along three main avenues. The first two consist of the elaboration of a set of digital fundamental rights with a ‘constitutional’ status (‘Digital -Fundamental- Rights’), and the regulation of the enabling technologies (‘Technology Regulation’). Those avenues are intertwined and apply to both private and public sectors. The third avenue, ‘Digital Sovereignty’, is characterised by the prevalence of politics over law. It conflates a strategic dimension with value-based considerations. The article proposes ruling out the latter, referring to ‘Digital Strategic Autonomy’. Moreover, absent clear legal constraints, the envisaged ‘European preference’ in strategic public procurement, recently toned down by the European Commission, risks sliding into a national preference, fragmenting the internal market. Thus, the first two avenues should remain central to the EU’s digital welfare strategy, while the third one, though important, should act in the background

detail.abstract: This paper examines the diffusion of India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) from April 2017 through June 2026 using monthly payment-system statistics. The analysis combines the RBI/NPCI UPI product series for the early diffusion period with RBI Table No. 45 for the cross-instrument comparison. UPI transaction volume rises from 7.20 million transactions in April 2017 to 22,716.07 million in June 2026, a 3,155-fold increase, while average transaction size falls from approximately Rs. 3,154 to Rs. 1,273. The rail comparison shows that between November 2019 and June 2026 debit-card transaction volume fell 76.8%, CTS volume fell 50.8%, and credit-card volume increased 229.9%. A post-November-2019 bivariate log-linear regression estimates an elasticity of -0.457 (HAC p < 0.001) between UPI and debit-card volume. However, the coefficient changes sign in the model that controls for total retail-payment volume, illustrating the sensitivity of level regressions to common trends and aggregate-composition effects. A parallel credit-card regression is positive, consistent with coexistence rather than uniform substitution across payment rails. An early-period diffusion model also finds a positive association between banks live on UPI and transaction volume. The results therefore document a large-scale reallocation of payment activity but do not establish causal substitution or a definitive P2P-to-P2M mechanism. The principal contribution is a long-run monthly account of UPI diffusion linked to the changing composition of India's retail-payment system.

title: Measured, Not Assumed: Individual-Level Immigration Enforcement Records and the Local Contact-Removal Margin in the United States, FY2022-FY2026
affiliations: RUDN University, Peoples’ Friendship University of Russia and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Measured, Not Assumed: Individual-Level Immigration Enforcement Records and the Local Contact-Removal Margin in the United States, FY2022-FY2026

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable (analysis of public and FOIA-released administrative data).

detail.abstract:
United States immigration enforcement is normally measured in annual agency totals, which hide where enforcement happens and which events drive it. Using individual-level records released under FOIA covering fiscal years 2022 through 2026, this paper builds a monthly enforcement shock panel for 24 United States metropolitan areas, with 3,638 area-month records. The records are separated into contact events, such as detentions and encounters, and executed removals, so that each channel can be tested against local employment, wages, building permits and house prices.

The contact margin is at least as large as the executed-removal margin in the point estimates, with a ratio of 1.1384, although the interval around that ratio is wide because only 24 clusters are available. The local employment association is large, at-1.4609 log points per standard deviation, but it is not robust to small-cluster inference: a wild-cluster bootstrap gives a p-value of 0.519 against a conventional 0.0148, so it is reported as suggestive. Wage, permit and price responses are indistinguishable from zero, and three capacity instruments fail the first stage.

The contribution is a measured shock object and a disciplined set of answers about what it can support.

title: Pretrained Transformers Applied To Population Cancer Registries Improve Survival Prediction In Label-Scarce And Previously Unseen Cancers
affiliations: Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory, Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory, Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University, Xiamen University, Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory, Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory, Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory, Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory, Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory, Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory, Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory and Zhejiang University - Department of Clinical Laboratory

detail.title: Pretrained Transformers Applied To Population Cancer Registries Improve Survival Prediction In Label-Scarce And Previously Unseen Cancers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of China (No: 82402697, 82302612, 82403877 and 82472351), Natural Science Foundation of Zhejiang Province (ZCLQN25H2001, and LQN25H160028), Fujian Provincial Natural Science Foundation (Grant No. 2026J0011752) and the Scientific Research Foundation of State Key Laboratory of Vaccines for Infectious Diseases, Xiang An Biomedicine Laboratory (Grant No. 2025XAKJ0102004).

detail.abstract:
Background: Survival models in oncology are fitted one cancer at a time, from the outcome data of that cancer alone, and rare cancers seldom supply enough deaths for that to work. Population cancer registries hold millions of records across every cancer type, and a representation learned from them without outcome labels might supply what a small cohort cannot. We tested whether outcome-agnostic pretraining on registry data improves survival prediction when labelled data are scarce, including in cancers withheld from pretraining altogether.

Methods: We did a retrospective cohort study of malignant tumour records diagnosed between 2000 and 2023 in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) 17 registries, November 2025 release. Records with valid age, primary site, histology, and year of diagnosis were eligible; death-certificate-only and autopsy-only records were excluded. Patients were assigned to non-overlapping training, validation, and test partitions. A transformer encoder was pretrained by masked field-value modelling of verified diagnosis-time registry variables, without survival or any other outcome label. The encoder was then frozen and read by a linear Cox proportional hazards head. Nine further pretraining experiments each removed every patient group containing one target rare cancer. Discrimination for overall survival was measured by Harrell's concordance index, with secondary prediction horizons at 12, 36, and 60 months. Comparators were an architecture-identical randomly initialised frozen encoder, and conventional Cox regression fitted on matched or on all available labelled data.

Findings: Of 9,708,868 source tumour records, 9,425,135 (97·1%) were eligible. In the held-out test partition, the pretrained representation gave higher concordance than the randomly initialised frozen encoder in all nine cancers excluded from pretraining, by 0·0034 (95% CI 0·0014–0·0052) to 0·0368 (0·0111–0·0645). In an exploratory analysis across 67 cancers given 256 labelled patients each, the point estimate favoured the pretrained model over Cox regression in every cancer, with a median difference of 0·0283; nominal 95% CIs excluded zero in 54 of 67. The advantage was bounded: given all available labelled training data, Cox regression was the better model in seven of the nine rare cancers. Pretraining also failed to beat a frequency-based baseline on its own primary reconstruction metric.

Interpretation: Outcome-agnostic pretraining on a population cancer registry carried prognostic information into cancers it had never seen, and improved survival discrimination where cancer-specific labels were scarce. That advantage did not survive an abundance of labels, and it appeared without any gain on the pretraining objective itself, so reconstruction performance is a poor guide to downstream transfer. Registry pretraining is therefore best read as a way of making scarce labels go further, not as a replacement for conventional survival models in cancers that have data of their own. Validation in registries outside SEER and in other health systems, along with assessment of calibration and clinical utility, is needed before clinical use.

detail.abstract: Corporate purpose debates, in large part theoretical, have captured academic and industry attention in the recent past. This paper will examine the specific case of recent government investment in companies within the tech sector with a view to understanding the aims of such investment and, further, the implications of this for the idea of corporate purpose. The tech sector is particularly relevant because, at every stage in history, the cutting-edge technology of the time has been a matter of interest for governments and continues to be so at this current moment of fraught geopolitics. This paper uses case studies from the U.S. and Australia. The use of case studies allows us to delve into context-specific issues and, to an extent, glean some more generalizable takeaways. Based on the analysis of case studies in this paper, we argue that governments are pursuing strategic aims through their investments in the tech sectorsomething we call strategic socialism. To be clear, we are skeptical of this and caution against the long arm of the State. Government investors have the potential to influence corporate decision-making, possibly even de facto changing these companies' corporate purpose. To address this, we highlight the need for greater transparency around the relationship between government investors and the companies in which they own shares. We propose that companies with government involvement should state their corporate purpose on the official company website as a preliminary solution so as to ensure clarity and transparency. The paper not only contributes to our understanding of corporate purpose based on practical insights from the tech sector but also contributes to our broader understanding of the intertwining of business and government.

detail.abstract: Historical-pattern forecasts may fail when information moves prices beyond historical support. We audit next-session forecasts from a deployed Bitcoin system. Across 1,973 BTC/USD and 1,125 BITO origins, directional accuracy was 48.8% and 50.6%, with near-nominal interval coverage. On return-defined large-move sessions, accuracy fell to 36.7% and 37.5%, and all nominal-80% intervals missed. Headline-count spikes increased standardized error for both instruments, but directional degradation appeared only for BTC and was imprecise. These exploratory results do not measure investor behavior; they motivate research into which news changes behavior and how responses propagate into prices.

detail.abstract: When a bank closes a branch, the deposits move to the merged entity's nearby offices. Linking weekly posted rates at every U.S. branch to customers' cell phone records, we follow 1,301 closures, dated by foot traffic. Deposits at the entity's survivors within ten kilometres rise by twelve percent for at least two years while their visits fall by a quarter; rival branches gain nothing. The survivors' certificate rates fall, but the cut appears at every branch sharing their rate-setting account, and acquired branches adopt the acquirer's lower schedule within weeks. Consolidation moves deposits between branches; the network prices them.

detail.abstract: Therapeutic technologies often show recurring stages of product formation, generational renewal, independent confirmation, and subsequent expansion, but the time required for these transitions varies substantially across lineages and modalities. Using small molecules as a historical calibration domain and product-level therapeutic histories, this study measures the interval from the first viable lineage-forming product (P1) to the first materially upgraded generation (G2), and from G2 to the first independent product confirming the reproducibility of that generation (C2). Across smallmolecule lineages, P1→G2 intervals range from approximately four decades in some early lineages to 5-6 years in several later ones. However, substantial variation among lineages arising under similar pharmaceutical R&D conditions indicates that calendar era and system maturity alone do not fully explain the differences in maturation timing. G2→C2 intervals are generally much shorter than P1→G2. Among newer therapeutic modalities, observed P1→G2 intervals range from 11 to 15 years, whereas completed G2→C2 intervals are also substantially shorter. These patterns are consistent with differences in the capabilities available at P1 and the technological challenges that remain before a materially upgraded generation can emerge.

detail.abstract: An adverse human rights audit can put a supplier's business at risk long before a court examines the evidence. For workers at the same factory, even a sound audit may leave the question of compensation unresolved. This article examines the authority of ethical assessments in commercial relationships through these two disputes. I argue that the legal effect claimed for an assessment requires justification by reference to the particular obligation at issue. Debates about legal validity and authority provide the jurisprudential basis for the inquiry. The assessment of remedies draws on Shiffrin and Fried's disagreement over contract and promise. English contract and negligence cases, EU sustainability requirements and the public recognition of technical standards show how the problem arises in practice. I propose a statutory right to reasons and timely review for dependent suppliers in existing relationships governed by English law. Workers' claims require further examination of any protective function the buyer has undertaken and the harm caused by its performance.

detail.abstract: Systemic risk forecasts are sensitive to the assumed dependence model, yet the space of plausible specifications is vast. We study the role of dependence uncertainty in out-of-sample forecasting through the lens of a real-time Bayesian learner. We propose a sequential approach for pair-copula constructions that updates beliefs over competing specifications and that forecasts from predictive mixtures. We disentangle different sources of uncertainty and evaluate their relative importance under misspecification. In an application to systemically important US banks, averaging over dependence specifications improves density forecasts, while gains in conditional tail-risk forecasts are confined to the deepest tail configuration and are linked to the dispersion across different tail-dependence shapes.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the systemic fragmentation and inconsistent efficacy pervasive in contemporary corporate instructional design. The absence of an architectural standard often leads to extraneous visual and mental exhaustion, collapsing the distinction between passive content exposition and applied competency development. Drawing from Cognitive Load Theory and Experiential Learning Models, this paper develops the 4-Quadrant 20-Slide Instructional Architecture. The framework standardizes a single training session (spanning 60 to 90 minutes) into four balanced functional quadrants: (1) Engagement & Context Hub, (2) Core Conceptual Foundation, (3) Practical Simulation & Drill, and (4) Institutional Debrief & Action Plan. Setting a critical threshold of 20 slides-allocated symmetrically at 5 slides per quadrantfurnishes an engineering mechanism to eliminate cognitive fatigue and enforce measurable learning outcomes. Concurrently, it equips corporate learning and development (L&D) divisions with an auditable governance rubric to assess material rigor and ensure transfer of training.

detail.abstract: Trend strategies have long been praised for their appealing qualities as effective means of portfolio diversification, and for other attractive features that have been thoroughly documented in the literature, such as low correlation with equity markets bringing protection from drawdowns. Indexes such as the BarclayHedge BTOP50 Index and the Société Générale SG Trend Index track the performance of a basket of funds dedicated to trend-following and managed futures strategies (CTAs). However, misspecification and poor execution of a trend-following strategy can lead to severe risks. Building on the concepts from [Braun et al., 2024] and [Hurst et al., 2013], we expand the above work on replication of trend-following strategies in CTAs while substantially reducing the number of assets (hence the turnover) and diversifying in replication methodology, achieving a superior performance in terms of Sharpe ratio. We take as benchmark the SG Trend Index.
