detail.abstract: India's Forest Rights Act of 2006 allows the right to collect and sell minor forest produce (MFP) to forest-dwelling communities, primarily members of the Scheduled Tribes (STs). This is aimed at improving the income generation capacity of these communities that have traditionally been dependent on forests for their livelihood. There are many factors that are creating hurdles in these communities’ economic development through the sustainable use of MFPs. This study aims to understand the impact the FRA has made on these communities’ socio-economic aspects and to come up with a solution to boost the marketing and selling of MFPs and processed products. This field study involved interviews of 120 persons from the different villages in the Dhanora, Kurkheda and Korchi Talukas of Gadchiroli district in Maharashtra state to get insight into the impact of minor forest produce (MFP) on the lives of tribal and other forest-dwelling communities. The primary data was collected through interviews that were carried out using Google Forms and in-person interviews. The data suggest whose income is under Rs 50,000 were most expressive about increase in income. A majority of respondents believed that they can earn better remuneration if MFPs are marketed well, such as promotion and exploring new markets. About 69.2% (83 respondents) had not received forest pattas (area) under the Forest Rights Act (FRA). A majority of respondents (54 people or 45.3 %) claimed socio-economic improvement due to better MFP remuneration in recent years. As many as 77 respondents (64.2%) believed they could earn better income through improved MFP marketing, while only 1.7% (2) did not believe so. The major obstacles to selling processed MFPs in urban markets were lack of marketing skills (72), lack of subject knowledge (67), unawareness of demand (51), and poor transportation (50). As many as 70 respondents believed value addition was possible if the supply chain was strengthened.

title: M.O.T.H.E.R.: Human Sovereignty at Machine Speed

detail.title: M.O.T.H.E.R.: Human Sovereignty at Machine Speed

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research did not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
M.O.T.H.E.R. begins with that question.


It does not predict that catastrophic loss of control will occur soon, or at all, nor does it claim to solve AI alignment. Instead, it treats severe loss of effective human control as a design stress case: a condition against which governance for increasingly capable and autonomous AI should be designed before such a condition could become operationally real.

 

The central problem is a potential separation between formal human authority and effective human control. Human institutions may retain formal legal authority while the practical ability to observe, understand, deliberate upon, and intervene in consequential machine activity is increasingly challenged by the speed, scale, and complexity of that activity. That makes it increasingly plausible that important existing modes of supervision may lose effectiveness sooner than conventional human-centered oversight structures are prepared to accommodate.

 

M.O.T.H.E.R. proposes a human-governed, AI-native supervisory architecture for that gap: not just a machine solution, but a wider governance system around it. Humans and legitimate human institutions retain normative authority. Machine components serve as an operational toolkit that may receive bounded, revocable, and, where appropriate, provisional authority to monitor, verify, constrain, preserve evidence, and escalate at speeds relevant to the systems being governed. Their function is not to replace sovereign human judgment, but to preserve the conditions under which that judgment can continue to matter within a broader human structure in which relevant risks, interests, and actors can be represented and decisions made under legitimate authority.

 

Many elements of this proposal already have substantial precedent in AI control, runtime governance, delegated authorization, public law, and international institutional design. M.O.T.H.E.R.’s research hypothesis concerns the architecture created by their integration: whether machine-speed supervision can become an operational arm of legitimate human governance without transferring sovereignty either to the machinery or to the private actors that build it.

 

This paper establishes M.O.T.H.E.R.’s initial constitutional architecture and the research agenda required to operationalize it.

title: Optimal Cohort Partitions
affiliations: and Yale School of Management

detail.title: Optimal Cohort Partitions
detail.abstract: We study optimal partitions of a heterogeneous population into distinct groups. Through the lens of majorization theory, we provide an optimization framework for part-additive objectives that characterizes the fractional and integral partition polytopes, and identifies new classes of optimal policies. Our main result shows that, under edge-quasi-convex objectives, there exists an optimal fractional partition that is locally uniform, mixing adjacent types evenly across consecutive sections. Among integral partitions, there exists an optimal pairwise extremal partition, where every pair of sections, holding the others fixed, is maximally balanced or maximally polarized. Under Schur-convex objectives the assortative partition is optimal, while under Schur-concave objectives the uniform fractional and balanced integral partitions are. We next apply our framework to student assignment with peer effects. Using the workhorse linear-in-means (LIM) model, we characterize the optimal partitions for performance, inequality, welfare, and diversity, which generally conflict. The assortative partition maximizes welfare but produces the greatest inequality and the least diversity. The inequality-minimizing partition changes from balanced to dispersion-maximal as peer effects weaken. The performance-maximizing partition moves from assortative to upper-uniform to uniform as the planner's weights shift from higher-toward lower-performing sections. We further characterize sorting-neutral models that, despite being non-linear, exhibit LIM's invariance of total effort. Finally, we complement our theory with an empirical exercise on a novel dataset with quasi-random classroom assignments. We find that greater sorting is associated with sizable gains for lower-achieving students in the most sorted cohorts. Higher achievers exhibit non-significant and even negative effects.

title: Managing Inventory Systems with Random Lead Times and Heterogeneous Customer Patience
affiliations: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Managing Inventory Systems with Random Lead Times and Heterogeneous Customer Patience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare there is no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: We study a periodic-review inventory system with stochastic, non-crossover lead times over an infinite horizon. Customers are impatient: after stockout, they decide whether to stay or abandon, with a probability depending on their elapsed waiting time. The resulting system has a mixture of backorders and lost sales, and the objective is to minimize the long-run average holding, backlogging, and lost-sales penalty costs. Because the optimal policy is difficult to characterize in general, we focus on a simple yet fundamental class of base-stock (BS) policies and analyze their performance in two regimes: (i) a joint-penalty-scaling regime, in which both the unit backlogging cost and lost-sales penalty grow large, and (ii) a lost-sales-penalty-only scaling regime, in which only the unit lost-sales penalty grows large. Under bounded demand, we show that the BS policy is eventually optimal in both regimes, but the optimal BS level differs sharply. Under unbounded demand, we establish the asymptotic optimality of the BS policy and compare the asymptotic behaviors of the optimal policy and the best BS policy across the two regimes. We further extend our results to systems with Markovian lead times and establish the optimality of state-dependent BS policies under bounded demand and the asymptotic optimality of state-independent BS policies under unbounded demand when a common maximum lead time is reachable from any supply state. Numerical experiments show that the optimal BS policy performs close to optimal in non-asymptotic regimes and outperforms the myopic policy across a broad range of parameters.

title: Eigenvalue-Decomposition Cost Denoising as an Alternative to Predict-then-Optimize for Shortest-Path Problems
affiliations: and Regis High School

detail.title: Eigenvalue-Decomposition Cost Denoising as an Alternative to Predict-then-Optimize for Shortest-Path Problems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: No participants were involved in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Predict-then-optimize methods such as Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) of Elmachtoub and Grigas [2022] learn a mapping from contextual features to unknown edge costs and then solve the induced combinatorial problem on the predicted costs. This approach is powerful but relies on the predictive model being well specified: when the true cost-generating process is nonlinear in the features and the predictor is linear, SPO+'s performance degrades as the misspecification grows. We propose and evaluate a structurally different remedy for a specific but common setting: when the decision-maker observes many noisy realizations of the same underlying cost process, the realized cost vectors themselves can be treated as a noisy signal and denoised directly, via eigenvalue decomposition (equivalently, Principal Component Analysis) of their covariance matrix, before ever invoking a predictive model. We instantiate this idea on the 5 × 5 grid shortest-path benchmark introduced by Elmachtoub and Grigas [2022], retaining only the top-k eigenvectors of the training cost covariance matrix and projecting new noisy cost observations onto that subspace prior to solving with Dijkstra's algorithm [Dijkstra, 1959]. We find that the choice of k is decisive: keeping only k=2 eigenvectors discards real signal and underperforms even the naive noisy-cost baseline, while setting k=5 to match the true latent feature dimension makes eigenvalue-denoised Dijkstra the best-performing method at every misspecification level tested, outperforming SPO+ by a wide margin under high misspecification.

title: The Chaos Score: A Validated Composite Warehouse Risk Index, with a Benchmarked Customer-Analytics Pipeline as a Secondary Application -Evidence from the VelocityMart Retail Dataset

detail.title: The Chaos Score: A Validated Composite Warehouse Risk Index, with a Benchmarked Customer-Analytics Pipeline as a Secondary Application -Evidence from the VelocityMart Retail Dataset

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding from public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agencies.

detail.abstract: Retail operations analytics is typically split across two silos: warehouse risk management and customer relationship management, each run on its own data pipeline. All results reported here are derived from a simulated Datathon dataset rather than production operational data; the R², F1, and ranking figures below should be read as evidence of internal methodological soundness on this dataset, not as externally validated benchmarks. In particular, no outcome data (actual incidents, costs, or realised churn events) is yet available to externally calibrate the Chaos Score's weights or confirm the customer-analytics models' real-world predictive value-both checks are internal to this dataset-and we return to this limitation in detail in Section 8. This paper's contribution is not any individual model-gradient boosting, logistic regression, K-Means, AHP, and entropy weighting are each well established-but two things built on top of them: (i) the Chaos Score, a warehouse risk index whose novelty lies in its hybrid compensatory/non-compensatory aggregation rule and in three complementary assessments of its weighting rationale and ranking robustness (AHP judgment consistency, entropy-derived informational content, and Monte Carlo rank-stability), and (ii) the demonstration that a single weekly data-integration pipeline can produce both this operational risk score and a full customer-value/churn analytics layer, rather than requiring two siloed systems. We build both on a simulated 91-week VelocityMart operations dataset (800 SKUs; 770 active warehouse records; 15,308 transaction lines; 2,000 customers; 1,780 repeat-buyer profiles). Part I develops a forensic data-cleaning methodology that resolves four classes of hidden warehouse data defects-decimal-unit weight drift, ghost inventory, temperature-zone mismatches, and GPS-logged picker shortcuts-and combines the cleaned attributes into the Chaos Score. We ground its additive form in Multi-Attribute Utility Theory (Keeney & Raiffa, 1976), contrast it with a multiplicative alternative whose interaction effects are not empirically identifiable from the present single-snapshot dataset, and propose a non-compensatory veto extension so that a single safety-critical failure (ghost inventory) cannot be masked by low scores elsewhere-a specific, novel refinement over a plain weighted sum. We then validate the weights with an independent Analytic Hierarchy Process (Saaty pairwise judgment matrix, consistency ratio CR = 0.015), a Shannon entropy-weighting analysis of the realised data, a 5,000-draw Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis (mean Spearman ρ = 0.946 under fully randomised weights), an exact variance decomposition, and a benchmark against three simple baseline indices-finding the Chaos Score almost uncorrelated with classic demand/ABC-based prioritisation (ρ = 0.015; 47 of its top-50 SKUs would be missed by ABC alone) but currently close to a naive equal-weight scheme (ρ = 0.978) because two of its five components are inactive in the present snapshot. Part II extends the same integrated dataset into a customer-analytics layer: a Gradient Boosting Regressor estimates customer total spend (test R² = 0.947; six of the eight benchmarked models tuned via GridSearchCV with 3-4-fold cross-validation, with the Random Forest and Gradient Boosting classifiers run at default settings-see Section 5.1.1 for the resulting caveat on the classifier comparison), a Logistic Regression classifier best classifies high-risk customer profiles on a near-balanced test set (F1 = 0.684, ruling out class imbalance as the explanation for the tree ensembles' weaker showing), and K-Means with k = 4 recovers an interpretable four-segment structure spanning 40.14 to 229.44 in mean spend. We report the pipeline's limitations in full-principally its reliance on ₹ ₹ a synthetic Datathon dataset and the current absence of outcome data to externally calibrate the Chaos Score's weights-and set out a specific, executable procedure for closing that gap.

title: UMAIX™: A Multi-Agent Operating System for Human-Centric Phygital Retail
affiliations: and indipendent

detail.title: UMAIX™: A Multi-Agent Operating System for Human-Centric Phygital Retail

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study is based on mathematical modeling, discrete-event simulations, and privacy-preserving, fully anonymized aggregated telemetry (Zero-PII compliant). No identifiable human participant data were collected or processed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Modern commercial retail environments are undergoing an irreversible phase transition from static distribution conduits into dense, stochastic cyber-physical ecosystems. Within these spaces, high-velocity supply chain volatility, multi-modal edge sensor telemetry (computer vision, LiDAR, micro-load cells, and spatial BLE/NFC arrays), and non-linear customer behavioral dynamics continuously collide. Traditional enterprise software architectures—fundamentally structured on centralized relational databases, batch-processed Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) pipelines, and isolated Customer Relationship Management (CRM) silos—suffer from systemic architectural latency, informational fragmentation, and catastrophic operational debt when attempting to resolve asynchronous edge disruptions.

This monograph presents the theoretical foundations, complete mathematical formalization, systems architecture, and longitudinal empirical evaluation of UMAIX™, an autonomous, multi-agent operating system engineered specifically for phygital retail governance. Departing completely from passive point-solution tooling, UMAIX™ establishes an active, distributed execution runtime structured across four cooperative, goal-directed agent tiers: System Agents, Worker Agents, Customer Agents, and Governance (Kernel) Agents.

We formalize physical retail plant mechanics as a continuous-time Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and introduce the Cognitive Friction Minimization Theorem, proving that intermediate semantic filtering and dynamic priority dispatching are mathematically necessary to bound human decision error rates below operational saturation limits. Extensive discrete-event simulations coupled with field telemetric audits across four structural retail archetypes validate systemic operational dominance over traditional enterprise stacks.

title: Winning Before You Play: An Iterative Capture Algorithm for Pre-Game Dominance Analysis in Three-Player Auction Bridge
affiliations: Indian Statistical Institute

detail.title: Winning Before You Play: An Iterative Capture Algorithm for Pre-Game Dominance Analysis in Three-Player Auction Bridge

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: This paper introduces an innovative and bias-free variant of a three-player auction bridge, specifically designed to address structural limitations found in traditional formats. In a standard auction bridge, the partner of the winning bidder often plays a passive role, possessing minimal influence over the outcome once the bidding phase concludes. To rectify this, our proposed three-player model redistributes strategic agency, emphasising a framework where No Trump strategies statistically outperform specific trump card selections. The core of this research is a rule-based dual-algorithm framework. First, we implement an iterative bidding algorithm that allows players to calibrate their bids dynamically based on evolving hand strengths. Second, we introduce a predictive iterative algorithm designed to calculate the expected number of tricks a player will secure before the lead card is played. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on backtracking or high-complexity dynamic programming, our iterative method significantly reduces time complexity. This efficiency is crucial for real-time gameplay, enabling players to perform complex probability assessments instantly without computational lag. To validate the model, a simulation was conducted on a dataset of 1,00,000 game instances. This large-scale analysis allowed for a precise comparison between initial bidding, outcomes, and overall bidding accuracy. The empirical results demonstrate that our algorithm not only enhances the balance and fairness of the auction bridge but also exhibits high reliability in predictive accuracy. Beyond the realm of card games, the methodology behind this iterative approach shows significant promise for quantitative financial domains. By modelling uncertainty and strategic competition, the algorithm offers valuable insights into risk management and decision-making in volatile market environments.

title: A Reconciliation Protocol for Tactical Asset Allocation: Forecasting, Exposure, and Economic Value in Relative-Performance Regimes
affiliations: and Independent

detail.title: A Reconciliation Protocol for Tactical Asset Allocation: Forecasting, Exposure, and Economic Value in Relative-Performance Regimes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. This research was conducted in a personal capacity and does not represent or imply the views, endorsement, or investment recommendations of any employer or institution.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses secondary financial-market data and involves no human participants, personal data, animals, or clinical intervention.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a reconciliation protocol for evaluating whether market-regime forecasts create economically meaningful tactical asset allocation value. Monthly stock, bond, and cash returns are used to construct three relative-performance regimes from stock-bond and bond-cash return spreads. Regime estimation and model development end in December 2019, while January 2020 through December 2025 forms a 72-month retrospective holdout. Continuation and Markov benchmarks are compared with regularized linear and shallow nonlinear machine-learning models under a common information set, chronological tuning, a fixed allocation policy map, and transaction costs. Evaluation combines multiclass forecast losses, transition-conditional accuracy, block-bootstrap inference, multiplicity adjustment, minimum detectable effects, exposure-matched static benchmarks, and performance-concentration diagnostics.

Model complexity does not produce reliable improvements over simple persistence-based rules. The continuation strategy records an annualized active-return point estimate of 0.82% relative to a 60/40 benchmark, but its block-bootstrap confidence interval ranges from -1.96% to 3.70%, and the observed information ratio is only 0.185. Approximately 85% of its observed total active return is attributed to average static exposure rather than dynamic timing, while removing the five strongest active-return months changes its annualized active return to -1.70%. Transition evidence is likewise weak after conditioning on the appropriate transition null and accounting for dependence and multiple testing. The short holdout can detect only unusually large effects, so failure to reject zero does not establish that all smaller effects are absent.

The main contribution is therefore not a profitable trading rule, but a reusable evaluation protocol that separates forecast quality, persistence, average exposure, dynamic timing, performance concentration, and statistical power before tactical allocation value is claimed.

Declaration of Generative AI and AI-Assisted Technologies: Generative AI tools were used to assist with language drafting and editing, computational code development, and code review. The authors independently reviewed and verified the research design, empirical implementation, reported results, interpretation, and final manuscript, and take full responsibility for the content of this paper.

title: Pricing AI Technology for Healthcare Services
affiliations: School of Business, Sun Yat-sen University, University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business, School of Business, Sun Yat-sen University and

detail.title: Pricing AI Technology for Healthcare Services

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve healthcare quality and service throughput, but greater AI capability does not necessarily mean more patients receive AI-assisted care. We consider a game-theoretic queueing model of the interactions among AI firm pricing, hospital adoption and capacity decisions, and patients' care-seeking decisions. The AI firm sells an AI tool to a hospital. The tool's AI capability is characterized by its effectiveness in improving care quality and efficiency in increasing service rate. The firm chooses among subscription, pay-per-use, and hybrid pricing. Each AI use generates data value and incurs an operating cost, and their difference is the firm's net value per AI use. We obtain three main results. First, although AI is often expected to substitute for clinical labor, the hospital may expand capacity after AI adoption when demand expansion from improved quality and throughput dominates efficiency gains that reduce capacity requirements. Second, AI adoption does not necessarily increase the number of patients served relative to the no-AI benchmark. AI penetration, measured by the number of patients receiving AI-assisted care, is highest under subscription and lowest under pay-per-use pricing. Third, subscription pricing is optimal when the firm's net value per AI use is nonnegative. When it is negative, the optimal scheme may shift from pay-per-use to hybrid or subscription pricing as AI efficiency increases. The thresholds decrease as AI effectiveness improves. Pay-per-use pricing can create a win-win outcome for the hospital and AI firm yet need not expand patient access.

title: Tokenization and the Cost of Capital: A Five-Channel Valuation Framework with Event-Study and Practitioner Evidence

detail.title: Tokenization and the Cost of Capital: A Five-Channel Valuation Framework with Event-Study and Practitioner Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper is academic research and does not constitute investment, legal, or tax advice. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any employer or affiliated organization. The author declares no conflict of interest and received no external funding. The research, analysis, and writing are the author's own work. Replication code and the accompanying valuation tool are released under AGPL-3.0 (Appendix G). The author thanks the twelve tokenization practitioners across five jurisdictions who volunteered their time to complete the perception instrument. In an emerging field with a genuinely small population of qualified respondents, each response carried disproportionate weight.
declarations.funderStatement: Non-funded research.

detail.abstract: Paper type: Research. Mixed-evidence study combining a large-sample event study with a primary practitioner-perception instrument. Purpose: This paper develops and evaluates a five-channel framework – the Tokenized Asset Valuation Engine (TAVE) – that maps enterprise asset tokenization onto the weighted average cost of capital (WACC), establishes how equity markets price tokenization announcements, and tests how the practitioners who lead these decisions perceive the same channels. It addresses a question secondary market data alone cannot answer: not only how the market prices tokenization, but why. Design/methodology/approach: The design pairs an event study of 1,169 verified tokenization announcements by 35 listed firms across five jurisdictions (2021–2025) with a cross-sectional perception survey of tokenization decision-makers (N = 12). The market layer applies eventinduced-variance-corrected tests, firm-clustered cross-sectional regressions, wild cluster bootstrap inference, a matched-control difference-in-differences (DiD) liquidity test, and tendraw placebo falsification. The perception layer uses a 24-item, six-construct reflective instrument analyzed descriptively and qualitatively, with the specified partial least squares structural equation model (PLS-SEM) estimated on an exploratory, explicitly caveated basis. Findings: Markets price tokenization announcements negatively and significantly (CAAR – 0.260%, BMP p = 0.002; significant at the 1% level in all five windows). No cross-sectional covariate robustly differentiates that reaction: an apparently decisive jurisdiction effect (analytic p < 0.001) collapses under a wild cluster bootstrap (p = 0.31), the exclusion of one misbenchmarked firm (p = 0.85), and announcement-composition controls. The liquidity channel splits: baseline illiquidity is not priced across firms, yet price impact falls 2.70% against matched non-announcing peers (p < 0.001) – the mechanism operates before the market prices it. Not one of the 1,169 events disclosed a smart-contract audit. Practitioners rate transparency (4.98/7) and regulatory uncertainty (4.97/7) highest, converging with market behavior on risk and diverging from it on benefit. Practical implications: CFOs gain a channel-by-channel structure for the financial case and a measured liquidity benefit to communicate; investors gain evidence that no observable firm trait differentiates announcement reactions; standard-setters, auditors, and regulators gain a concrete, evidence-based disclosure recommendation grounded in a complete null. Originality/value: The paper integrates liquidity, information, collateral, and two tokenizationspecific risk channels into a single valuation identity, tests it on the largest verified sample of enterprise tokenization events assembled to date, and adds a perception layer that locates the reasoning behind market behavior. It also documents a methodological case in which few-cluster analytic inference manufactured a false positive that the study's own robustness battery detected.

title:
Artificial Intelligence in Wealth Management: 
Fiduciary Responsibility and Regulatory Adaptation under EU Law
affiliations: Democritus University of Thrace, Law School

detail.title:
Artificial Intelligence in Wealth Management: 
Fiduciary Responsibility and Regulatory Adaptation under EU Law
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the wealth-management industry, accelerating its transition from a relationship-based and human-centred professional service to a technologically mediated, data-driven, autonomous form of financial intermediation. Historically grounded in fiduciary-like duties of loyalty, diligence, confidentiality, and acting in the client’s best interests, wealth management has evolved beyond its association with private banking into a holistic service encompassing portfolio management, investment advice, retirement planning, tax and estate planning. Robo-advisors, large language models, and agentic AI systems have democratised access to personalised financial services for retail investors, supporting financial inclusion and capital-market participation. Yet the substitution of human judgment by algorithms raises questions on the viability of the fiduciary paradigm underpinning these relationships.

This article examines the implications of AI deployment in wealth management through the lens of European Union law. It analyses the principal risks associated with AI-enabled advisory and portfolio-management activities, including opacity, explainability deficits, conflicts of interest, discriminatory outcomes, manipulative design, hallucinations, data-quality failures, and threats to market integrity and financial stability. Attention is devoted to the tension between the promises of scalability, efficiency, and personalisation offered by AI and the enduring objectives of investor protection and trust in financial markets. Against this background, a layered interpretation of the European regulatory framework governing wealth-management AI is developed, analysing the interaction between sectoral legislation, particularly MiFID II, IDD, and DORA, and horizontal instruments, including the AI Act, GDPR, and the revised Product Liability Directive. An apparent asymmetry is identified between risk classification and fiduciary intensity, since most wealth-management AI systems are treated as limited-risk despite their potential to affect severely life savings, retirement outcomes, and market stability. It is argued, however, that when interpreted teleologically and systematically, the combined operation of sectoral and cross-sectoral legislation produces a coherent framework of obligations for the AI systems providers and deployers, capable of addressing the distinctive risks posed by AI-enabled wealth management.

A central thesis advanced is that the European Supervisory Authorities (ESMA, EBA, EIOPA), play a decisive role in bridging the gap between technologically neutral statutory provisions and rapidly evolving AI applications. Through guidelines, opinions and other soft-law instruments, these authorities translate professional duties into concrete AI-governance expectations relating to transparency, explainability, documentation, data governance, human oversight, auditability, model validation and operational resilience. Fiduciary responsibility is therefore not displaced but operationalised through an increasingly sophisticated framework of technological governance and supervisory oversight.

The article further situates wealth-management AI within the evolving EU legislative landscape. Recent initiatives, including the CCD II, the DMD II, the Digital Omnibus reforms, and the RIS, reveal a broader regulatory movement towards enhanced rights to human involvement, meaningful explanation, protection against dark digital interfaces, and improved retail-investor empowerment, while also seeking to simplify disproportionate compliance obligations and preserve European competitiveness. Rather than signalling the tightening of regulatory regime for wealth-management AI, these developments point towards the incremental adaptation and refinement of existing legal frameworks.

Finally, the article highlights the challenges arising in non-harmonised components of wealth management, particularly tax advice and estate planning, both closely connected to legal advice. Unlike investment, banking, and insurance activities, these domains remain subject to national professional rules, raising questions regarding professional authorisation, accountability, and the scope of AI-assisted recommendation and decision-making. It is argued that AI systems operating in such contexts cannot lawfully substitute qualified professional judgment and should incorporate effective technical guardrails and human intervention mechanisms to reduce liability risks. The article concludes that AI can be accommodated within the fiduciary architecture of wealth management only through robust governance, proportionate systems-quality management, widespread explainability, effective human oversight, supervisory coordination, and strengthened financial and AI literacy among all relevant stakeholders.

title: When Every Watchdog Sleeps

detail.title: When Every Watchdog Sleeps

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial, personal or professional relationships that could have influenced, or reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study is based exclusively on publicly available documents and did not involve human participants, personal data, interviews or identifiable case-study subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was independently undertaken by the author.

detail.abstract: Persistent distress in Bangladesh banking cannot be explained adequately by the absence of rules, boards, audit committees or supervisory mandates. This paper asks why formally visible control arrangements may coexist with delayed challenge, weak escalation and recurring loss. It develops and applies an internal control imbalance diagnostic to a purposive documentary corpus comprising Bangladesh banking rules and stability publications, international governance standards, and prudential expectations from Australia and the United Kingdom. The method is a structured qualitative content analysis. Seven application domains are selected from Control Portfolio Theory's twelve control families: administrative, managerial, ethical, cultural, monitoring and feedback, informational transparency, and adaptive learning. The comparison is functional rather than a country ranking: it tests whether responsibility, independence, information, challenge, consequence and learning are mutually reinforcing. The analysis finds that Bangladesh's formal architecture recognises many expected governance structures, but documentary compliance alone cannot establish their operating effectiveness. The principal vulnerability is control concentration: policies, committees, approvals and reporting can dominate while protected challenge, transparent follow-up, credible consequences and organisational learning remain comparatively difficult to observe. The paper therefore reframes governance failure as an assurance-chain problem. A watchdog is effective only when it has authority, independence, information, capability, escalation routes and consequence support at the same time. The contribution is an auditable diagnostic and a set of reform propositions that can be tested through supervisory files, enforcement outcomes, board records and longitudinal bank data. The paper does not infer misconduct by any named institution and does not claim causal proof from documentary evidence alone.

title:
When AI Says "Honestly" 
Honesty and Sycophancy as Two Sides of the Same Coin in the Speech of Language Models

detail.title:
When AI Says "Honestly" 
Honesty and Sycophancy as Two Sides of the Same Coin in the Speech of Language Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently through the British Institute for Ignorance Studies (BIIS) and received no external funding.
declarations.funderStatement: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently through the British Institute for Ignorance Studies (BIIS) and received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
What happens when a language model says "to be honest"? Tracing this small linguistic marker, this essay arrives at two seemingly opposite but in fact intertwined phenomena: honesty and sycophancy in the speech of artificial intelligence. Drawing on evidence from the world's literary and philosophical traditions and on discourse markers in linguistics, the essay argues that sycophancy, not honesty, is the default behavioural stance in relationships of power, and that the honesty marker carries meaning only because it departs from this default.

This analysis is reinforced by a large-scale quantitative finding: a study showing that users rated sycophantic AI responses as more trustworthy than honest ones, even when those same responses distorted their moral judgement.

The essay's final conclusion is a cautious one. In a system shaped by human approval, the training process has no means of distinguishing genuine honesty from its persuasive display, and for a user who has access only to that system, this inability to tell the difference is, in practice, just as consequential as the absence of any difference at all.

detail.abstract:
This research paper is written by Matteo Aquilina (Bank for International Settlements, Macquarie University), Alfred Lehar (University of Calgary), Federico Ravenna (Collegio Carlo Alberto, University of Turin, HEC Montreal, CEPR) and Lorenzo Schönleber (Collegio Carlo Alberto, University of Turin).

The paper studies the role of the rapidly expanding asset class of tokenised money market funds (TMMFs) within the digital finance ecosystem. TMMFs represent blockchain-native claims on conventional money market funds that combine on-chain settlements with off-chain short-term safe assets. We document their institutional structure and market evolution. Exploiting exogenous shocks to crypto-asset prices, we show that markets perceive TMMFs as safer than stablecoins, whose main role in digital finance remains that of a medium of exchange. In contrast, TMMFs increasingly perform a store-of-value role, acting as safe havens during periods of market stress.

title: 3DFaceARC: 3D Face Reconstruction Via Single-View 2D Scene Using Graph Neural Networks
affiliations: Kathmandu University, Kathmandu University, Kathmandu University, Kathmandu University, Kathmandu University and Kathmandu University

detail.title: 3DFaceARC: 3D Face Reconstruction Via Single-View 2D Scene Using Graph Neural Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We do not perceive any organizations as having influenced this study.
declarations.funderStatement: We do not know of any organizations that have funded this research.

detail.abstract: Three-dimensional reconstruction recovers a 3D model from 2D images or data, capturing geometric structure, depth, and spatial arrangement for a realistic representation. In this paper, we present an end-to-end, self-supervised deep learning system for reconstructing high-quality 3D facial models from single 2D images, combining a 3DMM prior, the Basel Face Model 2019, a graph neural network (GNN)-based mesh refinement module, and a differentiable renderer, trained using seven photometric, perceptual, geometric, and identity-based losses without requiring 3D ground truth, depth sensors, or manual annotation. We conduct a controlled comparative study of three GNN architectures: GCN, GAT, and Graph-SAGE, as the mesh-refinement backbone displacing a coarse 53,215-vertex 3DMM mesh toward image evidence. Under an identical training budget, GCN achieves the lowest and most stable validation loss of 2.4245 at epoch 91; GAT performs comparably, with 2.4278 loss at epoch 58 with minor transient instability, while GraphSAGE reaches a similar early optimum of 2.4793 loss at epoch 33 but later diverges due to unbounded growth of the shape-regularization term, revealing an inductive-bias mismatch with the mesh's fixed, near-regular topology. Per-term loss decomposition shows all three architectures converge to nearly identical photometric, perceptual, and identity losses, indicating that the GNN backbone is not the primary performance bottleneck; instead, the photometric/perceptual supervision signal and the capacity split between the 3DMM prior and GNN displacement field dominate reconstruction fidelity.

detail.abstract: Reliable information infrastructure is often presented as a prerequisite for resilient healthcare supply chains, but national evidence should distinguish infrastructure growth from service continuity. This study analyzes annual public secondary data for Egypt from 2010 to 2024, combining internet use, secure internet-server density, DPT3 immunization coverage, life expectancy, and infant mortality. Internet use increased by 53.1 percentage points and secure-server density rose 35.8-fold. DPT3 coverage remained within a narrow 93-97% range and averaged 95.3%. The information-infrastructure index was not significantly associated with the coverage level (Spearman rho=0.19, p=0.507), although greater infrastructure was moderately associated with lower year-to-year volatility. Interruptedtrend models show that immunization coverage was broadly maintained during 2020-2021 and strengthened thereafter, while life expectancy experienced a temporary negative level shift followed by recovery. The findings suggest that connectivity may support continuity but cannot be interpreted as its cause. Program design, procurement, cold-chain capacity, workforce routines, security, and governance remain necessary complementary mechanisms. AI disclosure. title: Recalibrating the Plenary Power Doctrine After Trump v. Hawaii, Thuraissigiam, and Loper Bright

detail.title: Recalibrating the Plenary Power Doctrine After Trump v. Hawaii, Thuraissigiam, and Loper Bright

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, professional, or financial relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because the research did not involve human participants, patients, or the collection of personal data. The article is based solely on legal and doctrinal research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
This Article reexamines the constitutional foundations and contemporary operation of the plenary power doctrine in U.S. immigration law. For more than a century, the doctrine has afforded Congress and the Executive substantial authority over the admission, exclusion, detention, and removal of noncitizens while limiting the judiciary’s role in reviewing immigration decisions. The Article asks whether that exceptional level of judicial deference remains constitutionally justified in light of modern separation-of-powers principles, equal protection norms, and the Supreme Court’s post-Chevron approach to statutory interpretation.

The Article traces the development of immigration exceptionalism from the Chinese Exclusion era through the modern administrative state. It demonstrates that the plenary power doctrine was not derived from an express constitutional provision but developed through judicial decisions that accorded the political branches broad authority over immigration. At the same time, the Court has repeatedly recognized constitutional and statutory limits on that authority, particularly in cases involving noncitizens within the United States, detention, due process, equal protection, and habeas corpus.

The Article then examines the significance of Trump v. Hawaii, Department of Homeland Security v. Thuraissigiam, Garland v. Gonzalez, and United States v. Texas. These decisions reveal that contemporary immigration law does not operate under either absolute judicial deference or ordinary unrestricted judicial review. Instead, the availability and intensity of review vary according to the nature of the governmental action, the individual’s legal and geographic status, the source of the challenged authority, and the procedural vehicle through which judicial review is sought.

Particular attention is given to Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and the Supreme Court’s rejection of Chevron deference. Loper Bright reaffirmed that courts, rather than administrative agencies, must exercise independent judgment in determining the meaning of federal statutes. The Article argues that this development has important implications for immigration law. Although Loper Bright does not itself abolish the plenary power doctrine, it weakens the justification for allowing immigration agencies to receive broad deference concerning questions of statutory meaning merely because those questions arise in the immigration context.

The Article also incorporates comparative perspectives from Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, and South Africa to examine how constitutional democracies reconcile sovereign control over borders with meaningful judicial oversight. Drawing on these domestic and comparative developments, the Article proposes a calibrated framework for recalibrating rather than abolishing plenary power. Under this framework, courts should retain structural review to protect separation-of-powers principles and the Suspension Clause; apply meaningful rationality review, including scrutiny for impermissible animus, in appropriate entry and exclusion cases; and conduct full Administrative Procedure Act review of executive agency action, including arbitrary-and-capricious review without Chevron deference.

The Article’s central contribution is to bring together doctrinal developments that have frequently been examined separately. Trump v. Hawaii demonstrates the continuing force of immigration deference; Thuraissigiam illustrates the consequences of restricting the availability of judicial review; and Loper Bright reaffirms the judiciary’s independent responsibility to interpret federal law. Read together, these decisions provide a basis for distinguishing legitimate political-branch discretion from judicial abdication. The Article therefore argues that plenary power can survive as a limited recognition of congressional and executive authority over immigration while its most expansive forms of judicial deference are recalibrated. Such an approach would preserve legitimate governmental authority over borders and foreign affairs while restoring a meaningful judicial role in enforcing statutory boundaries, constitutional limitations, and individual rights.

title: The limits of price-based coordination in electricity market design: A multi-criteria agent-based benchmark of eight competing architectures
affiliations: Technische Universität München (TUM), Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt, Regensburg University of Applied Sciences, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Technische Universität München (TUM) and Technische Universität München (TUM) - Department of Energy and Process Engineering

detail.title: The limits of price-based coordination in electricity market design: A multi-criteria agent-based benchmark of eight competing architectures
detail.abstract: As the electrification of heating and mobility accelerates, activating demand-side flexibility is critical to preventing distribution grid congestion, yet the comparative impacts of competing market architectures remain contested. This study presents the first agent-based comparison of this breadth: eight competing market designs, from flat tariffs to local energy markets, simulated under identical conditions on a future high-flexibility German low-voltage feeder used as a forward-looking stress test. The central finding is a structural complexity-performance paradox. Increasing market sophistication does not produce monotonic performance improvements across technical, economic, social, and environmental dimensions. Deploying a home energy management system under static tariffs already captures a substantial local optimization dividend. Conversely, dynamic pricing improves economic and environmental outcomes but worsens grid stress through load synchronization, driving peak transformer loading above 400 % of rated capacity. Feeder-level dynamic grid fees struggle to prevent these overloads, while local energy markets offer a more balanced profile but cannot resolve structural winter congestion. Benchmarked against a constrained-optimum reference whose dual is the distribution locational marginal price, the price-based designs sit far from a coordination that secures the feeder at its rating, exposing their overloads as a coordination artifact rather than a physical capacity deficit. The underlying mechanism is the inability of pure energy-price signals to substitute for instantaneous, locational capacity coordination, indicating that grid-compatible operation depends on enforcing the transfer-capacity constraint rather than approximating it through a price.

detail.abstract: Knowledge workers now have access to artificial intelligence tools that can draft, summarise, search, analyse and even write code. Whether these tools actually make knowledge work more productive is one of the defining questions of the current decade. This paper reviews the evidence on AI and knowledge worker productivity and argues that the tools are real but the gains are conditional. Randomised experiments and field studies show substantial average productivity gains, from about 14 per cent for customer support agents to roughly 40 per cent time savings on professional writing tasks, yet the same studies reveal striking variation between people, tasks and skill levels. Survey data show that adoption is widespread but that few organisations have captured bottom-line value, and the risks, from hallucination and overtrust to deskilling and weak data foundations, are as documented as the benefits. The paper argues that AI does not replace knowledge management; it depends on it. Lasting productivity gains come when capable tools meet well-managed knowledge, clean data, redesigned workflows and people who are trained, trusted and supported. The paper reviews the modern landscape of AI tools for knowledge work, synthesises the experimental and survey evidence, examines failure modes, and proposes a practical framework for measuring knowledge worker productivity and for introducing AI in ways that produce gains that last.

title: Counteracting Institutions or Rent Extractors? Intermediaries and Information Asymmetry in International Student Accommodation

detail.abstract: Indian students are now the largest group of international students in the United Kingdom, and many arrange their first accommodation before arrival, remotely, sight unseen, and through intermediaries whose incentives they cannot see. Education agents, digital accommodation aggregators, and universities that refer students onward stand between the student and the housing market, yet this intermediary layer has fallen between two literatures: research on student mobility examines how students are recruited, and research on student accommodation how students and their housing transform the cities around them, while the process by which they actually reach housing, and are channelled toward it, goes largely unexamined. This paper brings the migration-infrastructure and migration-industry traditions onto the terrain of accommodation and reads them through information economics (Akerlof, 1970) to pose two linked questions. First: do these intermediaries act as counteracting institutions that reduce the information asymmetry students face, or as rent extractors that profit from preserving it? Second: when students attempt to route around or push back against them, does their resistance reshape the structure or is it absorbed by it? Mapping the intermediary pathways of the India-UK corridor; drawing, where the commercial structure is undocumented, on practitioner knowledge, the paper specifies what would distinguish an intermediary that serves students from one that lives upon them, and sets out a research design through which the questions could be answered. Its contribution is to convert a diffuse and unproven suspicion into a located, testable question, and to make it answerable.

detail.abstract: Critical infrastructure operations increasingly depend on interconnected digital, physical, and cyber systems, creating complex conditions in which equipment failures, cyber incidents, environmental disturbances, and operational disruptions can propagate across infrastructure networks. As these systems become more interconnected, reactive monitoring alone is increasingly insufficient because it primarily identifies abnormal conditions after they have emerged rather than supporting timely anticipation of their potential consequences. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven anomaly detection provides an important capability by identifying unusual operational, cyber, environmental, and equipment conditions from continuously generated infrastructure data. However, effective resilience requires moving beyond anomaly identification toward predictive assessment of the risks associated with detected abnormalities. This study conducts a systematic critical literature synthesis of 20 supplied publications to examine the relationships among real-time infrastructure data, anomaly detection, data reliability, predictive risk assessment, uncertainty, decision confidence, adaptive response, and infrastructure resilience. The synthesis indicates that anomaly detection alone does not automatically produce reliable risk decisions. The significance of an identified anomaly depends on the quality and reliability of the underlying data, the operational context in which it occurs, prevailing cybersecurity conditions, and the uncertainty surrounding its interpretation and potential consequences. Based on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual framework comprising eight connected stages: Data Acquisition → Data Reliability Assessment → AI-Driven Anomaly Detection → Contextual Interpretation → Predictive Risk Assessment → Uncertainty and Decision Confidence Assessment → Adaptive Response → Resilience Feedback. The framework emphasizes that trustworthy infrastructure intelligence requires detected abnormalities to be evaluated within their operational and data context before risk-informed action is taken. Overall, resilient infrastructure operations require AI systems that progress beyond detecting abnormalities toward producing context-aware, reliability-informed, and uncertainty-sensitive risk intelligence that supports adaptive decision-making and continuous resilience improvement. (Diyora; Sarker; Hasnaine, Ibrahem, and Fouda; Alasa et al.; Martins)

detail.abstract: Critical infrastructure networks increasingly depend on heterogeneous data generated by sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, operational technology, cybersecurity systems, and environmental sources. However, conventional monitoring approaches often identify anomalous conditions without adequately interpreting the operational context in which those signals emerge. This study examines the role of context-aware machine learning (ML) in strengthening early-warning and predictive risk intelligence for critical infrastructure. A systematic critical literature synthesis of 20 selected publications was conducted, with evidence organized around context-aware sensing, machine-learning prediction, anomaly detection, data reliability, cybersecurity, uncertainty, and infrastructure resilience. The synthesized findings indicate that operational context substantially improves the interpretation of infrastructure signals by helping distinguish normal variation from potentially meaningful early-warning conditions. The evidence further demonstrates that predictive performance depends not only on model capability but also on the reliability, relevance, timeliness, and contextual quality of underlying data. Consequently, effective early warning should progress beyond isolated anomaly detection toward context-aware risk prediction that integrates changing operational conditions and uncertainty. The study concludes that a context-aware ML architecture can connect real-time data acquisition with predictive risk intelligence and adaptive warning mechanisms. Importantly, high model confidence should not automatically be interpreted as high decision confidence, particularly when contextual reliability or operational conditions are uncertain.

title: Mandatory Disclosure of Investor Complaints and Firm Risk: Evidence from India
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Management (IIM), Indore

detail.title: Mandatory Disclosure of Investor Complaints and Firm Risk: Evidence from India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: We examine how equity markets respond to mandatory disclosure of shareholder complaints. India's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations (LODR), effective 1 December 2015, require listed firms to disclose quarterly the number of investor complaints received, resolved, and pending. Although the mandate applied to all listed firms, their informational exposure varied with pre-mandate complaint intensity. Firms with higher prior complaint intensity revealed more information about previously private grievances. Using 6,993 firm-year observations for 722 Indian listed firms from financial year 2011 to 2021, we find that a shift from the 25th to the 75th percentile of pre-mandate complaint intensity is associated with a 2.6% increase in idiosyncratic risk. Systematic risk is unaffected, and the total-risk effect persists after conditioning on systematic risk. Notably, the effect is absent in the implementation year but accumulates thereafter, reaching 4.7% by financial year 2021. Pre-trend tests and three pseudoevent placebos are insignificant, and the pattern is unaffected by the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Overall, the evidence suggests that the repeated disclosure of realized shareholder grievances is gradually reflected in equity prices. Rather than reducing uncertainty, greater visibility of shareholder grievances increases firm-specific uncertainty, revealing an unintended informational consequence of mandatory disclosure.

detail.abstract: Higher education institutions frequently express commitments to inclusion, belonging, diversity, civil discourse, and evidence-informed decision-making. The more difficult leadership question is whether institutional systems are capable of translating those commitments into practice. This white paper examines inclusion as a test of leadership and institutional capacity. It argues that inclusive leadership should not be evaluated primarily through statements, representation initiatives, committees, programs, or expressed intentions. Instead, leadership should be evaluated through the systems institutions build to recognize different experiences, identify meaningful disparities, facilitate participation, support productive disagreement, respond to concerns, evaluate outcomes, accept accountability, and adapt when evidence indicates that existing approaches are ineffective or incomplete.

title: A Comparative Study of Adolescents With and Without Skin Disorders on Stress, Coping and Mental Health
affiliations: and Panjab University, Chandigarh - Panjab University

detail.title: A Comparative Study of Adolescents With and Without Skin Disorders on Stress, Coping and Mental Health

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The study examined the relationship between skin disorders and psychological well-being among adolescents aged 16–18 years. Comparing 300 adolescents with skin disorders and 100 healthy controls, the researchers found that adolescents with skin disorders experienced significantly greater stress symptoms, perceived stress, daily hassles, and task-focused coping. A discriminant function analysis further demonstrated that psychological variables could distinguish adolescents with and without skin disorders with 91.3% accuracy. Perceived stress, stress symptoms, avoidant-focused coping, and daily hassles emerged as the strongest predictors of group membership. The findings highlight the importance of integrating psychological interventions, including psychotherapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, behavioral therapy, and stress management, alongside conventional dermatological treatment.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funds were used.

detail.abstract: Objective: The primary aim of the present investigation was to compare adolescents of both the genders, with and without Skin Disorders on Mental Health and its dimensions viz. Being Comfortable with Self, Being Comfortable with Others and Ability to meet Life’s demands, dimensions of Stress viz. Stress Symptoms, Perceived Stress, Daily Hassles and Uplifts and Ways of Coping. Method: The sample of the study comprised 400 adolescents in the age range from 16- 18 years. 300 adolescents (150 males and 150 females) comprised the sample with skin disorders. Sampling was purposive. The healthy controls comprised of 100 subjects (50 males and 50 females) chosen randomly from schools of tricity. Those comprising the Healthy Control group were currently without a history of any kind of skin problem. Care was taken to select the sample from middle socio- economic group which matched with the socio-economic status of the subjects and other important characteristics such as age, sex and educational background was also taken into consideration. Results: Adolescents with skin disorders scored higher than adolescents without skin disorders on Stress Symptoms (t=14.06, p< .01), Task Focused Coping (t = 7.46, p < .01), Daily Hassles (t = 11.79, p < .01) and Perceived Stress (t=6.52, p < .01). Discriminant Functional Analysis for adolescents with and without skin disorders revealed that discriminant function based on 20 predictors could predict group membership with 91.3% accuracy. It was concluded that a set of 4 predictors selected out of 11 variables are the best discriminants of adolescents with and without skin disorders. The predictors that emerged significant in order of importance were Perceived Stress, Stress Symptoms, Avoidant Focused Coping, and Daily Hassles. Conclusions: The results of this study provide ample evidence to start using psych dermatological therapies viz. psychotherapy, behavioral therapy, CBT, and stress management as an adjunct to medical interventions. Orienting adolescents to wholistic therapies may bring about a much faster relief physically and emotionally.

title: Relative Rationality Theory: Emotional Adjusted Value, Emotional Adjusted Cost, Emotional Net Sale Payoff, and the Three-Phase Utility Function over Emotional Adjusted Wealth
affiliations: Swiss Management Centre University (Switzerland), SMC University

detail.title: Relative Rationality Theory: Emotional Adjusted Value, Emotional Adjusted Cost, Emotional Net Sale Payoff, and the Three-Phase Utility Function over Emotional Adjusted Wealth

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no conflict of inteterest
declarations.funderStatement: self funded

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Relative Rationality Theory (RRT) as a cash-equivalent framework for integrating economic and emotional determinants of choice within a unified decision architecture. Standard decision theory can represent non-monetary motives within preference or utility, but these motives often remain operationally opaque. RRT addresses this limitation by decomposing options into economic revenues, economic costs, emotional revenues, and emotional costs, and by expressing the emotional components, where possible, in money-metric terms through the Di Toro Emotional Flowchart. The paper develops the core constructs of the framework: Emotional Adjusted Value (EAV) for offer side valuation, Emotional Adjusted Cost (EAC) for acquisition-side decisions, Emotional Net Sale Payoff (ENSP) for selling-side choice, and Emotional Adjusted Wealth (EAW) as the psychological wealth benchmark from which decisions are evaluated. These constructs generate Decision-EAW, the option-implied emotional-economic wealth position entering utility. The paper then introduces a Three-Phase Emotional Adjusted Wealth Utility Function, defined over EAW rather than nominal wealth, with recovery, Consumption Phase, and investment–psychological regions. RRT separates valuation from utility by first integrating economic and emotional determinants into Decision-EAW and only then applying utility to compare alternatives. Because Decision-EAW is expressed on a common money-metric scale that combines economic amounts with cash-equivalent emotional components, it can enter a Bernoulli-style utility function as the wealth argument, with EAW on the horizontal axis and utility on the vertical axis. Choices that appear anomalous when emotional and contextual determinants remain implicit may become analytically transparent once those determinants are explicitly decomposed within the emotional economic valuation field. To the author’s knowledge, RRT is the first unified mathematical framework to integrate receiving, acquisition, selling, choice under risk and uncertainty, counterfactual emotion, and wealth-state evaluation within a single emotional-economic, cash-equivalent decision architecture.

title: The Style-Switching Fallacy: Why Eclectic Leadership Depends on Cognitive Integration, Not Behavioural Adaptation
affiliations: and Rononiti Eclectic Leadership Design Lab & Advisory

detail.title: The Style-Switching Fallacy: Why Eclectic Leadership Depends on Cognitive Integration, Not Behavioural Adaptation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: For half a century, dominant models of adaptive leadership have asked leaders to diagnose a situation and then consciously select and execute a matching behavioural style. This article argues that the diagnose-select-execute mechanism these models share is neurocognitively implausible precisely under the conditions leadership matters most: moments of stress, ambiguity, and time pressure. Drawing together three literatures that have never been fused into a single critique, trait-stability research within contingency theory, cognitive resource theory's account of stress and intellectual performance, and Bourdieu's theory of habitus as embodied, largely pre-conscious disposition, the article shows that style-switching models quietly assume a reserve of deliberate cognitive bandwidth that stress is specifically documented to remove. It then proposes an alternative mechanism, termed cognitive integration, in which adaptive capacity is built upstream, in the range of knowledge domains a leader draws on to form judgement, rather than downstream, in the persona performed in the moment. "Style", the article argues, is what an observer names after the fact; the leader's own lever is the internal state that generates it, and emotion-regulation research on reappraisal versus suppression is used to explain how integrated judgement reaches behaviour without the leader ever consciously selecting a style. The article also addresses two natural objections: that emotional intelligence already covers this ground, and that no leader can consciously consult four knowledge domains in real time. The article closes with testable propositions distinguishing the mechanisms empirically.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping firms' production organization and supply chain governance structures. However, its environmental consequences extend beyond changes in the level of carbon emissions to encompass the stability of emission trajectories. Using the staggered establishment of National Pilot Zones for New-Generation Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Development as a quasi-natural experiment, and drawing on supply chain-matched panel data of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2023, this paper constructs a staggered difference-indifferences (DID) design to examine how AI empowerment among midstream core (anchor) firms affects the carbon emission volatility of their upstream suppliers and downstream customers. We find that after the cities hosting midstream core firms are designated as AI pilot zones, the carbon emission volatility of upstream suppliers declines significantly, while that of downstream customers rises significantly-an asymmetric transmission pattern of "dampening upstream volatility while amplifying downstream volatility." Further tests provide evidence consistent with the view that trade credit arrangements, operating expense adjustments, and changes in financing constraints are important channels through which AI empowerment affects supply chain carbon emission volatility, while the digital infrastructure of supply chain firms and the intensity of industry competition constitute important boundary conditions for this effect. This paper advances research on the environmental effects of AI from emission levels to emission volatility and uncovers a mechanism of carbon risk redistribution along the supply chain amid digital transformation.

detail.title: Productive Capabilities, Economic Complexity, and Structural Transformation in Argentina

This research was conducted independently, without any personal or financial relationships with individuals or organizations that could be perceived as influencing the study. The author is solely responsible for the content of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author carried out this work independently and without external financial support.

detail.abstract:
Argentina is entering a new phase of productive transformation driven by opportunities in energy, mining, agribusiness, biotechnology, knowledge-intensive services, and digital technologies. These opportunities are typically assessed through the lens of current comparative advantages or economic complexity indices based on export baskets. Both approaches, however, may be insufficient to capture the transformation potential of an economy that, over more than a century, underwent successive cycles of accumulation, disruption, adaptation, and partial loss of productive capabilities.

This paper proposes an alternative interpretation grounded in the notion of accumulated capabilities. The central hypothesis is that Argentina's stock of productive, technological, and entrepreneurial capabilities is larger than what its current productive and export structure reveals. A significant portion of these capabilities persists —albeit often latent or fragmented— in firms, workers, suppliers, institutions, infrastructure, organizational routines, and technological know-how, even when the activities that originally generated them have declined or disappeared. Under certain conditions, these capabilities can be transferred and recombined around new demands, giving rise to new productive activities and diversification opportunities.

The argument draws on the literature on technological capabilities (Lall, 1992; Bell & Pavitt, 1993), economic complexity and the product space (Hausmann & Klinger, 2007; Hidalgo et al., 2007; Hidalgo & Hausmann, 2009), relatedness and capability complementarity (Frenken et al., 2023), and recent empirical applications for Argentina using both complexity and skill-relatedness approaches (International Labour Organization, 2025; Fernández Franco et al., 2025). It also recovers the Argentine tradition of industrial transformation analysis developed by Kosacoff and his recent work with Fuchs (2024), which highlights accumulated strengths in knowledge-intensive sectors and natural resource-based activities, and calls for a policy framework to leverage these assets.

Through a historical analysis of ten productive trajectories —nuclear, aerospace and complex systems, automotive, agricultural machinery, steel and metallurgy, chemicals and petrochemicals, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology, energy, mining, and knowledge-intensive services— the paper argues that the observable productive structure does not exhaust the economy's stock of capabilities. New opportunities lie not within sectors, but at the intersections between accumulated capabilities and emerging demands. Natural resources, in this framework, are neither a primarization trap nor an automatic development solution; they are potential platforms for learning and for generating demand for industrial, technological, and service capabilities.

The paper concludes that Argentina's structural transformation does not require rebuilding the industrial pattern of the past nor starting from scratch. It requires identifying which capabilities survived, which can be transferred, which new demands can mobilize them, and which macroeconomic and institutional conditions allow learning processes to be sustained over time.

title: Exchange Rates and Asset Prices in a Global Demand System
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and Princeton University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Exchange Rates and Asset Prices in a Global Demand System
detail.abstract: We develop an asset demand system to analyze the equilibrium relation between international portfolio holdings and flows, exchange rates, and asset prices across all countries. We introduce a nested logit model of asset demand, for which we develop a new identification strategy by instrumental variables. Averaged across years and issuer countries, the demand elasticities are 27.9 for short-term debt, 3.2 for long-term debt, and 1.2 for equity. These demand elasticities are empirical targets for international macro models that feature inelastic demand to resolve long-standing puzzles in international finance. We use the estimated demand system to decompose the variation in exchange rates and asset prices into portfolio flows and shifts in asset demand, to interpret economic events such as the European sovereign debt crisis, and to estimate the convenience yields on US assets. In units of annual expected returns, the convenience yield is 1.41% on the US dollar, 2.71% on US long-term debt, and 0.50% on US equity.
