detail.abstract: Contemporary institutions possess increasingly sophisticated systems of regulation, auditing, data collection, and procedural control, yet major governance failures continue to develop without timely institutional recognition. This apparent contradiction suggests that the existence of formal oversight mechanisms does not necessarily ensure that organizations remain capable of identifying the gradual deterioration of their own operational behavior. This monograph introduces Institutional Drift Theory as a conceptual framework for explaining how institutions may progressively diverge from their formal purposes while preserving an appearance of procedural continuity and administrative normality. The study distinguishes the Formal Institution, constituted by official mandates, rules, structures, and control mechanisms, from the Behavioral Institution, formed by the routines, expectations, incentives, interpretative practices, and patterns of adaptation that guide decision-making in practice. Institutional Drift occurs as repeated exceptions, fragmented responsibilities, weakened escalation practices, and prolonged exposure to anomalies gradually alter what the organization recognizes as normal, material, or worthy of intervention. Under these conditions, institutional failure may emerge not from an absence of information, but from a declining capacity to connect dispersed evidence, challenge familiar explanations, and reinterpret recurring signals as manifestations of systemic risk. Drawing upon governance theory, public administration, organizational sociology, behavioral analysis, institutional economics, compliance studies, and systems thinking, the monograph develops a five-stage model of institutional deterioration and advances Behavioral Governance as a complementary approach to conventional oversight. The governance crisis surrounding Brazil’s Instituto Nacional do Seguro Social is employed as an analytical context through which the framework’s explanatory potential can be examined, without substituting theoretical interpretation for judicial, administrative, or investigative determinations. The study argues that effective institutional resilience depends not only upon stronger controls or greater informational capacity, but also upon the preservation of institutional curiosity, interpretative sensitivity, and the ability to recognize when repeated exposure has transformed exceptional conditions into accepted organizational reality. Institutional Drift Theory therefore redirects governance analysis from the visible moment of failure toward the behavioral transformations through which institutional self-correction is progressively weakened.

detail.abstract: Today, strategic employee relations requires companies to establish effective mechanisms for employees to raise concerns, resolve workplace disputes, and participate in processes that affect their working conditions. This study examines the extent to which strategic employee relations practices and grievance-management systems contribute to workplace stability, employee voice, organizational justice, conflict resolution, and organizational performance. To synthesize evidence on formal grievance procedures, employee voice, organizational justice, conflict management, mediation, dispute-resolution systems, and workplace outcomes, the study uses a structured literature-based method. The literature reviewed shows that grievance systems provide important institutional means for employees to communicate workplace concerns and seek organizational responses. It also appears that employees assess grievance procedures not only by outcomes but also by their perceptions of procedural fairness, respectful treatment, participation, and transparency. Approaches that emphasize participation can supplement formal procedures by strengthening employee voice and helping identify workplace problems early. Effective conflict management and dispute resolution practices can also help maintain trust and promote positive workplace relationships. Overall, the evidence supports viewing grievance management as a strategic employee relations mechanism rather than merely an administrative or disciplinary procedure. By incorporating principles of voice, fairness, participation, and conflict resolution into grievance systems, organizations can adopt a formal way of addressing workplace concerns that supports both employee relations and corporate stability.

title: Geopolitical Risk and the Deep Out-of-the-Money Put Puzzle: Tail Geometry across Global Equity Markets
affiliations: Hong Kong Chu Hai College, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology and Hong Kong Chu Hai College

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk and the Deep Out-of-the-Money Put Puzzle: Tail Geometry across Global Equity Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Deep out-of-the-money index puts are systematically overpriced, yet the observable factor reshaping equity left tails across countries remains unidentified. Using daily data for 45 global equity indices (2005-2024), we identify geopolitical risk (GPR) as that factor. Embedding GPR in a non-stationary Peaks-over-Threshold model yields closed-form tail geometry decomposing GPR effects into scale and curvature channels. GPR activates the left tail in 30 of 43 markets with a sign reversal: safe havens compress their tails under stress while emerging markets widen them. Emerging-market tail curvature is 1.42 times that of developed markets, and stronger institutions monotonically dampen tail escalation.

title: Project Development with Delegated Bargaining: The Role of Elevated Hurdle Rates
affiliations: Rice University, Rice University, Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business and

detail.title: Project Development with Delegated Bargaining: The Role of Elevated Hurdle Rates
detail.abstract: During project development, costs are endogenously determined through delegated bargaining with counterparties. In surveys, nearly 80% of CFOs report using an elevated hurdle rate, the implications of which we explore in a delegated bargaining model. We show that elevated hurdle rates can convey a bargaining advantage that exceeds the opportunity cost of forgone projects, whether hurdle rate buffers arise for strategic or non-strategic reasons. Using CFO survey data, we find buffer use is negatively related to the cost of capital and ex ante bargaining power, consistent with the model, and that realized returns exhibit “beat the hurdle rate benchmark” behavior.

title: Carbon Pricing and the Green-Credit Trap
affiliations: and Wuhan University of Technology

detail.title: Carbon Pricing and the Green-Credit Trap

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: Carbon pricing is the canonical emissions instrument, but the transition it sets in motion must be financed. We study it in a two-sector macro-finance model in which green and brown production are funded by constrained intermediaries and green claims are structurally harder to pledge. A carbon price lowers emissions, but it also reprices brown assets and weakens intermediary balance sheets. Intermediaries relieve the resulting tightness by rationing balance-sheet-intensive green exposure, and that apparent relief is where the trap springs: weaker green investment erodes deployment capacity, green productivity, and green pledgeability, and makes brown-sector abatement less efficient. Under the benchmark calibration, asymmetric green finance opens a green-capital shortfall of about 10% within fifteen years relative to a symmetric finance counterfactual---a scar that survives conservative robustness checks. Through the deployment-dependent abatement channel, the emissions gap over the same horizon accumulates to about 31% of initial steady-state annual emissions. A one-sided green credit guarantee insuring only the policy-induced deterioration in green pledgeability repairs much of this damage; once its resource cost is internalized, welfare selects moderate rather than full support. Treating the carbon price and guarantee as a restricted Ramsey problem shows they answer to different fundamentals: the welfare-preferred carbon price is disciplined by the social cost of carbon, the optimal guarantee by the fragility of green finance. Support should be sized to the balance sheet it repairs, not the ambition of the tax---so in a second-best economy, targeted financial support can restore the transmission of carbon pricing itself.

title: SYSTEMIC INSOLVENCY OF SWITZERLAND: A QUANTITATIVE DIAGNOSIS UNDER THE SVWORLD STANDARD 73.5 v2.3.2

detail.title: SYSTEMIC INSOLVENCY OF SWITZERLAND: A QUANTITATIVE DIAGNOSIS UNDER THE SVWORLD STANDARD 73.5 v2.3.2

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No
declarations.funderStatement: No

detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive 13-step diagnostic assessment of the Swiss Confederation under the SVWORLD Standard 73.5 v2.3.2. Based on concrete sums, rigorous calculations, and verified official data from international, national, statistical, and financial reports, all conclusions in this study are conclusively proven. The assessment yields a Raw Resilience Coefficient of 0.0075 (final CVR: 0.0072), unequivocally placing Switzerland in the deepest Red Zone of structural insolvency among all advanced economies-approximately 3.3 times worse than the United States.

title: Does Early Entry with Dynamic Pricing Work?
affiliations: Nova School of Business & Economics, Nova School of Business and Economics and

detail.title: Does Early Entry with Dynamic Pricing Work?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no competing interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This project has received funding from the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under grant agreement number 101095593 (project HI-PRIX: Health Innovation Next Generation Payment and Pricing Models).

publicationDetails.detailsText: Nova SBE Working Paper Series No. 692

detail.abstract: Under standard entry, a pharmaceutical product reaches the market only once health technology assessment (HTA) is completed; under early entry, it enters immediately after regulatory approval (typically by the FDA or EMA) at a discounted price that is later adjusted once HTA concludes (conditional pricing approach). We develop a two-period model that characterizes when early entry schemes dominate standard entry regimes, and identify three failures that can undermine this dominance. First, imperfect commitment by either the payer or the manufacturer narrows the static conditions under which early entry dominates. Second, the absence of formal HTA during the early entry period allows manufacturers to act as unrestricted monopolists, inflating the list price and neutralizing the discount entirely. Third, when commitment is the outcome of a repeated relationship, a larger discount raises the manufacturer's short-run gain from deviating, so that a discount large enough to make early entry attractive can be too large for cooperation. These three failures point in a common direction: the discount, the policy lever for adjusting dynamic pricing, is at best ineffective and at worst counterproductive, unless the initial list price is capped at a level the payer can verify before assessment.

title: The Economics of Walking About and Predicting Unemployment
affiliations: Dartmouth College - Department of Economics and University College London

detail.title: The Economics of Walking About and Predicting Unemployment
detail.abstract: Unemployment is notoriously difficult to predict.  In previous studies, once country fixed effects are added to panel estimates, few variables predict changes in unemployment rates.  Using panel data for 29 European countries over 439 months between 1985 and 2021 in an unbalanced country*month panel of just over 10000 observations, we predict changes in the unemployment rate 12 months in advance based on individuals’ fears of unemployment, their perceptions of the economic situation and their own household financial situation.  Fear of unemployment predicts subsequent changes in unemployment 12 months later in the presence of country fixed effects and lagged unemployment.  Individuals’ perceptions of the economic situation in the country and their own household finances also predict unemployment 12 months later. Business sentiment (industry fear of unemployment) is also predictive of unemployment 12 months later.  The findings underscore the importance of the “economics of walking about”. The implication is that these social survey data are informative in predicting economic downturns and should be used more extensively in forecasting.  We also generate a 29 country-level annual panel on life satisfaction from 1985-2020 from the World Database of Happiness and show that the consumer level fear of unemployment variable lowers well-being over and above the negative impact of the unemployment rate itself.  Qualitative survey metrics were able to predict the Great Recession and the economic slowdown in Europe just prior to the COVID19 pandemic.

detail.abstract: Modern medicine has largely been organized around a reactive principle: symptoms appear, disease is identified, and treatment begins. Artificial intelligence, longitudinal biological data, multi-omics, advanced imaging, biological-age measurements, wearable sensors, and emerging digital-twin technologies may gradually invert that model. This paper proposes the concept of Biological Foresight: a healthcare architecture in which artificial intelligence continuously estimates not simply an individual's present health, but the probable future trajectories of organs, biological systems, disease risks, and aging processes. Rather than waiting for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, cancer, frailty, or metabolic dysfunction to cross conventional diagnostic thresholds, future health systems may increasingly detect deviations years earlier and identify periods during which intervention could produce the greatest preventive benefit. The central economic and medical proposition is therefore larger than "anti-aging." The emerging industry is the prediction, prevention, and management of biological deterioration before irreversible disease becomes established.

title: Zombie Lending: Theoretical, International and Historical Perspectives
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business, New York University (NYU) - Department of Finance, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Nova School of Business and Economics and Frankfurt School of Finance & Management

detail.title: Zombie Lending: Theoretical, International and Historical Perspectives
detail.abstract: This paper surveys the theory on zombie lending incentives and the consequences of zombie lending for the real economy. It also offers a historical perspective by reviewing the growing empirical evidence on zombie lending along three dimensions: (i) the role of under-capitalized banks, (ii) effects on zombie firms, and (iii) spillovers and distortions for non-zombie firms. We then provide an overview of how zombie lending can be attenuated. Finally, we use a sample of U.S. publicly listed firms to compare various measures proposed in the literature to classify firms as "zombies." We identify definitions of zombie firms that are adequate to investigate economic inefficiency in the form of real sector competitive distortions of zombie lending. We find that only definitions that are based on interest rate subsidies are able to detect these spillovers and thereby provide evidence in support of credit misallocation.

title: Money, Information, and Central Bank Communication
affiliations: University of Liverpool Management School

detail.title: Money, Information, and Central Bank Communication

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: We develop a monetary model in which sellers acquire information about demand to guide investment, and their collective effort improves the central bank's information. Better information can worsen underinvestment and reduce welfare. Central bank information disclosure can crowd out private information acquisition. Unlike discretionary disclosure, commitment to a disclosure rule internalizes how disclosure affects information production and buyer liquidity. The central bank may therefore disclose less to preserve socially valuable private information or more to crowd out excessive acquisition. Monetary policy shapes these incentives through buyer liquidity, so the disclosure ranking between commitment and discretion can reverse as inflation changes.

title: Selective Spillover of the Fed Funds Rate: Evidence of Heterogeneous Cointegration in ASEAN-3 Capital Markets and Exchange Rates

detail.title: Selective Spillover of the Fed Funds Rate: Evidence of Heterogeneous Cointegration in ASEAN-3 Capital Markets and Exchange Rates

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors

detail.abstract: This study examines the selective and heterogeneous spillover of United States Federal Reserve (Fed) monetary policy to three ASEAN emerging economies, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand, across two market channels, the nominal exchange rate and the domestic equity index. Using monthly data from January 2021 to July 2026 (T = 67 observations), the Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR) is tested against the nominal exchange rate (USD/IDR, USD/MYR, USD/THB) and the benchmark stock market index (IHSG, KLCI, SET Index) of each country through six separate Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds testing models. Unit root tests (ADF, PP, and KPSS) confirm that all series are integrated of order one, satisfying the precondition for bounds testing. The results show that only the Indonesia and IHSG pair exhibits a statistically confirmed long-run cointegrating relationship with the EFFR, while the exchange rates of all three countries, together with the Malaysian and Thai equity indices, show no evidence of long-run cointegration. For the Indonesia and IHSG model, the error correction term is negative and highly significant, with a speed of adjustment of 30.5 percent per month, yet the long-run coefficient on the EFFR itself is not statistically significant. These findings indicate that Fed rate spillover to ASEAN-3 markets is selective rather than uniform, a pattern that most plausibly reflects active exchange rate management by domestic monetary authorities and differing depths of capital market integration across the three countries. The study offers implications for macroprudential policy design in emerging ASEAN economies facing continued normalization of US monetary policy.

title: Non-binding declarations and endogenous credibility in sequential allocation

detail.title: Non-binding declarations and endogenous credibility in sequential allocation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Non-binding declarations can affect sequential allocation even when they neither constrain the receiver nor commit the sender. We study a rank-contingent declaration by an informed agent whose willingness to accept depends on allocation timing. The receiver can allocate immediately, preserve a later opportunity, or abandon the sender. Greater credibility of future refusal lowers the value of waiting relative to both immediate allocation and abandonment, contracting the waiting region from both sides and polarizing behavior between acceleration and exclusion. These allocation margins determine which sender types imitate genuine refusers, making credibility an endogenous fixed point of allocation-induced message-pool composition. Holding receiver-side primitives fixed, the informative equilibria characterized here admit an exact branch representation as the reward from early allocation varies, with local folds supporting multiplicity. A larger reward strengthens imitation incentives and shifts the credibility map downward: both extremal credibility levels weakly fall, and informative equilibria disappear above a global existence ceiling. Receiver-side incidence can attenuate or reverse this erosion. A sports-draft implementation provides a microfoundation and shows how acceleration can alter other players' allocations. More broadly, the mechanism extends to sequential allocation settings in which communication changes the value of waiting and allocation margins shape sender incentives.

title: Demystifying the Bergomi-Guyon expansion
affiliations: Bloomberg LP and CUNY Baruch College

detail.title: Demystifying the Bergomi-Guyon expansion

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Alòs, Gatheral and Radoičić derived the Bergomi-Guyon expansion of the implied variance smile from the forest expansion of the cumulant generating function. Its coefficients are sums of products of diamond trees, with prefactors that are polynomials in the log-strike k. Matching moments order by order produces, at order eps^l, terms of degree greater than l in k that mysteriously cancel.

We show that, in suitable variables, the matching condition can be formulated as a nonlinear heat equation. The resulting recursion computes the prefactor of each product of trees from those of products of fewer trees, without generating the higher-degree terms; its only model-independent input is a cumulant series, which we compute in closed form. Consequently, at order eps^l every prefactor has degree exactly l in k. The prefactors are universal and need only be computed once. Code and coefficients are provided.

detail.abstract: Malawi's mobile commerce business units were either spun-off or hived-down from the mobile network operators effective 1st January 2019 in compliance with the Reserve Bank of Malawi Directives. This study explored both regulatory and financial reporting consequences for a period of six years and noted significant improvement in the bank and cash holdings but results revealed substantial gaps which required further investigations in the matters dealing with foreign currency exchange dealings as these were not reported in the financial statements. Further investigations were proposed on the value added tax which appeared to be excluded by one reporting entity while both entities appeared to practice adverse transfer pricing mechanisms which worked to the disadvantage of the mobile network companies which they solely rely on. Both reporting entities also revealed distorted statement of cash flows due to inherent complexities in understanding at which point the reporting entities claimed their cash in view of the fact that they were and are still not members of the national switch which is the payment system in Malawi but have to go through the sponsoring banks which offer instant E-Value while the reconciliations are done later which sometimes takes months. The study recommends robust supervision to reduce contagion risk.

title: Energy Intensity, Carbon Intensity, and the Producer-Consumer Divide: Asymmetric Productivity Effects and Implications for Energy Transition

detail.title: Energy Intensity, Carbon Intensity, and the Producer-Consumer Divide: Asymmetric Productivity Effects and Implications for Energy Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Energy transitions are commonly assumed to advance productivity and energy security together. This paper tests that assumption using a global panel of up to 108 countries over 1990–2023 (N = 2,591 country-years), asking whether the productivity return to energy intensity, carbon intensity, and energy import dependence differs systematically between net energy-exporting (“Petro”) and highly import-dependent (“HID”) economies. An augmented Cobb–Douglas productivity model with country and year fixed effects interacts these classifications with a set of energy-security regressors to identify group-specific slopes. The results show that energy-exporting and import-dependent economies draw productivity premiums from asymmetric energy margins: the energy-intensity penalty is substantially smaller for exporters than for import-dependent economies, though it remains negative for both groups, and neither group gains from electrification; a positive productivity return to carbon intensity, by contrast, is confined to import-dependent economies — a sign reversal across groups; exporters additionally show a distinct penalty for drifting away from deep net-exporter status, consistent with a specialization-based reading of energy security. Introducing these variables substantially attenuates estimated labor and capital elasticities, direct evidence that capital, labor, and energy are non-separable inputs to production. These findings argue against designing energy-transition policy, or the growth models used to evaluate it, around a single pooled energy-productivity relationship: a country's position in global energy trade is a first-order determinant of which transition levers are productivity-compatible, not a second-order control variable to be averaged away, with direct implications for how energy should be modeled in the aggregate production functions used throughout the energy-economics literature.

title: The Real Cost of Waiting to Sell

detail.title: The Real Cost of Waiting to Sell

keywords: private company liquidity JEL Classification: G11

detail.abstract: Owners of lower-middle-market businesses tend to treat the choice to wait before selling as a small delay, a season or a year. The mechanics of a private sale make it a much longer commitment than that. Buyers price on a multi-year record and a sale process runs close to a year, so a single strong year cannot lift the price and the decision to wait becomes a multi-year bet in practice. This paper reframes the decision as an allocation problem. The comparison that matters is not the business today against the business in three years. It is the return the business will earn on the capital locked inside it against the after-tax return that same capital would earn diversified and liquid, plus a premium for holding nearly all of one household's wealth in a single illiquid asset. We compute that premium rather than assert it, using the standard mean-variance result that a market pays an owner only for the systematic part of the risk they carry. For a typical owner the premium works out near nine percent a year and rises sharply with the volatility of the business, which places the breakeven return on retained equity in the low-to-mid teens in real terms. That range is directionally consistent with the private equity premium literature, in which private business returns have been found no higher, or only modestly higher, than public equity returns despite far greater concentrated risk. When a business compounds retained capital above the hurdle, holding is the better allocation. When it does not, selling and reallocating is. Two facts weigh against casual waiting: most businesses that go to market never sell, and the risks of the intervening years fall largely outside the owner's control.

title: Total Factor Productivity Across the Integrated Assessment Model Landscape: A Comparative Framework and a Complementary Module

detail.title: Total Factor Productivity Across the Integrated Assessment Model Landscape: A Comparative Framework and a Complementary Module

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Integrated assessment models (IAMs) treat total factor productivity (TFP) — the residual linking capital and labor to output growth — very differently, and this treatment is rarely tested empirically against cross-country data, despite evidence that energy efficiency, carbon intensity, and energy security shape that residual. This paper classifies TFP/GDP treatment across ten representative IAMs (GCAM, REMIND, MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM, WITCH, DICE/RICE, IMAGE, AIM/CGE, POLES-JRC, E3ME/GEM-E3, and the Energy Policy Simulator), benchmarks each model's capacity to reproduce an empirically documented, country/group-specific energy-productivity heterogeneity, and proposes a reduced-form CO-STIRPAT-type complementary TFP module with an integration architecture for coupling it to each model family. The classification draws on published model documentation across four dimensions — TFP/GDP endogeneity, regional parameter heterogeneity, explicit energy-trade accounting, and capital/labor endogeneity — and is benchmarked against producer/consumer (net-exporter versus import-dependent) interaction coefficients from a companion cross-country panel analysis, with four integration patterns specified to match each IAM family's structure. None of the ten IAMs can currently reproduce the benchmark heterogeneity internally: the shortfall is total for eight models with exogenous or residually calibrated TFP/GDP paths, partial for GCAM's under-activated trade-accounting channel, and least severe for the macro-econometric models E3ME and GEM-E3. This is the first study to benchmark TFP-treatment practice across this range of IAM traditions against a common empirical standard and to specify a model-family-matched integration architecture for a reduced-form TFP module rather than a single-model patch, addressing a forecast-reliability question with direct consequences for the policymakers and firms who rely on IAM-based technology-transition scenarios.

detail.abstract: Non-controlling interests (NCI) are part of the equity of the consolidated financial statements of the reporting entities in line with IAS 1-Presentation of Financial Statements and IFRS 3-Business Combination. The NCI are sometimes the most significant items in the statements of financial position as well as statements of changes in equity for some reporting entities but rarely featured in the auditor reports under the key audit matters. There is thus a huge possibility of increasing audit risk where auditors express inappropriate audit opinions. One way to avoid this is to enhance the use of the analytical procedures when evaluating the NCI to enable auditors to explore and evaluate various causal effect relationships. This study evaluated accounting for non-controlling interests of Malawi's listed companies. The results indicate serious exceptions in the measurement and valuation of the non-controlling interests exacerbated with the related parties (especially controlling interests) of the reporting entities being classified as non-controlling interests in the subsidiaries. Non-controlling interests in the sub-subsidiaries relationships were not properly accounted for in other instances leading to incorrect overstatement of the NCI. The exceptions noted herein would have been lessened if external auditors were adopting and applying the appropriate analytical procedures in the non-controlling interests. It is recommended that appropriate training in analytical procedures be reinforced on external auditors.

title: A Myerson Completion Conjecture for Shapley-Shubik Power: Exact Representation Beyond Weighted Voting

detail.title: A Myerson Completion Conjecture for Shapley-Shubik Power: Exact Representation Beyond Weighted Voting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Simple games need not be weighted. Adding a communication graph does not make weighted voting universal at the level of exact rule representation: an elementary counting comparison shows that, for sufficiently many players, there are more simple games than weighted-game/graph pairs. At the level of power, however, the question is different. The inverse-power literature largely asks how closely a weighted game can approximate a target power vector, and existing results show that weighted games can often approximate broader classes very well. This note asks for zero error. A five-player simple game is exhibited whose Shapley-Shubik vector is not attained by any weighted voting game, but is attained exactly as the Myerson value of a weighted game on a path. Exact enumeration further finds that every Shapley-Shubik vector generated by a simple game with at most six players is attained by a weighted game with a communication graph. These examples motivate the Myerson completion conjecture: every Shapley-Shubik vector of a finite simple game has an exact weighted-game/graph representation.

detail.abstract: The Blackwell order is widely used in economic theory to compare information structures. However, it has potential as a metric for measuring intergenerational mobility as well. I provide a novel geometric characterization of the Blackwell order using its lower contour set. This characterization allows me to visualize the Blackwell order and its completions for two and three states, and provides an equivalent statement of Blackwell informativeness. I then use my visualization to analyze completions of the Blackwell order and their relationship to intergenerational mobility.

detail.abstract:
This paper re-examines the practices of modern Islamic banking through the lens of classical Islamic economic principles. By applying what we term the “Sabbath Pond Test”—a metaphor drawn from the Qur’anic account of a community that circumvented the prohibition on fishing on the Sabbath—we assess whether contemporary Islamic financial products avoid the substance of riba (usury) or merely its form. Drawing on Qur’anic injunctions, Prophetic Hadith, and Hanafi jurisprudence (including works like Ahkam al-Qur’an, Kitab al-Amwal, Kitab al-Kharaj, and Usul al-Shashi), the paper critically analyzes a hypothetical case study of an Islamic mortgage structure that imitates an interest-bearing loan via sale, lease, and buy-back arrangements. We then present classical, interest-free financing alternatives such as Musharakah and Mudarabah, as well as public finance measures from early Islamic history that prioritized risk-sharing and social welfare. The study finds that while Islamic banks like Meezan Bank claim Sharī‘ah compliance by contract technicalities, there is an urgent need for greater transparency and alignment with the maqasid (objectives) of Sharī‘ah — emphasizing justice and economic substance over form.

AI Assistance Disclosure: Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) were used for language refinement, paraphrasing, structural editing, clarity improvements, formatting and citation-style consistency checks, preliminary source discovery and citation suggestions, and translation into other languages. The idea of applying the Sabbath Pond analogy to contemporary Islamic banking originated with the author. The author is accountable for the manuscript’s content; no AI tool is credited as an author.

Academic preprint; not a fatwa or financial advice. Archived at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21545850. Web edition: https://irshados.com/ebooks/islamic-banking-sabbath-pond-test-reevaluation/

title: Augmented Viable System Model (AVSM): Algorithmic homeorhesis and the recursive governance of non-ergodic socioeconomic systems

detail.title: Augmented Viable System Model (AVSM): Algorithmic homeorhesis and the recursive governance of non-ergodic socioeconomic systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.funderStatement: Funding from BI Partner or the Research Council of Norway's industrial PhD scheme.

detail.abstract:
The fragility of contemporary socio-economic structures — and of the models used to represent them — originates not in policy failure or any single statistical assumption, but in the category error of treating evolving socio-economic systems as stable objects whose state space, structure, parameters, agents, preferences, and equilibrium conditions are fixed in advance.

This paper formalises the Augmented Viable System Model (AVSM), a seven-level homeorhetic architecture grounded in the HIDCHANS ontology (Haarberg, 2026a). Where Beer's Viable System Model pursues stability through homeostatic set-points, AVSM operationalises algorithmic homeorhesis: the stabilisation of canalised developmental trajectories rather than fixed states. Creodic viability is defined not as restoration of equilibrium but as the capacity to adapt and persist along evolving creodes within moving viability boundaries.

Nine formal contributions include a proof that AVSM is a proper superset of VSM via a function-preserving embedding; a generalisation of Ashby's law of requisite variety to a requisite homeorhetic variety condition, recovering Ashby's law exactly as its zero-velocity degenerate case; algorithmic homeorhesis structured as optimal control on a Riemannian manifold; and five emergent properties shown jointly necessary and sufficient for creodic viability.

Companion paper: HIDCHANS (SSRN Abstract ID 7196840).

title: Unrealized Equity Gains in Reported Earnings: A Verified Series from XBRL Filings, 2018-2025

detail.title: Unrealized Equity Gains in Reported Earnings: A Verified Series from XBRL Filings, 2018-2025

declarations.funderStatement: Independent Researcher

keywords: cyclically adjusted price-earnings JEL Classification: M41
earnings quality; fair value accounting; ASU 2016-01; XBRL; data quality; insurance accounting; cyclically adjusted price-earnings

detail.abstract: Accounting Standards Update 2016-01, effective for fiscal years beginning after 15 December 2017, requires changes in the fair value of equity securities to be recognized in net income rather than in other comprehensive income. Reported earnings at holders of large equity portfolios therefore incorporate unrealized gains and losses on positions never sold. This paper measures the aggregate magnitude directly from SEC XBRL disclosures, then verifies fifteen of the largest constituents line by line against their source filings. Scanning the 700 largest filers and retaining only the dedicated unrealized-gains concept, only USD-denominated facts, and only the figure the Commission designates as canonical for each annual period yields 104 companies and a cumulative pre-tax total of approximately $315.4 billion for fiscal years 2018 through 2025. The distribution is the paper's central result and it was not the expected one. Berkshire Hathaway alone accounts for 86.7% of the series. Five insurers account for 91.0%. The remaining ninety-nine companies-including every large technology firm in the sample-account for 9.0%. Alphabet contributes $10.6 billion across eight years; Amazon and eBay are net negative. The standard did not distribute a distortion across corporate America. It changed how a small number of insurers report a portfolio they have always held. Two further findings follow. The series is substantially self-cancelling: losses in 2018 and 2022 erase 27.1% of the gains recorded in the other six years before any smoothing. And removing the entire series from the earnings input to the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio moves that measure from 42.18 to approximately 42.9-about two percent. A separate contribution concerns the reliability of structured filing data. Hand verification of fifteen filers found restatements at six of them, three periods at one filer where the magnitude was unchanged and the sign reversed, and one widely used concept that returns a point-in-time balance rather than a period flow while capturing items that never enter net income. An earlier hypothesis of the author's, formed from four companies in a single quarter, is stated and withdrawn. The collection reproduces all fifteen verified filers exactly. The method, concept list, and complete code are printed in Appendix A, so the series can be reproduced, extended, or refuted by any reader.

title: The 2026 FDI Screening Regulation: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: The EU’s new foreign direct investment screening regime is considerably more European than its predecessor, but it is still not a genuinely EU screening system. This paper examines how the 2026 FDI Screening Regulation transforms the voluntary and fragmented 2019 framework into a system of mandatory minimum harmonisation and compares the approaches. Its ‘good’ lies in closing important jurisdictional and enforcement gaps and establishing a common baseline for national screening. Its ‘bad’ lies in the substantial procedural and substantive fragmentation that remains. The deeper ‘ugly’ is structural: the Regulation recognises Union-wide security risks but leaves ultimate decision-making with the Member States, while adding another layer of review without adequately coordinating FDI screening with merger control, the Foreign Subsidies Regulation and other transaction-control regimes. It thus centralises information and influence without centralising legal authority.

title: WDSTNet_Pro: Leakage-Aware Three-Stream Gated Fusion for Reproducible Brain Tumor MRI Classification
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: WDSTNet_Pro: Leakage-Aware Three-Stream Gated Fusion for Reproducible Brain Tumor MRI Classification
detail.abstract: Brain-tumor classification results on public MRI datasets can be difficult to interpret when repeated images or correlated slices are present. We evaluated WDSTNet_Pro, a three-stream model with a full-image Swin Transformer, a deterministic brain-focused EfficientNet-B0 branch, and an eight-map, two-level bior4.4 Gray8 discrete wavelet transform branch. Each stream produces a 512-dimensional representation, and the three representations are combined by feature-wise softmax gating. Development used all 5,712 images in the official Kaggle Training directory with grouped five-fold cross-validation. The 1311-image testing directory was evaluated only after checkpoint selection and inference settings had been fixed. The five-fold EMA ensemble reached 99.39% accuracy and 99.34% macro-F1, with eight misclassifications. A normalized-pixel hash audit, performed independently of the predictions, identified 30 repeated test observations. Retaining one representative from each exact-hash group left 1,281 images; the same eight errors remained, corresponding to 99.38% accuracy and 99.33% macro-F1. The 95% image-level bootstrap confidence interval for clean-set accuracy was 98.91%–99.77%. In a controlled architecture ablation on the first three validation folds, the full model reached 99.04%, the Swin-only baseline 98.92%, and scalar three-way gating 99.10%; these differences were within the observed fold-to-fold variation. By comparison, replacing the five-model ensemble with a single validation-selected EMA checkpoint increased the clean-set error count from 8 to 13. These results suggest that, on this saturated benchmark, evaluation design and inference averaging have a clearer measurable effect than additional architectural complexity. The study therefore emphasizes auditable evaluation rather than a claim of architectural superiority. Patient identifiers were unavailable, and no external cohort was used.

title: Simulation of Ventricular Contraction with Left Bundle Branch Block Using a New Multiscale and Multiphysics Model
affiliations: Brno University of Technology, Brno University of Technology and Brno University of Technology

detail.title: Simulation of Ventricular Contraction with Left Bundle Branch Block Using a New Multiscale and Multiphysics Model
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: The paper deals with simulation of the impact of the left bundle branch block on the ejection fraction of the human left ventricle. Using a new multiscale and multiphysics model based primarily on finite element method for description of the electrical and mechanical processes in the myocardium and Windkessel model for hemodynamical calculations, it evaluates also changes in ventricular motions or strain and stress distributions induced by the block.Methods: Electrical activation of left ventricle under healthy conditions and during the branch block is modelled by the monodomain equation coupled with an artificial ionic model designed to reduce the computational demands of the monodomain equation. Conduction velocity in myocardium is considered orthotropic. The activation maps are subsequently used in the simulations of ventricular mechanics to distribute the beginning of contraction throughout the finite-element mesh. Passive mechanical behaviour of myocardium is described by a new orthotropic hyperelastic model. Active stresses, induced by muscle contraction, are incorporated by means of the time-dependent active strain tensor. Contraction starts from a prestressed reference configuration representing the enddiastolic state of the ventricle. Pressure development during ejection phase is controlled by two-parametric Windkessel model.Results: Calculated activation maps show that the left bundle branch block prolongs electrical activation by 50 % which agrees with clinically observed prolongation of the QRS complex in ECG. Results indicate that the left bundle branch block does not substantially reduce the pumping efficiency of the ventricle; ejection fraction in the diseased state decreased by only 2.3 % relative to the healthy conditions which agrees with some of the previously published clinical studies. Changes in displacements and strains, predicted by the model, correspond to clinical and experimental observations.Conclusions: Performed analyses confirmed that the model captures basic characteristics of the left bundle branch block-induced mechanical dyssynchrony, reported in literature. Specifically, apical displacements were increased in the presence of the block and strain analysis demonstrated delayed contraction of the lateral wall relative to the septum.

detail.abstract: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) holds a position of near-monopoly dominance at the leading edge of global chip fabrication, making it simultaneously an ordinary case of industry concentration and an extraordinary case of geopolitical consequence. This paper examines TSMC through PESTLE analysis, Porter's Five Forces, and a set of complementary strategic frameworks (dynamic capabilities, technology S-curves, Dunning's OLI, GVC governance theory, institutional theory, and the Resource-Based View) to ask how political, economic, and technological forces are actively reshaping-rather than merely surrounding-TSMC's industry structure and global business strategy. It further asks whether TSMC constitutes a genuine "global choke point," examining what a disruption to its operations would mean for the global value chain. Drawing on industry market-share data, TSMC's global expansion strategy (Arizona, Kumamoto, Dresden), and its sustainability commitments amid mounting emissions and energy pressure, the paper finds strong qualitative support for TSMC's structural centrality to global chip supply, while deliberately stopping short of quantifying disruption scenarios that current evidence cannot responsibly support. The paper concludes that TSMC's dominance is real but narrower, and more conditional, than headline market-share figures alone suggest.

title: A UAV-borne edge computing system for early tea anthracnose detection based on a frequency-aware lightweight model
affiliations: Zhejiang University of Science and Technology, Zhejiang University of Science and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A UAV-borne edge computing system for early tea anthracnose detection based on a frequency-aware lightweight model
detail.abstract: Tea anthracnose, a prevalent disease of Longjing 43—a cultivar extensively grown in eastern China—severely compromises leaf quality and yield. Its frequent infection of tender leaves during the harvest season makes early and accurate diagnosis critical for timely disease management and reduced economic losses. Yet early-stage infected leaf textures nearly indistinguishable from healthy backgrounds, so conventional visual detection often fails. In low-altitude UAV inspections, heavy models cannot meet the real-time constraints of edge computing, whereas conventional lightweight models rely on aggressive downsampling that over-smooths the high-frequency textures of tiny lesions, thereby limiting early recognition.​To address these limitations, we propose a UAV-borne edge computing system driven by a frequency-aware lightweight model. The framework adopts an inverted "Pruning-then-Tuning" architecture. First, spatial and channel reconstruction techniques suppress background redundancy to reduce computational cost. Second, frequency-preservingg Haar wavelet downsampling replaces traditional strided convolutions to preserve high-frequency details. The core innovation—the Spatial-Wavelet Learnable Fusion Tuner (SwlFT)—integrates learnable wavelet transforms with an adaptive spatial-frequency gating mechanism, effectively enhancing weak pathological textures obscured by background noise.To bridge algorithmic design with field application, we constructed a UAV-borne optical pod utilizing the Jetson Orin Nano. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model improves mean Average Precision (mAP@50) by 5.5% over the baseline while reducing FLOPs by 14.6%. Validated across multi-site field inspections comprising 131 minutes of flight data, the hardware-software co-designed system sustained a stable 32.40 FPS without thermal throttling. This framework provides an accurate and field-deployable solution for precision agriculture.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest related to this study. The authors have no financial or personal relationships that could influence the findings or interpretation of the results.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, biological samples, or primary data collection. Therefore, ethical approval and informed consent were not required.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how environmental degradation and climate change affect health outcomes in India, measured through life expectancy at different stages of life. Using state-level panel data, the analysis covers both rural and urban areas and examines life expectancy at birth to adolescence, adulthood, and older ages. Life expectancy data are drawn from the Sample Registration System based abridged life tables published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, while information on income, urbanization, carbon emissions, and surface temperature is taken from Global Data Lab. The study first applies fixed effects and random effects panel models and uses the Hausman test to select the appropriate specification. The presence of cross-sectional dependence is confirmed using the Pesaran test, and Panel Corrected Standard Error models are then employed to obtain reliable estimates. To capture age-specific health risks more clearly, fractional logit models are used to estimate how changes in income, climate conditions, and emissions affect the probability of surviving. The results show that higher income consistently improves life expectancy and survival probabilities across all ages in both rural and urban India. In contrast, higher surface temperature and carbon emissions reduce life expectancy, with stronger effects at adult and older ages. Urbanization by itself shows limited direct effects, but its interaction with emissions suggests that rapid urbanization can partly offset environmental damage through better infrastructure and services. Overall, the findings highlight that economic growth alone is not sufficient to improve health outcomes if environmental damage continues to rise. The study underscores the need for growth paths that combine income improvement with effective climate and environmental policies to ensure longer and healthier lives in India.

detail.abstract: Published estimates of how equity market signals relate to mortgage-backed security outcomes differ in sign across otherwise similar specifications. We assemble these scattered coefficients through an AI-agent-assisted systematic review in which the agent performs retrieval, screening, and extraction while a finance domain expert holds exclusive authority over every coefficient and classification judgment. Screening yields ten confirmed estimates from two studies. The apparent disagreement resolves into a moderator: the benchmark asset against which the MBS convenience premium is measured determines the sign of the volatility effect. Within one baseline regression, a one-point increase in VIX raises the premium measured against AAA corporate bonds by 3.207 basis points and lowers the premium measured against Treasury securities by 1.257, both significant at the 1% level. Because estimates measured against different benchmarks belong to different strata, we report no pooled effect size. We have identified no comparable synthesis of this literature.

title: Disaggregating the Cause of Inflation: Why Assigning Inflation a Single Supply or Demand Verdict Repeats the Same Convention Error as Measuring It

detail.title: Disaggregating the Cause of Inflation: Why Assigning Inflation a Single Supply or Demand Verdict Repeats the Same Convention Error as Measuring It

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: A prior paper (Hwang, 2026) argued that the general price level is not a natural object price indices imperfectly approximate, but a convention — a weighted average constructed for specific institutional purposes, embedding contestable normative choices about whose experience counts. This paper argues that the same structural pathology recurs one stage later in the pipeline, at the point where a measured price change is assigned a cause. Once a convention (CPI) is fixed, decomposing a given print into its constituent categories is mechanical and uncontroversial. Explaining why each category moved is not mechanical, but it is also not, in the majority of cases, theoretically indeterminate: a distributed infrastructure of sector-specific monitoring (agricultural, energy, automotive, housing), together with a family of empirical methods — narrative identification (Romer & Romer, 1989), sectoral price-quantity sign-restriction classification (Shapiro, 2022), and survey-disciplined structural decomposition (Bernanke & Blanchard, 2023) — resolves most component-level causal questions with tractable, checkable evidence. The genuine theoretical indeterminacy — the identification problem in its strict form — is confined to a much smaller residual: broad-based, sticky, expectations- and wage-driven co-movement that no sector analyst owns because it is not a property of any single market. The public and professional discourse systematically fails to observe this division of labor, collapsing what is actually a three-part composite — a majority of tractably checked components, a small zone where the sector evidence itself is genuinely mixed, and a residual that is the legitimate domain of macro theory — into a single causal label ("demand-pull" or "cost-push") applied to the whole print. This is the same error the measurement paper diagnosed: forcing a heterogeneous, disaggregated reality into a single headline claim because that is what is discursively convenient, and treating the resulting label as a discovered fact rather than an interpretive simplification. The costs are structurally identical in kind to those catalogued in the measurement paper — forecasting failures (both from misapplying a residual-tier framework to a genuinely mixed print, and from under-specifying the residual tier's own proxies, as the 2021–22 unemployment-based Phillips curve failure illustrates), politically weaponizable ambiguity ("greedflation" debates fought without reference to which components were actually margin-driven), and public confusion about what any given policy response can and cannot address. The paper also confronts directly the strongest objection to its own framework — that sector-level "checking" is itself theory-laden, and that the checked/mixed/residual tiering is a judgment call rather than an algorithm — and argues that both objections are correct as far as they go without undermining the paper's reform, which does not eliminate judgment but relocates it to the most granular and honestly reported level. The paper proposes a modest, achievable reform in the same spirit as its predecessor: routinize component-level causal attribution, with an explicit confidence tier distinguishing checked (sector-evidenced) from mixed and residual (identification-limited) categories, as a standard supplement to CPI and PCE releases.

detail.abstract:
This preprint examines how recovery identity may evolve once substance use has stabilized and recovery becomes part of a longer life history. It introduces **recovery identity configuration** as an integrative framework combining social identity, narrative identity, role-exit, recovery capital, stigma, and peer-support research.

The framework distinguishes recovery-identity salience, broader identity structure, and narrative-temporal integration, while treating stigma, institutional practices, and social opportunity as contextual conditions. Its central argument is that a strong recovery identity is not inherently restrictive; what may matter more is how it coexists with other valued identities and with the possibility of a meaningful future beyond the recovery role.

title: Stability in Contract

detail.title: Stability in Contract

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funders

detail.abstract:
Contract law involves the public and therefore coercive enforcement of private claims. The coercive nature of contract consists in the fact that contract enforcement goes beyond acknowledgement that the underlying claims are binding. This coercive element stands in need of justification. This Article develops a justificatory criterion of reflexive adequacy: contract law doctrine that is otherwise substantively just is nonetheless defective if its enforcement materially contradicts its public rationale. The state lacks the normative authority to rely upon an enforcement rationale that depends for its success upon opacity, effective suppression of remedial claims, or burdens that cannot be justified to those who bear them as participants in a reciprocal arrangement. This criterion operationalizes that feature of a just society that Rawls described as stability for the right reasons: just institutions must be capable of informed, reason-responsive support through their ordinary operation.

The criterion of reflexive adequacy can be applied to contract doctrine as both justification and critique. The Article illustrates the justificatory use of reflexive adequacy by reconstructing unconscionability doctrine as a response to two potential failures of stability to which contract is vulnerable. A failure of publicity is one that makes a consequential contractual term or mechanism practically inaccessible to a contracting party. A failure under the strains of commitment imposes a recurring burden that free and equal participants in the practice of contracting cannot reasonably be asked to bear. These failures cut across the orthodox procedural and substantive prongs of unconscionability doctrine. Either failure independently justifies withholding or limiting enforcement, but neither adhesion nor unequal bargaining power is sufficient on its own to establish such a failure.

The Article illustrates the critical use of reflexive adequacy by diagnosing the recent history of mandatory arbitration in consumer and employment contracts. Failures of publicity and excessive strains of commitment both arise within the regime established by the Supreme Court’s reading of the Federal Arbitration Act. The emergence of mass arbitration, with claimants filing individual demands in the thousands and firms resisting the fees assigned by the arbitration clauses they have drafted, is a stress test for stability. Whether contemporary arbitration practices are consistent with reflexive adequacy depends upon whether, empirically, contract drafters depend on counterparties not exercising their contractual rights, or instead genuinely seek to avoid exploitation of arbitration fee structures. The Article proposed that the Federal Arbitration Act be amended so that the enforcement of arbitration clauses in consumer and employment contracts is made conditional on use of federally certified providers who publish rules, outcome data, and redacted reasons for rulings disposing of statutory claims or affecting other cases. The proposal establishes a minimum standard for achieving the publicity that makes drafters and providers publicly accountable and informs further interventions aiming at substantive fairness.

detail.abstract:
This report benchmarks electricity cost and generation mix across 31 European markets (the EU-27, the UK, Norway, Switzerland, and Iceland) and five Middle Eastern markets, and introduces the EMEA AI Power & Innovation Competitiveness Index (“PCI-EMEA”) across the 20 countries most active in AI infrastructure siting. Six weighted components drive the Index: electricity cost, climate and cooling advantage, water stress, an illustrative tax position, regulatory and grid risk, and, new in this edition, an Institutional Integrity / Public-Sector Corruption Proxy (CPI) measured by Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index. Every component is built from a named external source or a stated, checkable formula (Section 2); the Index is best described as externally benchmarked and transparently modeled, not as an infallible ranking, and Section 2 states plainly where inputs are directly observed versus analyst-estimated.

PCI-EMEA is a country-screening tool, not a site-selection model: a strong national score narrows the field worth investigating, it does not certify that any specific site, substation, or parcel of land within that country is suitable. Constructability in particular is not scored here (Section 2.7, Section 8.5).

On tax: Ireland's R&D credit rose from 30% to 35% in Budget 2026 and is structured as a qualifying refundable credit; per HMRC guidance, the UK's RDEC is also treated as qualifying-refundable. Both are treated as qualifying refundable tax credits for purposes of the simplified model and therefore are not subject to the same 15% cash-tax floor applied here to non-QRTCs, but only Ireland's is large enough, relative to the illustrative company's R&D intensity, to produce a negative modeled cash-tax position; the UK's produces a positive, if reduced, one. Several other governments, Finland, Denmark, Portugal, Poland, and Italy among them, do operate real R&D incentives of their own (Section 5.1), but structured as ordinary deductions or non-refundable credits, which the Pillar Two floor neutralizes to the same 15% outcome once a company is large enough to be in scope. Five years ago, “which country has the lowest corporate tax rate” was close to the whole conversation. It no longer is, and increasingly, neither is “which country has an R&D credit”; what matters is whether that credit is refundable, and how large it is relative to what the company actually spends.

On regulation: the EU AI Act's high-risk system obligations, originally due 2 August 2026, were pushed to 2 December 2027 by a “Digital Omnibus” that entered into force on 27 July 2026. Article 50's transparency obligations apply from 2 August 2026, subject to the limited transition for Article 50(2) machine-readable marking described below: the disclosure obligations under Article 50(1), (3), (4), and (5), covering direct human-AI interaction, emotion-recognition/biometric-categorisation disclosure, deepfake and AI-generated public-interest text labelling, and how those disclosures must be presented, carry no grace period and are enforceable from that date. Only the machine-readable marking duty under Article 50(2) carries a narrow four-month grace period, to 2 December 2026, for generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 [18]. “The EU delayed the AI Act” is true only for the high-risk tier.

On Ireland specifically: data centres consumed approximately 23% of Ireland's metered national electricity in 2025, per the Central Statistics Office, up from 5% in 2015. The grid-connection framework that replaced the country's 2021-2025 de facto moratorium applies a tiered set of obligations from a 1 MVA de minimis threshold, with the largest projects, 10 MVA and above, required to provide dispatchable generation or storage covering the full extent of their maximum import capacity on a derated basis, and all qualifying projects required to match at least 80% of annual demand with additional Irish renewable electricity. That framework is real and binding, but newly implemented and not yet tested by a full construction cycle, which is why Ireland's regulatory-risk score remains the second-lowest in the set even as its tax position is the strongest.

title: Politics and Profit: Combining the Presidential Cycle and the January Effect
affiliations: Cambria Investment Management

detail.title: Politics and Profit: Combining the Presidential Cycle and the January Effect
detail.abstract: Does the intersection of two market anomalies set the stage for outsized performance?  The first is what is known as the Presidential Cycle. This theory goes that equity returns during the third and fourth years of a President's term are more favorable than the first two years.  A second market bias is the large outperformance of small cap stocks in January. Historically small caps outperformed large caps in 80% of all Januaries by 3 percentage points per year.  Historically across the 48 months in the four year cycle the January of Year 3 is the single biggest outperformer with median returns since 1927 of nearly 8% a month for small caps. Does this mean that January is guaranteed to be great? Again, nothing is guaranteed - Year 3 Januaries have varied from 27% to down 10%. While many of these tendencies are just that, investors can view them as head or tailwinds that could give bulls and bears pause.

detail.abstract: Standard Temporal Graph Networks (TGNs) are bounded by the 1-Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) graph isomorphism test, which implies they cannot detect cycle membership or cycle length from message-passing alone. We study this limitation empirically on the Bitcoin OTC trust graph, constructing a temporal cyclecompleting link prediction benchmark that isolates cycle-sensitive evaluation from generic link prediction. We implement and compare three models: TGN [Rossi et al., 2020] as the canonical baseline, TPNet as a path-aware extension, and Cy-cleFormer, a TGN augmented with cycle-basis positional encodings injected as additive residuals into the GRU memory update with LayerNorm stabilization. CycleFormer achieves consistently higher cycle-edge AUC than both baselines. Ablation studies isolate the contribution of residual injection, temporal horizon, cycle feature importance, and observation sparsity.

title: Analysis of the Economic Efficiency of UAV Delivery of Medical and Small-Sized Cargo: A Case Study of the East Kazakhstan Region

detail.abstract:
Introduction. The challenge of ensuring medical care accessibility in remote, sparsely populated regions remains a persistent global concern, particularly pronounced across the expansive territories of Central Asia. The effective implementation of “last-mile” delivery for essential pharmaceuticals and biomaterials demands innovative approaches unconstrained by the limitations inherent in ground-based transport infrastructure. The purpose of the study is to elaborate a model for deploying a delivery system based on unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) within the specific context of the East Kazakhstan Region (EKR) of the Republic of Kazakhstan.

Materials and Methods. A discrete-event simulation framework was constructed, integrating a logistics network module for the EKR’s medical facilities, an economic assessment module covering both capital and operating costs, and a socio-economic impact evaluation module. Validation was performed through benchmarking against findings from comparable studies and expert judgement; sensitivity was explored via Monte Carlo simulation.

Results. The optimal configuration, predicated on a public-private partnership model with an initial investment of 1.5 million USD (comprising 50 UAVs and 80 charging stations), was found to achieve financial breakeven within 3–4 years at an annual throughput of 50,000 deliveries. Calculations indicated that operational expenses could be reduced by an order of magnitude relative to conventional road transport, while medication delivery times could be shortened from 2–8 hours to 30–90 minutes. The principal impediment to implementation was identified not as technological deficiency but as regulatory constraints embedded in the Republic of Kazakhstan’s current aviation legislation.

Conclusion. The investigation confirms that UAV-based delivery for the EKR represents not merely a technically viable proposition but also an economically sound strategy for addressing transport accessibility deficits, with the potential to expand healthcare coverage in remote districts by 40–60%. The developed model offers a practical decision-support tool for administrators and is adaptable to other regions sharing similar geographical characteristics.

detail.title: Food Acquisition and Time Use – A Demand System Approach

This research used data from the USDA National Household Food Acquisition and Purchase Survey (FoodAPS).

detail.abstract: Limited time availability for food purchase and preparation (P&P) can hinder the ability to maintain a nutritious diet and, particularly among low-income households, is associated with increased food insecurity. We develop a framework to study the joint demand for Food-At-Home (FAH), grouped by time-saving features (convenience) and storability, Food-Away-From-Home (FAFH), and time spent on food P&P activities. Our demand system extends the Exact Affine Stone Index (EASI) model, and is estimated using a dataset created by merging the American Time Use Survey with the National Household Food Acquisition and Purchase Survey data. We find that convenience FAH and FAFH act as gross substitutes for Food P&P time; when the opportunity cost of time increases-in other words, as time becomes scarcer-the quantities demanded for convenience FAH and FAFH increases as well. For a subsample of households receiving SNAP benefits, the demand for FAH and for prepared foods appears resource elastic (that is, they increase as value of time and income increase). Our results support the importance of accounting for time cost when designing tools (such as the Thrifty Food Plan-TFP) aimed at achieving a nutritious diet with limited resources.

detail.abstract: This paper examines Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs) as a governance stress test, focusing on the interaction among national-security secrecy, scientific inquiry, institutional legitimacy, and public trust. It argues that decades of classification, stigma, and institutional risk management have produced a form of “manufactured ignorance” that may itself become a governance liability as the half-life of secrets collapses. The analysis relies on official U.S. government reporting, congressional testimony, high-quality multi-sensor cases, and credible civilian scientific efforts, with emphasis on chain of custody, replication, corroboration, and explicit uncertainty. Historical cases of classified programs and later reform are used to examine how governments manage disclosure, legitimacy shocks, and institutional remediation. The paper concludes with a proposed Disclosure Operations Manual: a policy framework for classification governance, decision gates, oversight, controlled dissemination, allied coordination, and independent validation intended to move potential UAP-related disclosure from ad hoc reaction toward a deliberate, law-bound, auditable process.

detail.abstract: Climate change has emerged as one of the most significant structural challenges facing Bangladesh's agricultural economy and rural livelihoods in the twenty-first century. This term paper reviews the relation between climate change, agricultural productivity and rural poverty on the basis of published and verifiable secondary data of Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), Soil Resources Development Institute (SRDI), World Bank and IPCC. This research did not utilize any new surveys, interviews or hypothetical data. According to the World Bank's Country Climate and Development Report (2022) for Bangladesh, Bangladesh could lose nearly one-third of its agricultural GDP by 2050 due to climate change. Without any action, agricultural land could shrink by around 6.5% nationally and 18% in the south by 2040. The same report projects that some 13.3 million people could be exposed to internal climate migration over the next 30 years. The survey conducted by the Soil Resources Development Institute (SRDI) found that about 1.056 million hectares of agricultural land in the coastal region is affected by salinity to different degrees. In contrast, the latest Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES 2022) conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics reveals that the national poverty rate has reduced from 48.9% in 2000 to 18.7% in 2022 but the rural poverty rate (20.5%) is still far higher than the urban poverty rate (14.7%). Since this study is based on secondary data, the relationships between climate, agriculture and poverty are interpreted as statistical associations and economic mechanisms, and not as causal effects. The paper closes with several policy recommendations centered on expanding climateresilient agricultural technology, region-specific adaptation strategies, irrigation management, and the diversification of rural income.

title: The Neurolaw of Propaganda: Empathy Loss, Black Swan Risks, and Precautionary Interventions

detail.title: The Neurolaw of Propaganda: Empathy Loss, Black Swan Risks, and Precautionary Interventions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial, personal, or professional conflicts of interest regarding the research, authorship, and publication of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant, financial support, or sponsorship from any funding agency, commercial organization, or institutional affiliate.

detail.abstract:
Historically, propaganda has been conceptualized predominantly across political science and
sociological scholarship as an ideological practice of persuasion and manipulation that
externally shapes public opinion. Today, cognitive neuroscience and digital advances show
that propaganda extends beyond rhetorical endeavor. It has evolved into a neurobiological
intervention that alters social perception, empathy, and decision-making circuits. This review
examines how media violence and hate speech induce socio-cognitive desensitization. It
analyzes how neuro-propaganda erodes empathic functioning in the mPFC, Anterior Insula,
and Amygdala, and how algorithmic architectures automate this decay. Beyond state-led
proactive interventions, this study highlights state anachronism—the temporal gap between
rapid technological growth and slow legal adaptation. Furthermore, it incorporates the
macroeconomic dynamics of surveillance capitalism into this core analysis. Using Black
Swan theory and the Precautionary Principle, the study evaluates the conceptual ambiguities
of neurotechnological manipulation and subsequent social disruptions. The core argument is
that uncertainty cannot validate refraining from regulatory action. Indeed, the very presence
of potential, unpredictable risks requires immediate precautionary intervention. Balancing
neuroscientific skepticism against neuro-paternalist overreach, this paper outlines systemic
strategies for a constitutional neuro-legal protection regime grounded in cognitive
sovereignty.
