From PostScript and Photoshop to PDF, Creative Cloud, Acrobat, Experience Cloud, Firefly, and agentic creative tools, Adobe has shaped how individuals, businesses, publishers, educators, marketers, and creative professionals produce and manage digital content. This paper examines Adobe through historical, technological, business, and ethical perspectives. It analyzes Adobe's transition from packaged software to cloud subscription platforms, its role in standardizing document workflows through PDF, its growing emphasis on generative AI, and its expansion into customer experience orchestration and brand visibility. Adobe's fiscal 2025 revenue reached $23.769 billion, with Digital Media accounting for about 74% of total revenue and Digital Experience accounting for about 25%, showing the company's strong subscription-driven platform model. (Adobe) The paper concludes that Adobe's future competitiveness depends on balancing professional-grade creative control, commercially safer AI, creator trust, pricing fairness, interoperability, and authenticity standards.

title: A Two-Phase Cloud Migration Framework for SME Digital Transformation in Sri Lanka's Travel Technology Sector
affiliations: , Staffordshire University and Staffordshire University

detail.title: A Two-Phase Cloud Migration Framework for SME Digital Transformation in Sri Lanka's Travel Technology Sector
detail.abstract: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Sri Lanka's rapidly digitizing travel and hospitality sector face persistent infrastructure challenges including single points of failure, inadequate data protection, and inability to handle seasonal demand spikes. This paper proposes a validated twophase cloud migration framework using Amazon Web Services (AWS). The first phase employs a lift-and-shift strategy, resolving immediate reliability and performance issues through multi-AZ EC2 deployments, RDS with automated failover, and CloudFront content delivery. The second phase re-architects monolithic applications into microservices using AWS Fargate, API Gateway, Lambda, and purpose-built databases. The framework achieves 99.95% availability (up from 95%), 60% page load improvement, and establishes a foundation for sustained growth. We provide architectural blueprints, implementation roadmaps, risk mitigation strategies, and cost-benefit analysis applicable to regional SMEs undergoing digital transformation.

detail.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in medicine, finance, security, law enforcement, and social media raises a number of challenges associated with privacy and the safety of personal data. Modern privacy regulation tools created for the management of static databases and centralized processing of data become more and more outdated and inefficient in regard to processing distributed and opaque data flows characteristic of AI technologies. The aim of this paper is the analysis of Privacy by Design (PbD) paradigman approach based on the integration of privacy features into the very foundation of AI application creation. In particular, relying on the list of PbD principles formulated by Ann Cavoukian and the corresponding extensions in regard to machine learning, this paper attempts to find out technical solutions like differential privacy, federated learning, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computations, and data minimization approaches that can be applied in accordance with PbD principles. This paper consists of two major sections. The first section provides theoretical analysis of PbD concepts within AI technologies. The second section covers technical approaches and their relevance. Three case studies covering medical AI technologies, recommendation systems, and facial recognition systems are examined to analyze the efficiency of current PbD solutions. As the results show, a lot of effort has been done in this field, but there is still much left to do..

title: Model Choice Boundary: Sourcing, Delegation, and Assurance for Runtime Model Selection in Enterprise AI

detail.abstract: Enterprises increasingly serve AI workloads through routing systems that allocate each request among models, providers, endpoints, service tiers, compute budgets, and fallback paths at runtime. Technical routing research establishes that such selection is feasible but takes the eligible set, the objective, and the authority structure as given. This paper treats the resulting management problem as one of decision rights. It introduces the Model Choice Boundary: the allocation of decision rights between an enterprise and one or more intermediaries over which eligible inference configuration performs a workload, under what objectives and constraints, using what evidence, and subject to whose residual authority. The framework separates the sourcing boundary, which concerns who operates the routing mechanism, from the authority boundary, which concerns who controls the decision. It decomposes model choice into meta decision rights over Eligibility, Objective, and Change, an operational Allocation right, an Intervention right, and adjacent rights over Evidence, Learning and Data, and Exit, and allocates them through workload routing mandates using five determinants. It separates baseline workload risk from incremental routing exposure and derives a four level assurance stack. Enterprises can delegate high frequency Allocation without surrendering strategic control, but only where retained rights are backed by mandate separating evidence and feasible correction. A sharp corollary follows: a mandate that names several goals without ordering them has delegated Objective, whatever the agreement says.

title: Neural Information Extraction and Consumer Preference Prediction: A Study of Product-Evoked EEG Signals
affiliations: Zhejiang University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Chongqing University

detail.title: Neural Information Extraction and Consumer Preference Prediction: A Study of Product-Evoked EEG Signals
detail.abstract: Accurate identification of consumer preferences is central to personalized recommendation and decision support in e-commerce. Existing approaches, however, rely primarily on consumers' self-reported evaluations and accumulated behavioral data, which may not fully capture their real-time preference states during product exposure. Previous research has established that electroencephalography (EEG) contains information predictive of consumer choices. A more critical issue is how to extract this information from high-dimensional neural signals and translate it into usable consumer preference predictions. This study examines this issue through a controlled experiment. The results indicate that models enhanced by feature selection effectively extract preference-relevant information from high-dimensional EEG data and achieve good predictive performance in both prediction tasks. Within the same prediction framework, EEG data perform better than self-reported data in both tasks. These findings extend neural prediction research from whether EEG contains preference information to how neural signals can be translated into usable preference information. They also highlight the key role of information extraction in connecting neural measurement with consumer preference prediction.

title: Does AI-Augmented Content Win Readers? Accountability and Readership in News Media
affiliations: George Mason University - Department of Information Systems and Operations Management and

detail.title: Does AI-Augmented Content Win Readers? Accountability and Readership in News Media

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: News media's use of artificial intelligence (AI) has prompted regulatory activity (e.g., NY FAIR News Act), which typically recommends editorial oversight and transparency regarding AI use as accountability measures. But do these measures together help outlets win readers? Since journalists typically lack full agency over content despite driving revenue, we study this question using a principal-agent framework that links production (editor-journalist) and market (reader-outlet) models through content quality, with agents privately differing in AI-use intensity and principals enforcing accountability through oversight and transparency. We analyze the production and market models individually and jointly. Individually, we find that while costless oversight is always recommended, costly oversight can limit the oversight rents that heavy AI users extract. Further, transparency demand is not unconditional but depends on the content's alignment with readers' beliefs. Indeed, the so-called "transparency discount" is not guaranteed, and readership can increase with transparency when readers value news more than belief alignment. Yet, joint analysis reveals a transparency inversion paradox: an outlet can gain readership by disclosing AI use that degrades content, but lose readership by disclosing use that improves content. Thus, our study demonstrates regulatory weaknesses that can help advise recent legislative efforts on AI use in media.

title: Beyond Delivery Success Rate: A Device-Aware, Recency-Weighted Framework for Cash on Delivery Risk Management in South Asian E-Commerce

detail.title: Beyond Delivery Success Rate: A Device-Aware, Recency-Weighted Framework for Cash on Delivery Risk Management in South Asian E-Commerce

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed as Risk Analytics Lead at Daraz Bangladesh, a subsidiary of Alibaba Group, where the research was conducted. The analytical framework described in this paper was developed and deployed as part of the author's professional responsibilities. All data used in this study is proprietary to the platform and has been anonymised in accordance with GDPR-level data governance standards. No external funding was received for this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted as part of the author's professional work at Daraz Bangladesh (Alibaba Group).

detail.abstract: Cash on delivery (COD) remains the dominant payment method across South Asian ecommerce markets, accounting for a majority of order volume in Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Nepal. Unlike prepaid transactions, COD defers revenue realisation to the moment of doorstep handover, exposing platforms to significant gross-to-net (G2N) margin leakage when deliveries fail. Existing buyer risk frameworks in these markets rely primarily on delivery success rate (SR) as the core scoring signal. This paper identifies three structural limitations of SR-based scoring: it treats all historical failures as equally weighted regardless of recency, it is blind to item-level cancellations and returns that erode G2N without affecting SR, and it operates at the account level, leaving device-level multi-account evasion undetected. We present a multi-metric COD risk framework deployed across four South Asian markets that addresses each limitation directly. The framework introduces a recency-weighted SR model that assigns greater weight to recent buyer behavior, an item-level G2N evaluation rule that surfaces buyers with high SR but significant cancellation leakage, and a Universal Mobile Device ID (UMID) based COD block mechanism that detects and restricts buyers evading account-level controls across linked devices. A delivery time lag analysis further shows that failed delivery concentration is strongly associated with package aging in the logistics pipeline, enabling separation of buyer-intent failures from logistics-driven failures. Threshold simulation across intervention cohorts, evaluated against lifetime profit margin contribution, demonstrates that more selective rule thresholds outperform broader ones on commercial impact while maintaining meaningful failed delivery reduction. The framework has been deployed in production and contributes a practitioner-validated approach to COD risk management in markets where standard e-commerce risk playbooks do not fully apply.

title: Navigating the Noise: AI Artifact Assurance — Extending Task-Technology Fit to Account for the Human Review That Generative AI Outputs Require

detail.title: Navigating the Noise: AI Artifact Assurance — Extending Task-Technology Fit to Account for the Human Review That Generative AI Outputs Require

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract:
Purpose – Generative artificial intelligence has entered everyday organizational change management (OCM) work, where practitioners use it to draft communications, training content, technical explanations and manager scripts. Existing guidance treats the selection problem as one of tool capability, asking which model performs best. This paper argues that the question is misspecified for change work and develops an alternative construct, AI artifact assurance, defined as the process through which a change team qualifies an AI-generated work product against task-specific requirements, critical-defect thresholds and human-review needs before the artifact is circulated or used.

Design/methodology/approach – This is a conceptual paper following a theory adaptation design (Jaakkola, 2020). Task-technology fit theory is adapted to the case of probabilistic, artifact-producing technologies by importing two bodies of work it does not currently accommodate: noncompensatory decision theory and information quality management. The paper is explicitly non-empirical; it develops constructs, propositions and boundary conditions, and specifies how each proposition may subsequently be tested.

Findings – Three theoretical moves are advanced. First, the appropriate unit of assurance in change work is the artifact rather than the tool, because defect risk is a property of the task-artifact pairing rather than of general model capability. Second, artifact quality in high-consequence change work is noncompensatory: a single critical defect disqualifies an artifact irrespective of aggregate quality, which implies a lexicographic screen rather than a weighted index. Third, and most consequentially for theory, the expert effort required to render an output usable, termed human assurance burden, is constitutive of task-technology fit rather than external to it. Five propositions formalize these claims.

Research limitations/implications – As a conceptual contribution the framework is argued rather than tested. The propositions are stated so as to be falsifiable, and a research agenda specifies the observable measures and designs through which each may be examined.

Practical implications – The framework yields a governance routine that is durable across model generations because it evaluates outputs rather than vendors: classify the task, identify the dominant defect risk, screen for disqualifying defects, read the required review burden, and decide whether to use, revise, regenerate, escalate or reject the artifact.

Originality/value – The paper relocates AI evaluation in change management from the model level to the artifact level, formalizes noncompensatory quality for organizational artifacts, and extends task-technology fit by treating required human assurance as a dimension of fit. It offers change scholarship a governance construct that does not expire as underlying models change.

Keywords Organizational change management, Generative artificial intelligence, Artifact assurance, Task-technology fit, Information quality, Noncompensatory decision making, AI governance

Paper type Conceptual paper

title: AI Governance and Strategic Decision-Making in Organizations: A Systematic Literature Review

detail.title: AI Governance and Strategic Decision-Making in Organizations: A Systematic Literature Review

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of organizational strategic decision-making, changing how organizations analyze information, assess alternatives, and develop strategic responses. However, the growing use of AI also raises important questions about how these systems should be governed, particularly with regard to transparency, accountability, bias, ethical risks, and regulatory compliance. Although research on AI governance and AI-supported decision-making has expanded considerably, the existing literature remains fragmented across information systems, strategic management, organizational studies, ethics, and public policy. This fragmentation makes it difficult to develop a clear understanding of how AI governance is connected to strategic decision-making within organizations.

This study aims to systematically review the existing literature on AI governance and strategic decision-making in organizations. The review will examine the theoretical and conceptual frameworks used to explain this relationship, the models and mechanisms proposed for integrating AI into organizational strategic processes, and the main risks and ethical challenges identified in previous research. A systematic literature review will be conducted following PRISMA guidelines using major academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, EBSCO Business Source Complete, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar. The review will focus primarily on literature published between 2015 and 2025, with particular attention to research published from 2020 onward.

The study is expected to provide an integrated synthesis of current knowledge on AI governance and strategic decision-making, identify major theoretical and methodological patterns, and highlight important gaps for future research. It will also provide practical insights for organizational leaders and policymakers seeking to develop effective AI governance structures that support responsible and strategically aligned use of AI.

detail.abstract: Frontier AI labs and nonprofit organizations are increasingly partnering to deploy frontier AI in support of nonprofits' missions worldwide, and philanthropic funders have invested hundreds of millions of dollars to support organizations in deploying AI for social impact. However, the rapidly growing AI for Social Good (AI4SG) ecosystem lacks a clear understanding of the support these partnerships provide, how they form, and what drives their success. This paper reports the findings of an empirical study of bespoke partnerships between frontier AI labs and nonprofits, drawing on interviews conducted between April and July 2026 across 24 organizations-frontier AI labs, nonprofits, philanthropic funders, and advisory organizations-and on four case studies of partnerships serving last-mile communities in low-and middle-income countries. We identify important conditions for success and common sources of friction across partnerships, and find that partnerships can improve by strengthening governance, formalizing expectations, and supporting nonprofits' capacity to sustain solutions after the partnership ends. We find that funders play a vital role in convening and coordinating these partnerships, though their strategies can in some cases concentrate resources narrowly and influence nonprofits' technology choices. Our research contributes recommendations for AI labs, nonprofits, funders, and advisory organizations within the AI4SG ecosystem.

detail.abstract: Deviation and out-of-specification investigations are among the most resource-intensive activities within pharmaceutical quality systems, and their quality directly shapes inspection outcomes, CAPA effectiveness, and patient safety. Generative AI, and in particular large language models (LLMs) coupled with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), has attracted growing interest for accelerating investigation drafting while preserving evidentiary rigor, and a small but expanding body of peer-reviewed work has already tested this directly on pharmaceutical manufacturing records. This paper synthesizes that literature and examines the design requirements for a retrieval-grounded decision-support system intended to assist, not replace, qualified investigators across deviation review, root-cause analysis, and CAPA documentation. Rather than claiming an unoccupied gap, the paper positions itself against the closest existing work: a benchmarking study of GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Claude-2 on real manufacturing deviation records; an enterprise-deployed pharmaceutical regulatory-compliance RAG assistant; a peer-reviewed governance mapping of the 2025 draft EU GMP Annex 22; and a review of LLMs in healthcare quality management already addressing deviation and CAPA workflows against the EU AI Act, GAMP 5, ISO 13485 and ISO/IEC 42001. The narrower gap identified here is that the closest systematised review of digital innovation in pharmaceutical manufacturing quality, searching to 2023, confined its AI theme to artificial neural, convolutional and fuzzy cellular neural networks, with generative AI and large language models absent from its included literature. The paper further shows that the evaluation rubric such a system would require substantially overlaps with existing RAG evaluation frameworks (RAGAS, ARES, RAGChecker) rather than constituting a new instrument, and that the draft EU GMP Annex 22 currently restricts dynamic, generative models from critical GMP applications, a constraint bearing directly and unresolvedly on any such proposal. No performance results are claimed; this is a structured narrative synthesis and design analysis, not a validated deployment. detail.abstract: This study evaluates an AI-based personalized revision framework for Secondary School Certificate students using a synthetic dataset of 1,000 learner records. The simulated cohort was balanced between an experimental condition receiving adaptive, AI-informed revision recommendations and a control condition receiving standard teacher-guided revision. Each record included baseline achievement, eight weekly assessments, posttest and four-week retention outcomes, topic-level mastery, revision-plan completion, study behaviour, confidence, attendance, and demographic characteristics. Data quality checks found no missing values, duplicate learner identifiers, exact duplicate records, or out-of-range values. Baseline performance was nearly identical between groups (44.25% versus 44.30%, p = .956). In the synthetic model, the experimental group achieved a mean post-test score of 67.07%, compared with 53.58% in the control group. Mean learning gains were 22.82 and 9.28 percentage points, respectively, producing a simulated difference of 13.54 points. An ANCOVA controlling for baseline achievement yielded an adjusted experimental coefficient of 13.54 points, 95% CI [13.02, 14.05]. Retention loss was smaller in the experimental condition, and confidence gains and plan completion were higher. Because the observations were generated rather than collected from students, inferential statistics describe the internal behaviour of the simulation and must not be interpreted as evidence of effectiveness in Bangladesh schools. The main contribution is a reproducible evaluation framework, dataset schema, decision logic, and prototype Student Performance Tracker and Smart Revision System that can be validated through a future randomized or quasi-experimental field study.

detail.abstract:
International-relations scholarship has long organised statecraft around three broad logics: realist competition over security, liberal-institutionalist cooperation around trade and regimes, and constructivist attention to norms, identity and legitimacy.

This paper argues that a fourth, underdeveloped logic — the deliberate cultivation of population wellbeing as a basis for cooperation, trust and legitimate influence — deserves systematic treatment alongside the other three, and proposes the term Wellbeing Diplomacy to name it. Locating the concept within soft-power and smart-power theory (Nye, 2004), regime theory (Krasner, 1983) and the epistemic-communities literature (Haas, 1992), we show how a global mental-health burden exceeding one billion people, an AI-driven labour transition, and a wellness economy now worth USD 6.8 trillion have together created both a governance gap and a strategic opportunity.

We argue that Indic wisdom — anchored in Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam ("the world is one family"), Ayurveda, Yoga, and Sarve Bhavantu Sukhinah — functions not merely as a normative resource but as a practical catalyst, capable of simultaneously building diplomatic trust and generating measurable services-export value for India: AYUSH and herbal exports already exceed USD 689 million annually, India's wellness-tourism market is valued near USD 28 billion and climbing toward USD 38 billion by 2030, and traditional-medicine recognition is now being written into bilateral trade agreements such as the India–Oman CEPA and the India–New Zealand FTA.

The paper develops a five-domain operational framework, a dedicated analysis of India's wellbeing-services export opportunity under the WTO's GATS trade-in-services modes, and a preliminary, non-definitive Wellbeing Diplomacy Index. It closes with an explicit accounting of risks — cultural instrumentalisation, over-commercialisation, measurement fragility and sovereignty overreach — together with conflict-of-interest, funding and ethics declarations, and a research agenda addressed to the global scholarly and policy community.

The paper is offered as a foundation for further inquiry, not a finished doctrine.

title: ASSESSING THE COMMERCIAL IMPACT OF THE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT TAX INCENTIVE IN MERGERS & ACQUISITION TRANSACTIONS IN NIGERIA

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No affiliation

detail.abstract:
For more than five decades, Nigeria's principal investment incentive was the pioneer status incentive (“PSI”) granted under the repealed Industrial Development (Income Tax Relief) Act. It had a blanket approach where a company producing an approved pioneer product enjoyed a complete holiday from company income tax for a defined period. The relief attached to profits, and it applied so far the beneficiary continued operating within the pioneer line of business. The Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 (“NTA”), which came into force on 1st January 2026, repealed that Act[3] and replaced the pioneer status incentive with the economic development tax incentive ("EDTI"), a credit computed by reference to certified capital investment rather than realised profit.

The economic development tax credit ("EDTC") is an entitlement evidenced by a certificate issued to a named company, granted by the President, computed on capital expenditure certified in respect of identified assets at an identified location, and published in the Federal Gazette. It is, in commercial terms, an asset. For instance, for a company that has committed the N10,000,000,000.00 (Ten Billion Naira) of qualifying capital expenditure ("QCE") required to enter the coal mining sub-sector, the credit is worth N500,000,000.00 (Five hundred million Naira) a year for five years, with a carry-forward window of a further five years. It's then worth stating the value in terms of equity in a financial transaction between two entities.

The question that follows is: does the incentive survive the transaction? The Act answers in a single subsection of four paragraphs. This article examines that subsection and the transactions it governs, identifies the transaction it does not govern, considers the complicated relationship with the general business restructuring rules elsewhere in the Act, tests whether parties may lawfully contract around it, and sets out the practical steps that acquirers and targets should now be taking.

detail.abstract: ROSAI — Role-Oriented Skills Assessment for AI — is a framework developed by Prasanjit Saha for assessing professional AI readiness relative to the mix of responsibilities expected from a role. Rather than treating AI readiness as a universal attribute, ROSAI represents a target role as a continuous composition across Product/Business, Software Engineering, Data/ML, Operations/Transformation, Design/UX, and Leadership/Governance. This role composition dynamically determines the relative importance of seven AI capability dimensions: AI Fluency, Applied AI Judgement, Build & Execution, Evaluation & Reliability, Data & ML Capability, Responsible AI & Governance, and Business & Organizational Impact. The framework produces three separate interpretation signals: ROSAI Score, Evidence Strength, and Assessment Confidence. This Version 1.0 paper defines the conceptual model, high-level scoring architecture, role-relative weighting mechanism, role-critical safeguards, assessment architecture, validation roadmap, limitations, and relationship to existing AI literacy and workforce competency frameworks. ROSAI v1.0 is presented as a practitioner-designed framework and testable methodology; it has not yet undergone psychometric validation or independent peer review.

detail.abstract: The uncontrolled spread of fabricated and misleading content across digital platforms has turned automated fake news detection into an urgent research priority. Approaches built around hand-crafted linguistic features and shallow classifiers struggle to capture the contextual subtleties that separate deceptive narratives from genuine reporting [8]. Transformer-based language models, beginning with BERT and its successors, have reshaped the field by learning deep, bidirectional representations of text that generalize reasonably well across domains and writing styles [2], [3]. This paper reviews the trajectory of transformer-based fake news detection research, synthesizes reported performance across widely used benchmarks such as LIAR, FakeNewsNet, and ISOT, and proposes a hybrid detection framework that combines a fine-tuned transformer encoder, a metadata-aware attention fusion layer, and a post-hoc explainability module. The comparative analysis draws on more than two dozen studies published between 2017 and 2025 to surface recurring strengths, failure patterns, and open problems, including vulnerability to large-language-model-generated misinformation and inconsistent generalization across datasets of differing granularity. The paper closes with concrete research directions for improving the robustness, interpretability, and multilingual coverage of transformer-based detection pipelines.

detail.abstract: Global retail enterprises operating across multiple countries, business lines, and product categories face a fundamental analytics challenge: the proliferation of disconnected data systems that prevent leadership from obtaining a unified view of organizational performance. This paper presents a case study of a comprehensive retail analytics transformation program executed at a Fortune 100 athletic goods company (approximately $30 billion in annual revenue, ~79,000 employees) between 2015 and 2016. The initiative addressed a fragmented analytics landscape comprising more than twenty disparate data systems-spanning SAP, Oracle, flat files, and custom APIsthat served different business units, geographies, and functional domains. The transformation was delivered in two sequential phases: first, an Enterprise Product Catalog Online Transformation that unified SKU-level product data across all business units and global markets for four-quarter forward planning; and second, a Global Analytics Dashboard that consolidated actuals-versus-forecast reporting across sales, inventory, and demand metrics for all countries, business lines, and product categories. The analytics platform replaced manual, ad-hoc reporting processes with a self-serve, on-demand Tableau-based dashboard accessible to all business unit leaders globally. This paper contributes a practitioner-oriented framework for enterprise analytics unification in multinational retail environments, addressing the technical challenges of multi-source data ingestion, cross-system deduplication, format harmonization across heterogeneous platforms, and stakeholder alignment when business units maintain conflicting definitions of operational metrics.

detail.abstract:
Research on artificial intelligence and work now spans exposure, productivity, work organisation, hiring, displacement, training, career behaviour, health, household adjustment and social protection. The question an individual worker asks : " What does this transformation mean for my own occupational, material and health future? ", nevertheless requires a different inferential task. This paper develops a worker-centred evidence-chain review and a Worker Evidence Translation Protocol (WETP) that identifies how far population evidence can responsibly support worker-facing orientation. The approach is an adversarial, purposive synthesis rather than an exhaustive systematic review. It separates outcome depth from design and identification strength, and records observation time, population, technology, institution, durability and required transport for each claim.

Two results are distinguished. First, there is a structural observability limit: broad generative-AI diffusion began only in late 2022, so a genuinely long-run same-person trajectory from AI-related work change to durable material outcomes cannot yet be observed. This is a calendar constraint, not a literature-gap finding. Second, and empirically more informative, chain coverage is uneven. Current evidence directly observes exposure, adoption, work reorganisation and selected worker-state margins: Danish administrative data show rapid task reorganisation with precise two-year null effects on recorded earnings and hours, while U.S. payroll data through June 2026 show a widening employment gap for workers aged 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations, operating mainly through reduced hiring rather than separations. Downstream transition, recovery and household mechanisms are substantively documented, but largely in displacement, robotics or household settings that require technological and institutional transport. The principal evidence gap is therefore the bridge linking current work change to feasible transition and downstream recovery for the same workers. WETP operationalises this boundary through a worker context profile, evidence cards, explicit "do not infer" statements and five descriptive actionability levels.

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to interrogate the operational fissures between the African Continental Free Trade Area's Digital Trade Protocol and the practical demands of transboundary environmental governance in the Lake Victoria Basin. It examines how the Protocol's provisions on data governance, cross-border data flows, and emerging technologies collide with sovereignty claims embedded within the Lake Victoria Basin Commission's institutional architecture. The paper argues that data innovation, as imagined by continental trade law, presupposes an interoperability that East Africa's fragmented environmental data regimes do not yet possess. It further contends that artificial intelligence, increasingly deployed for water-quality forecasting and hyacinth prediction, risks entrenching a new algorithmic dependency unless African states assert a coherent doctrine of environmental data sovereignty. Drawing on doctrinal analysis, comparative regional practice, and continental policy instruments, the paper builds critically upon existing scholarship on African data governance and transboundary water law. It concludes by proposing a basin-level data trust and an interoperability clause reconciling the Protocol with basin-specific legal instruments, thereby advancing a genuinely African jurisprudence of data-driven environmental stewardship.

detail.abstract: This work concerns an alternative framework for performing engineering economic calculations from the viewpoint of industrial capital by using the Marxian categories of constant capital and variable capital. It presents a dynamic macroscopic economic model that describes the capital production process of a single company for the cases of both discrete and continuous production cycles. Explicit formulae are developed for the growth of constant capital, variable capital and surplus value over time. Measures of profitability like the rate of return, rate of profit and payback period are derived from the model, which is illustrated by two examples. In the first example, the model is applied to three different investment scenarios adapted from a well-known textbook on plant design and economics for chemical engineers whereas, in the second one, it is applied to the cost data of a plant manufacturing an active pharmaceutical ingredient from Duboisia leaves. Compared to conventional engineering economics, which is based upon the opportunity-cost viewpoint of finance capital, the Marxian model can describe both simple and expanded reproduction and yields a deeper insight into the capital accumulation process of the company.

detail.abstract: In recent decades, many methodologies have been proposed to help stakeholder groups decide on the best ideas to implement in order to meet a prespecified objective. Despite their frequent usage across many domains including healthcare, political science and business management, no mathematical framework unifying such methods has yet been constructed. With the birth of ideometrics in 2025 - an emerging science studying the generation, evaluation and prioritisation of ideas, it would be fitting to develop a formal quantitative classification and description of idea prioritisation methods. Firstly, notation will be developed in order to classify methods under idea-criteria evaluability, from which the concept of a prioritisation attainment sequence (PAS) will be introduced. The PAS captures (i) how criteria used for idea evaluation are weighted, (ii) how ideas are scored and aggregated across participants, and (iii) how the criterion weights and aggregated idea scores can be combined to form a vector of ideas indexed by priority. The PAS of the following commonly used methods will be computed for illustration: multi-voting; nominal group technique; Delphi process; RAND/UCLA appropriate method; paired comparison method; group analytic hierarchical process, and the Child Health and Nutrition Research Initiative method. The mathematical framework developed in this paper provides a standardised approach towards understanding how ideas are currently evaluated and prioritised.

title: Causal Engram Circuits for Factual and Hallucinated Memory in Large Language Models
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Causal Engram Circuits for Factual and Hallucinated Memory in Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce fluent yet factually incorrect statements—a failure that mirrors false memory in biological systems. Whether such errors arise from causally identifiable and manipulable circuit elements has remained unknown. Here we adapt the engram framework from systems neuroscience and combine causal mediation analysis with a double-dissociation logic to localize, verify, and rewrite factual and false memory traces in GPT-style transformers. We discover that sparse sets of knowledge neurons—canonical ensembles of approximately 8–15 units—function as memory engrams: silencing them selectively erases target-fact retrieval while matched controls remain intact; exogenous activation forces the fact into output even under neutral prompts. Rigorous controls, including patterned activation and non-engram amplification, confirm identity-specific sufficiency. Critically, counterfactual fine-tuning creates false memory engrams that deviate geometrically toward lexical co-occurrence subspaces; formal mediation analysis reveals that this geometric corruption causally mediates 65% of the pathway from falsity to erroneous output. Exploiting this divergence, we construct an unsupervised Memory Credibility Score that predicts hallucination propensity without behavioural testing, generalizing across relations and model scales. The framework extends to multi-hop and temporal reasoning and enables reversible, context-dependent memory control unavailable to permanent weight-editing methods. Our findings establish a causal sufficiency-and-necessity account of factual retrieval, diagnose representational pathologies underlying hallucination, and deliver a precision toolkit for understanding and certifying knowledge in LLMs.

title: The Historical Plurality of Capitalism: Belonging, Civilizational Routes, and the Limits of Global Convergence

detail.title: The Historical Plurality of Capitalism: Belonging, Civilizational Routes, and the Limits of Global Convergence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract:
Capitalism has never developed as a single institutional system. This paper argues that its historical plurality is not merely a transitional consequence of different stages of development but a durable feature of human institutional evolution. Using the Philosophy and Economics of Belonging, the paper explains capitalist plurality through imperfect belonging, institutional differentiation, and the unusually rapid diachrony of human societies.


Different geographical environments, historical experiences, religions, family structures, political systems, and conceptual traditions have generated distinct civilizational routes through which markets, property, firms, states, labor, finance, and technological change have been institutionalized. Capitalism transforms these inherited arrangements, but it is simultaneously interpreted, constrained, and transformed by them.


The paper then examines the implications for twenty-first-century globalization. Production, finance, trade, technology, data, artificial intelligence, migration, and environmental effects increasingly operate across national borders, while political legitimacy, enforceable authority, solidarity, and reciprocal obligation remain substantially national or regional. The resulting global belonging deficit constitutes a central institutional problem of contemporary capitalism.


The paper argues that neither global institutional homogenization nor fragmentation provides an adequate response. The future of capitalism requires strong, flexible, and tolerant global institutions capable of governing interdependence while accommodating legitimate differences among national and civilizational forms of belonging. Capitalism should therefore be understood as a permanently plural global system whose stability depends on improving the institutional correspondence between an increasingly global economy and the diverse societies within which economic activity remains embedded.

title: When Regulatory Metrics Disagree: A Multi-Layer Audit of Regulatory Output in the First Year of the Second Trump Administration
affiliations: Stanford University - Hoover Institution and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: When Regulatory Metrics Disagree: A Multi-Layer Audit of Regulatory Output in the First Year of the Second Trump Administration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: The research was not funded.

detail.abstract: Administrative scorecards, rule publications, codified text, and agency burden estimates measure different aspects of regulatory output. We compare them during the opening year of the second Trump administration. We match the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) FY2025 ledger to a census of 2,334 Federal Register final rules, classify burden direction through blinded large-language-model review with verified quotations, measure changes in the electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR), and audit agency estimates. OIRA's regulatory-budget account reports 646 deregulatory and five significant regulatory actions (129:1). A separate census covering the administration's first 365 days identifies 481 burdenreducing and 671 burden-increasing final rules under a common document classification. The eCFR contracts by 315,735 words and 6,338 RegData-style restriction terms (0.560 percent); for context, the annual RegData series records declines in only six of 55 year-to-year changes. These measures use different units, eligibility conditions, and reporting periods. We propose linked reporting that preserves each measure's scope, unit, and inferential limits.

title: How Network Hiring by Entrepreneurs Shapes Firm Formation and Performance

detail.title: How Network Hiring by Entrepreneurs Shapes Firm Formation and Performance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This material is based upon work supported by the National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship under grant DGE-1656518. I also acknowledge support from the Dixon and Carol Doll Graduate Fellowship Fund and the Hawley-Shoven Fellowship Fund through a grant to the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, as well as from the European Research Council under the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under grant agreement No. 851891, hosted by Statistics Norway (ref. 21/5634).

detail.abstract: Many entrepreneurs rely on their personal networks to hire their first employees. How important is this practice for the formation and performance of new firms? I study this question using Norwegian administrative data that allow me to link entrepreneurs to their firms, employees, and former coworkers. To identify causal effects, I develop an instrumental variables framework that jointly models entry and network hiring, allowing for endogenous selection on both margins. The results reveal three main findings. First, each ex-coworker hired in the firm's first year raises annual revenues in the following four years by over $250K and crowds in other hires, without reducing average productivity. Second, without the ability to hire ex-coworkers, a quarter of network-hiring entrepreneurs would not have started their firms at all. Third, counterfactual simulations show that, compared to entry subsidies, networks enable entry of entrepreneurs who create substantially more jobs, survive longer, and achieve higher value added per worker. Interpreted through the lens of a simple model, the data suggest that private information about coworker quality is a key driver of network hiring. Taken together, the results show that access to human capital through networks is an important determinant of entrepreneurial entry and success.

title: From Picking Winners to Absorbing Winners? DeepSeek and the Adaptive Reconfiguration of Chinese Industrial Policy

detail.title: From Picking Winners to Absorbing Winners? DeepSeek and the Adaptive Reconfiguration of Chinese Industrial Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is based exclusively on publicly available documents and secondary sources and did not involve human participants or interventions.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Debates about industrial policy remain organised around a question of foresight: whether states can identify, before market outcomes are visible, which sectors, technologies or firms warrant selective support. This article argues that the question is underspecified, because selection operates at distinct analytical levels and at distinct moments. Where selection-relevant technological trajectories turn over faster than firm-specific policy commitments can be recalibrated, the informational validity of ex ante firm selection decays before the policy cycle does. Under such temporal mismatch, the state's relative institutional advantage can shift away from identifying specific firms ex ante and toward integrating competitively validated capabilities ex post. I call the resulting mode "Absorbing winners": within a strategically designated and state-enabled sector, decentralised experimentation reveals competitively validated capabilities, after which state institutions and state-coordinated actors embed, adapt, scale and redeploy those capabilities across broader infrastructural, industrial and governance systems. The unit of intervention is the capability rather than the originating firm, and ownership transfer is neither necessary nor sufficient. The argument is developed through process tracing on DeepSeek, tested against a negative case (Meta's Llama in Chinese public systems), and specified through four disconfirming observations. The article connects the mechanism to absorptive capacity and complementary-asset theory, inverting the classic latecomer direction: a state absorbing a domestically generated frontier capability rather than a foreign one.

title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Hyperspectral Retrieval of Leaf Biochemical and Structural Traits
affiliations: University of Valencia, University of Valencia and University of Valencia - Image Processing Laboratory

detail.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Hyperspectral Retrieval of Leaf Biochemical and Structural Traits

keywords.keywords: Gaussian Processes \sep Neural Network \sep Vegetation traits retrieval \sep Global Spectra-Trait Initiative \sep band ranking \sep dimensionality reduction

detail.abstract: Leaf biochemical and structural traits provide essential information on plant functioning, nutritional status, productivity, and responses to environmental stress.Reliable retrieval of these traits from hyperspectral reflectance requires models that provide both accurate predictions and meaningful uncertainty estimates.This study therefore evaluates and compares probabilistic machine learning regression algorithms (MLRA) that jointly provide point predictions and model-based uncertainty estimates.Specifically, Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), and Deep Gaussian Processes Regression (DeepGPR) were assessed for estimating leaf mass per area (LMA), nitrogen content per unit area (N$_\textrm{area}$), nitrogen content by dry mass (N$_\textrm{mass}$), phosphorus content per unit area (P$_\textrm{area}$), phosphorus content by dry mass (P$_\textrm{mass}$), and leaf water content (LWC) using leaf-level spectra from the Global Spectra-Trait Initiative (GSTI) database.The original spectra comprised 2151 wavelengths spanning 350-2500 nm.Principal Components Analysis (PCA) was evaluated as a dimensionality-reduction approach for all models, whereas Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) was applied within GPR for wavelength selection.Model performance was assessed using \(R^{2}\), normalized RMSE and model uncertainty estimates were assessed using Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP), and Mean Prediction Interval Width (MPIW).GPR provided the most consistent balance between predictive accuracy, PICP, and MPIW.The most accurate LMA retrieval was obtained using PCA-GPR with a Matérn-\(3/2\) kernel and 12 PCs (\(R^{2}=0.94\), nRMSE=0.17, PICP \(=0.98\)).The strongest N$_\textrm{mass}$ result was achieved using GPR-ARD with an RBF kernel and 40 selected wavelengths (\(R^{2}=0.92\), nRMSE=0.07, PICP \(=0.97\)).PCA-GPR also produced the most accurate results for P$_\textrm{area}$ and P$_\textrm{mass}$, while GPR-ARD and PCA-GPR yielded similar accuracy and uncertainty estimates for LWC.BNNs produced narrow but strongly under-covering prediction intervals, whereas DeepGPR generally achieved high PICP with substantially wider intervals.Overall, GPR combined with PCA or ARD offered the most reliable framework for probabilistic hyperspectral trait retrieval.

title: From Mandela to Meta: Democratization of The Right of Publicity, Persona, and Image Rights in Cyberspace
affiliations: and King's College London

detail.title: From Mandela to Meta: Democratization of The Right of Publicity, Persona, and Image Rights in Cyberspace

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
Image rights, historically divided across privacy, publicity, and personality-rights doctrines, are increasingly adjudicated outside of court, by the content-moderation systems of Meta, TikTok, YouTube, and X. This Article argues that these platforms have become de facto adjudicators of image-based harm, resolving image disputes at a volume and speed no national court system can match. 

The Article first surveys the fragmented legacy frameworks, U.S. privacy and publicity law, and European and Chinese personality-rights regimes, showing that none was designed for a modern world of microcelebrities, generative AI, and borderless global circulation. It then examines platform policies on consent, impersonation, and non-consensual imagery, arguing that their convergence across services and jurisdictions has produced a lex digitalis: a privately developed, global body of image-rights norms. Drawing on the classical Roman law categories of ius naturale and ius gentium, the Article characterizes this convergence as a digital analogue to natural law and the law of nations. The convergence reflects substantive commitments to dignity and autonomy that are treated as self-evidence across platforms, even absent any formal international agreement. 

The Article concludes that this platform-driven order has inadvertently produced a more universal and accessible image right than any single national legal system offers. This is a silver lining of sorts: a positive and unintended consequence of the platforms' development of a de facto global law is the immediacy of a more uniform networked approach. At present, protection of image rights in the analog world remains fragmented across jurisdictions, a patchwork of inconsistent regimes rather than a coherent whole. Cyberspace, by its nature, is global and demands global legal rules and solutions. The image-related rules of major platforms have quietly coalesced into precisely such a lex digitalis: a global body of uniform rules, standards, and policies that structures how, and which, types of images may or may not circulate online. In effect, platforms have extended image rights in a more uniform and internationally harmonized form than any single legal system has achieved on its own. 

There is also a second, and no less unintended positive consequence of content moderation rules. The more individuals share their images online, the more necessary robust image rights protection is to the digital world. It is, therefore, fundamental that all natural persons have digital recourse to protect their "image" which arises automatically at birth. Every individual, famous or not, is entitled to protect their digital image on equal footing. Real cases involving one-day-old babies, bus drivers, streetsweepers, models, and ordinary social media users illustrate how this protection allows individuals to safeguard their unique attributes and identity, and with them, their dignity, reputation, and privacy, in cyberspace. At present, the democratization of image and persona rights is a pressing and profoundly needed development.

title: Environmental Governance: Optimal Institutional allocation and Political conflict
affiliations: QUANT AI LAB

detail.title: Environmental Governance: Optimal Institutional allocation and Political conflict
detail.abstract: This paper develops a comparative-institutional model of environmental governance in which a fixed amount of institutional effort is allocated between governmentled environmental regulation (GLER) and non-state voluntary environmental governance (NVEG). The socially optimal allocation balances their relative environmental effectiveness against channel-specific implementation costs and the interaction costs generated by their coexistence. The model identifies GLER-only, NVEG-only, and mixed regimes. A mixed architecture is optimal when interaction costs are sufficiently low. Higher interaction costs reduce institutional diversity and lead to specialization, with the ordering of the thresholds determining which channel is retained. When GLER is more environmentally effective, greater environmental severity shifts the optimal allocation toward GLER. The political extension introduces groups bearing different shares of environmental damages and institutional costs. Relatively damageexposed groups favor GLER, whereas relatively cost-exposed groups favor NVEG. Political influence determines the direction of these opposing pressures around the social optimum, as summarized by a politically weighted damage-cost ratio. The framework shows that opposition to mandatory environmental regulation (GLER) can arise from distributional and institutional conflict without implying indifference to environmental damages.

title: The Operating-Layer Dominance Hypothesis: Why Agentic Trading Alpha Is an Interface Problem, Not a Model Problem A Position Paper on Architecture, Live Evaluation, and Alpha Limits in Multi-Agent Trading Systems

detail.title: The Operating-Layer Dominance Hypothesis: Why Agentic Trading Alpha Is an Interface Problem, Not a Model Problem A Position Paper on Architecture, Live Evaluation, and Alpha Limits in Multi-Agent Trading Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any people or organizations that could be perceived to have influenced this work. The author is an independent researcher and AI systems architect; no third party funded, commissioned, or reviewed this paper prior to submission. The author has authored books published independently on Amazon on related topics (AI systems architecture and financial markets), which is disclosed here for full transparency but did not influence the content or conclusions of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper does not involve human participants, patient data, or original data collection; it synthesizes previously published research and independent engineering observation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author without financial support from any institution, company, or grant body.

detail.abstract: Research and capital in agentic trading systems overwhelmingly target model improvement-larger language models, deeper reasoning chains, richer memory. This position paper argues the field is optimizing the wrong layer. We synthesize three independent bodies of evidence-multi-agent coordination architecture, production-scale live evaluation, and empirical alpha-decay studies-under a single testable claim: the Operating-Layer Dominance Hypothesis. In any agentic trading system executing real capital, output-behavior variance is predominantly explained by interface and execution parameters, not by model reasoning content. We ground this in a six-month, population-scale production record (n≈7.5M model invocations) showing agent fixed effects explain 60% of behavioral variance, and leaderboard-render boundaries causally shift trade routing via regression discontinuity. We corroborate this with an independent engineering observation from a real institutional deployment, and specify a falsification condition absent from prior literature. We conclude that deterministic execution-layer control, not model capability, is the binding constraint on agentic alpha.

title: A Myerson Completion Conjecture for Shapley-Shubik Power: Exact Representation Beyond Weighted Voting

detail.title: A Myerson Completion Conjecture for Shapley-Shubik Power: Exact Representation Beyond Weighted Voting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Simple games need not be weighted. Adding a communication graph does not make weighted voting universal at the level of exact rule representation: an elementary counting comparison shows that, for sufficiently many players, there are more simple games than weighted-game/graph pairs. At the level of power, however, the question is different. The inverse-power literature largely asks how closely a weighted game can approximate a target power vector, and existing results show that weighted games can often approximate broader classes very well. This note asks for zero error. A five-player simple game is exhibited whose Shapley-Shubik vector is not attained by any weighted voting game but is attained exactly as the Myerson value of a weighted game on a path. Exact enumeration further finds that every Shapley-Shubik vector generated by a simple game with at most six players is attained by a weighted game with a communication graph. These examples motivate the Myerson completion conjecture: every Shapley-Shubik vector of a finite simple game has an exact weighted-game/graph representation.

title: Digital Economy and Green Productivity in China: Evidence on Innovation-Productivity Gaps and Spatial Spillovers

detail.title: Digital Economy and Green Productivity in China: Evidence on Innovation-Productivity Gaps and Spatial Spillovers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
The rapid development of the digital economy has created new opportunities for improving productivity and promoting sustainable economic development. However, the productivity consequences of digital transformation remain uncertain, as the expansion of digital capabilities does not necessarily translate into equivalent improvements in economic performance. This paper examines the relationship between digital economy development and green productivity in China, with particular attention to the potential innovation–productivity gap and regional spillover effects.

Using a provincial panel dataset covering 30 Chinese provinces from 2011 to 2022, this study constructs measures of digital economy development and Green Total Factor Productivity (GTFP) and employs panel econometric models to investigate the impact of digitalisation on green productivity. Furthermore, mediation analysis and heterogeneity analysis are conducted to explore the underlying mechanisms and regional differences. A Spatial Durbin Model is further applied to examine whether digital economy development generates spatial spillover effects across regions.

The empirical results reveal a potential disconnect between digital innovation capability and productivity improvement: while digital economy development significantly promotes green innovation, such innovation gains are not fully translated into higher green productivity. While digital transformation creates opportunities for technological advancement and innovation, the conversion of digital capabilities into productivity gains depends on the effectiveness of innovation utilisation and regional economic conditions. The findings also reveal the importance of spatial interactions, suggesting that the effects of digital economy development extend beyond individual regions through interconnected economic networks.

This paper contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it extends research on digital economy and sustainable development by examining the relationship between digital transformation and green productivity from a regional perspective. Second, it highlights the importance of the innovation–productivity conversion process in understanding why digital advantages may not always generate proportional productivity improvements. Third, by incorporating spatial econometric analysis, this study provides new evidence on the regional spillover effects of digital transformation in China.

title: Which Tool? Why a Single Interest Rate Cannot Do the Job the Checked/Mixed/Residual Framework Assigns to Inflation Policy

detail.title: Which Tool? Why a Single Interest Rate Cannot Do the Job the Checked/Mixed/Residual Framework Assigns to Inflation Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

keywords: central bank communication JEL Classification: E31

detail.abstract: Two prior papers (Hwang, 2026a, 2026b) argued, first, that the general price level is a convention rather than a discovered fact, and second, that assigning a single causal label to an aggregate price change repeats the same error one stage later-a print's causes decompose into a checked tier (sector-evidenced supply or demand shocks), a mixed tier (components like shelter where the evidence itself does not resolve cleanly), and a residual (broad-based, sticky, expectations-driven co-movement). This paper asks what follows for policy instrument choice once that decomposition is taken seriously. Its answer is that the standard toolkit-an economy-wide short-term interest rate applied uniformly regardless of a print's composition-is mismatched to two of the three tiers and only well-matched to the third. The rate transmits almost entirely through demand and has essentially no direct purchase on checked supply shocks; worse, in the mixed housing tier, rate increases can aggravate the supply side of the very component they are meant to cool, through a well-documented mortgage rate lock-in channel that suppresses listings and new construction (Batzer, Coste, Doerner & Seiler, 2024; Fonseca & Liu, 2024). The rate's legitimate domain is the residual, where it operates primarily through expectations-anchoring rather than through reversing whatever triggered the print. The paper maps each tier to instruments actually suited to it-strategic reserve releases and targeted trade or capacity measures for checked supply components; zoning, permitting, and construction-finance reform for the mixed housing tier; fiscal restraint and central bank communication, alongside the rate, for the residual-and confronts directly the strongest objection to this tier-matching logic: the Keynesian supply-shock literature (Guerrieri, Lorenzoni, Straub & Werning, 2022) shows that under low cross-sector substitutability and incomplete markets, a supply shock in one sector can generate a demand shortfall large enough to justify demand-side intervention even when the shock is genuinely supply-driven. The paper concedes this fully and refines its own prescription accordingly: the checked tier's default is supply-side and targeted, but the default is defeasible, and the correct demand-side response in the defeasible case is targeted, insured transfers to the affected sector-not an economy-wide rate move that falls on every interest-rate-sensitive sector regardless of relevance. A discussion of the empirically contested 1971-74 wage-price control episode and the mixed 2022 Strategic Petroleum Reserve record closes the paper by cautioning against overclaiming for any single instrument, checked-tier included.

title: Flight to Home or Flight to Safety? Global Tail Risk Cycles and Hedge Fund Returns
affiliations: IESEG School of Management, Univ. Lille, CNRS, UMR 9221 - LEM - Lille Economie Management, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Department of Economics and Koc University

detail.title: Flight to Home or Flight to Safety? Global Tail Risk Cycles and Hedge Fund Returns

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors of this study have no personal or financial relationships with people or organizations that may have influenced, or could be perceived to have influenced, their study.
declarations.funderStatement: Kamil Yilmaz's work for this paper was supported by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (TÜBİTAK) under grant number 121C271.

detail.abstract: We extend the mutual excitation (MUTE) testing framework to identify flight-to-home (FTH) episodes in high-frequency data-directional tail excitation from emerging market equities to U.S. stocks-and distinguish them from flight-to-safety (FTS). Our continuoustime approach detects directionality, temporal clustering, and tail propagation that daily threshold methods cannot. Using 1-minute ETF data over 2010-2021, we find FTH events more frequent and intense than FTS, heterogeneous across regions, and time-varying across regimes. Hedge fund strategies exhibit significant FTH exposure distinct from FTS. Optionimplied tail measures are orthogonal to FTH, suggesting that FTH captures a new dimension of realized tail dependence.

title: The International Trilemma of Liberalization, Security, and Sustainability
affiliations: and Bocconi University - Department of Law

detail.title: The International Trilemma of Liberalization, Security, and Sustainability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Pennsylvania Journal of International Law, Forthcoming

detail.abstract: Recent years have seen the growing and expanding use of legal tools to further geopolitical objectives. Trade-related measures serve as an important means of pursuing these objectives, either through explicit restrictions, conditions, or barriers on market access or indirect measures that have the effect of doing so. Many of these measures are undertaken unilaterally in a manner that contravenes international trade law or exploits exceptions on the basis of national security. In parallel, countries are pursuing sustainability objectives to address climate change—such as green industrial policy to foster investment in climate mitigation and adaptation, carbon tariffs, and sustainability commitments in bilateral trade agreements—through a range of policy measures with implications for international law. Increasingly, countries pursue security and sustainability objectives simultaneously, often by imposing conditions and restrictions on the trade of environmental goods that are deemed to be geopolitically important, thereby securitizing what should be a global public good. In other instances, countries prioritize security or sustainability objectives while still being bound to reciprocal commitments to liberalize market access under international trade law. These developments involve trade-offs between liberalization, security, and sustainability, which international trade law has failed to effectively address. This Article likens this problem to a trilemma in which different policy objectives are mutually incompatible. Employing comparative analysis of the United States and the European Union, this Article analyzes green industrial policies and related trade policy measures, assesses conflicts with international trade law, and considers the implications for governance of the global economy and responses to climate change. In response, this Article offers measures to reform the legal architecture of the international trading system as a means to reconcile the competing incentives and imperatives posed by climate change and geopolitics.

title: Knowledge and Capital as Co-evolving Productive Stocks: A Minimal Core of Grand Synthetic Economics
affiliations: Nanjing University

detail.title: Knowledge and Capital as Co-evolving Productive Stocks: A Minimal Core of Grand Synthetic Economics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests
declarations.ethicsApproval: N.A.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper develops a minimal evolutionary core in which physical capital and usable knowledge are distinct but co-evolving productive stocks. Usable knowledge is not raw information or a productivity residual: it is knowledge converted into productive service by absorptive capability, organizational routines, and complementary assets. A resource identity and two accumulation laws first yield a closed benchmark with a unique positive stationary position, local stability, exact capability elasticities, and capital-knowledge complementarity. The benchmark is then embedded in a heterogeneous-routine selection process. When the usable-knowledge stock crosses a routine-specific profitability threshold, high-capability routines expand; their expansion in turn accelerates knowledge formation. Under a transparent threshold condition, both a lowcapability and a high-capability regime are locally stable, generating history dependence and possible lock-in. A group extension also identifies the restricted conditions under which a more equal allocation of capability investment raises aggregate output. The contribution is synthetic rather than component-wise: it links accumulation, selection, institutional conversion, dimensional discipline, and empirically refutable regime dynamics. The paper concludes with a staged measurement and identification strategy using firm and industry panels, and states rejection rules for complementarity, capability conversion, convergence, and evolutionary path dependence.

title: Beyond the Trade-off: Joint Optimization of Efficiency, Equity, and Innovation
affiliations: Nanjing University

detail.title: Beyond the Trade-off: Joint Optimization of Efficiency, Equity, and Innovation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no competing interests
declarations.ethicsApproval: N.A.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Policy debates often separate redistribution, productive efficiency, and innovation. This paper develops a joint policy framework in which capital and usable knowledge co-evolve under creative destruction, fiscal instruments, and absorptive capability. A redistribution instrument, research support, and capability investment affect sustainable consumption, distribution-sensitive equivalent consumption, and net social innovation value through distinct but interacting channels. Raw metrics are normalized against explicit anchors, and policy maximizes the least-achieved target subject to a current-program budget. Under continuity and compact feasibility, an optimum exists and is weakly Pareto efficient. A target-instrument Jacobian distinguishes nominal instrument counts from independent local control. A fully specified computational experiment combines 40,000 policy draws with constrained local optimization. The best verified candidate has normalized instrument coordinates (0.227, 0.597, 0.288), a minimum achievement of 0.961, and a binding budget. Efficiency and innovation bind jointly, while equity exceeds the minimum. Across 120 structural perturbations with fixed baseline anchors, the median re-optimized minimum achievement is 0.958. These are mechanism illustrations rather than estimated policy rates or a certified global numerical optimum. The policy contribution is an auditable method for combining fiscal feasibility, distribution, innovation, and capability while exposing normative anchors, instrument redundancy, and state dependence.

title: Engineered Catastrophic Coupling – A Systems Failure In Real Time

detail.title: Engineered Catastrophic Coupling – A Systems Failure In Real Time

declarations.declarationOfInterest: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Engineered Catastrophic Coupling (ECC), a framework describing how financial risk generated by concentrated asset holders is systematically transferred onto households and public budgets — not only during acute market crises, but as a standing feature of current economic architecture. Using the AI investment boom as an applied case, the paper identifies the specific channels through which this transfer occurs, including credit tightening, fiscal stress, and asymmetric policy response, and distinguishes these direct transmission channels from self-reinforcing dynamics — such as market concentration — that sustain the underlying architecture independent of any single downturn. The paper argues that financial shocks under this architecture are increasing in both frequency and severity, as the system requires periodic crisis events to sustain asset valuations disconnected from underlying productive activity. It concludes by identifying the structural conditions that would need to hold for this pattern to be interrupted, while distinguishing ECC's claims about incentive alignment from claims of deliberate coordination, which the paper does not make.

AI Disclosure: The author used ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic) as research and writing assistance tools during the preparation of this manuscript, including for language refinement, structural feedback, and editorial review. All core ideas, arguments, and conclusions are the author's own.

title: Competition and the Cost of U.S. Infrastructure
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: Competition and the Cost of U.S. Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received support from internal research grants in the Department of Economics at Harvard University, including funding for data acquisition.

detail.abstract: Can limited competition in procurement auctions explain the high and rising price of road infrastructure in the U.S.? I assemble a new dataset covering the near-universe of state highway auctions between 2002 and 2024. I first document thin competition: one-or two-bidder auctions account for a third of awards, and this share has risen over the past decade. Using spatial variation in interstate bidder locations, I then estimate the average causal effect of competition on prices; an additional bidder reduces prices by ten percent. To decompose bids into markups and production costs, I develop a semi-parametric structural auction model that incorporates bidders' uncertainty over the number of competitors they face. I show that price increases over the past decade are more attributable to increasing markups than increasing production costs. Limited competition, in turn, is consistent with patterns generated by fixed costs of entering public procurement, but not broad construction-sector fixed costs. Embedding the markup estimates in a structural entry model, I estimate large auction-level-and even larger market-level-entry costs, suggesting an important role for procurement bureaucracy and regulatory barriers.

title: Sports FOMO: The Influence of Fear of Missing Out on Live Sports Consumption, Social Media Engagement and Purchase Intention
