detail.title: Sports FOMO: The Influence of Fear of Missing Out on Live Sports Consumption, Social Media Engagement and Purchase Intention

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study empirically examines an integrated model linking fear of missing out (FOMO) with live sports consumption, social media engagement and purchase intention, treating social media engagement as a mediator and fan identification and platform type as boundary-condition moderators. Data from 220 sport consumers in India were analysed using multi-item seven-point Likert measures. Internal consistency was acceptable to good across the five constructs (Cronbach's α = 0.751-0.883). FOMO positively predicted live sports consumption (β = 0.274, p < .001) and social media engagement (β = 0.484, p < .001), while social media engagement positively predicted purchase intention (β = 0.448, p < .001). The bootstrapped indirect effect of FOMO on purchase intention through social media engagement was significant (ab = 0.238, 95% CI [0.150, 0.339]). The direct FOMO-to-purchase path became non-significant once social media engagement was included (p = .250), indicating an indirect-only mediation pattern. Neither fan identification nor platform type significantly moderated the FOMO-engagement relationship. The results position social media engagement as the behavioural bridge that converts FOMO-driven psychological discomfort into commercially relevant fan behaviour, and offer a replicable, visually documented analytic template for future sport-consumer FOMO research.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. The author has no personal or financial relationship with any person or organization that could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study involved no human participants and no primary data collection. It analyzes publicly available secondary data only: aggregate statistics from government and private sources, and de-identified public-use survey microdata (Current Population Survey; Stack Overflow Annual Developer Survey).

detail.abstract: Generative AI coding tools raise productivity most for less-experienced workers, yet recent studies report falling early-career employment in AI-exposed jobs. I ask whether a "junior penalty" is visible for U.S. software developers in public data through mid-2026, testing three predictions of the task-based framework: fewer junior openings, a younger-skewing decline in employment, and falling relative junior pay. Software-development postings fell 54% after ChatGPT's release, the largest decline among the 41 Indeed occupational categories, but 58% of the fall from their 2022 peak predates the release. Software-developer employment kept growing, the occupation's age composition did not shift relative to 222 other occupations in CPS microdata, and the occupational wage distribution compressed. Only an opt-in developer survey shows a widening junior-senior pay gap. The evidence supports a hiring squeeze, but not yet an employment or wage penalty.

title: From Model Governance to Decision Governance: A Behavior-Centered Architecture for AI-Assisted Decisions in Regulated Financial Services

detail.title: From Model Governance to Decision Governance: A Behavior-Centered Architecture for AI-Assisted Decisions in Regulated Financial Services

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Deborah Ribeiro Nogueira is the Founder and CEO of Zayon, which provided the professional engagement context and practice-informed insights used as design inputs for this study. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author declares that there are no personal, financial, or commercial relationships with other people or organizations that could be perceived as inappropriately influencing or biasing the work presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human subjects, clinical trials, or medical interventions. The practice-informed insights utilized in this research consist strictly of aggregated, institutional, and fully anonymized operational patterns observed during professional engagements, ensuring that no individual or personal data was accessed or processed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was entirely self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence adoption in financial services has increased the importance of model validation, data governance, explainability, and human oversight. Yet consequential decisions are rarely produced by models in isolation. They emerge from socio-technical processes in which model outputs interact with evidence, rules, organizational authority, human interpretation, overrides, escalation practices, and institutional incentives. Existing research offers conceptually complementary but operationally fragmented perspectives on human–AI decision-making, human-in-the-loop systems, automation bias, socio-technical systems, algorithmic accountability, Decision Intelligence, and model risk management. Although recent work increasingly addresses meaningful human oversight and organizational accountability, it does not consistently specify how these mechanisms can be integrated across the lifecycle of individual AI-assisted decision episodes in regulated environments.

This paper conceptualizes and operationalizes behavior-centered Decision Intelligence through a decision-level operational architecture for regulated financial services. Its central premise is that the decision episode, rather than the model, should be treated as the primary operational integration unit through which evidence, decision assets, human behavior, authority, action, outcome, and accountability are connected. This shift does not replace the model as a unit of technical validation or as a governance object. Rather, it introduces a complementary integration layer connecting controls originating in different governance domains. The architecture comprises a Decision Lifecycle, Decision Assets, Governance Assets, a structured Decision Record, Decision Lineage, Behavioral Governance, Supervisability, and proportional Decision Risk Tiers.

The paper adopts a design-oriented conceptual research approach informed by design science. It uses structured conceptual literature synthesis to identify relevant constructs, practice-informed material to identify recurring operational patterns, and architecture development to translate these patterns into governance requirements, metrics, and propositions. The practice-informed material consists of anonymized observations of decision workflows, process discussions, solution demonstrations, and documented operational patterns encountered during professional engagements in financial services in Brazil and Latin America. It is used as design input and problem-grounding material, not as empirical evidence of prevalence or effectiveness. Five propositions are derived concerning decision-level traceability, behavioral observability, override governance, authority allocation as decision risk, and integrated Decision Governance. The artifact is assessed conceptually through requirements coverage, scenario walkthroughs, construct coherence, and boundary-condition analysis. Empirical effectiveness remains a subject for future research.

title: Detectable but Not Exploitable: Predictability and Trading Costs on the Casablanca Stock Exchange

detail.title: Detectable but Not Exploitable: Predictability and Trading Costs on the Casablanca Stock Exchange

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests. No position in any security discussed in this paper is or was held by the author.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Statistical detectability does not by itself establish economic exploitability. We measure the gap directly, on 73 securities of the Casablanca Stock Exchange, 2010-2026, using a panel laid on the exchange's own session calendar so that non-trading intervals are observed rather than inferred. Price recovery following such an interval is significant on 21 of 60 securities under standard inference and on 26 of 60 under pairs-bootstrap inference, in both cases more than seven times the false-positive rate (exact binomial p = 5.7 × 10⁻¹³ and p = 1.9 × 10⁻¹⁸), yet returns 0.228% over five sessions against a published round-trip fee floor of at least 1.10%. Across 56 testable securities none shows a significant surplus, 32 show a significant shortfall, and the mean shortfall of 0.87% at the published fee floor (p = 1.0×10⁻¹⁶) remains significant, at 0.43 points (p = 2.8×10⁻⁷), even with brokerage at zero and only the non-negotiable components remaining. Published fees, not estimated spreads, anchor the test: the Roll and Corwin-Schultz estimators differ by a factor of four and rank securities inconsistently. The conclusion is unchanged under every market-factor construction and sample window we test, and under inference that assumes nothing about the return distribution or the independence of the securities; the deficit narrows as the holding horizon lengthens and, at 20 sessions, is no longer significant.

title: Employer Power and the Price of Bank Credit
affiliations: , University of Rhode Island,  and San Diego State University

detail.title: Employer Power and the Price of Bank Credit

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding on this research.

detail.abstract: Employer labor-market power matters to creditors. Greater power lets a firm hold down labor costs when operating conditions deteriorate, preserving cash flow for debt service; but exercising that power can erode the human capital the firm depends on. Using Lightcast job postings and 7,204 bank loan facilities, we find that greater labor-market competition, and thus weaker employer power, is associated with higher spreads, shorter maturities, and a greater likelihood of secured borrowing. The spread relation is more significant among borrowers nearer default. Supplementary evidence from Amazon's HQ2 expansion points in the same direction. The set of employers competing for a borrower's workers is therefore priced in bank credit, and shows up in contract design as well as in the spread.

detail.abstract: The sachet economy phenomenon has developed as a marketing strategy for fastmoving consumer goods (FMCG) targeting populations with limited purchasing power, particularly in developing countries such as Indonesia. Sachet packaging enables consumers to acquire products in small quantities at lower entry prices, yet it often creates higher per-unit costs and severe environmental consequences due to the use of multilayer flexible packaging. This paper aims to analyze the sachet economy through macromarketing and micromarketing perspectives by integrating Bottom of the Pyramid (BOP) theory, the marketing mix, consumer behavior, producer strategies, supply chain dynamics, and the circular economy. The methodology employs a conceptual literature review based on national and international studies regarding consumer behavior, marketing strategies, distribution, packaging, and sustainability. The analysis demonstrates that sachets serve not only as an affordability mechanism, but also as a consumer cash-flow management tool and market penetration strategy. However, this model creates a structural dilemma between economic accessibility, corporate profitability, and environmental responsibility.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a conceptual model of competition among branded products in which market advantage may be determined not by a product's overall superiority across many attributes, but by a single attribute or a small set of attributes that acts as an entry screen for consumer choice. Such a factor is termed the Critical Attribute Bottleneck (CAB). The proposed diagnosis is framed as the starting point of a challenger's strategy in markets with pronounced noncompensatory choice.

title: When Do Physiological Measures Forecast Market Outcomes? A Random Utility Framework
affiliations: , INSEAD, Toyota Research Institute and University of Toronto

detail.title: When Do Physiological Measures Forecast Market Outcomes? A Random Utility Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors gratefully acknowledge support from the Toyota Research Institute.

detail.abstract: Physiological measures are increasingly used to understand consumer preferences and predict market-level outcomes, often from samples far smaller and less representative than a typical survey. It remains unclear when and why such measurements can provide information about preferences in the broader market. We address this question with a bias-variance decomposition, using a Random Utility framework. Utility is made up of a common component, shared across consumers, and an idiosyncratic component, capturing personal tastes. We show that when physiological measures partially mute the idiosyncratic component, they yield more precise estimates of common utility than survey measures, even with smaller samples. This same muting also limits the selection bias introduced by non-representative samples. We derive a condition specifying when physiological measures serve as better predictors of market outcomes than survey measures, as a function of preference heterogeneity, measurement error, sample size, and the magnitude of idiosyncratic muting. We recast this condition as a Participant Allocation Rule that weighs the relative cost of survey and physiological data collection, and illustrate its use with existing fMRI data. Our framework gives researchers and firms a principled basis for deciding when, and how much, physiological measurement is worth its cost.

detail.abstract: This paper synthesizes best practices for building and sustaining collaborative research partnerships among academia, industry, and policymakers in supply chain management. Effective collaboration bridges different incentives, timelines, and knowledge systems to produce actionable insights that improve supply chain resilience, efficiency, and policy relevance. Core strategies include co‑designing research agendas with stakeholders to ensure mutual value, establishing clear governance arrangements and intellectual‑property rules, and using pilot projects and living labs to translate theory into tested practice. Researchers adopted a structured approach, gathering and analysing qualitative data from a wide range of online literature sources and expert opinions. The study meticulously selected 35 peer-reviewed articles spanning from 2009 to 2024, each discussing the Best Practices for Collaborative Research in Supply Chain Networks. The data revealed the limitations of the growth of uncertainty to the Best Practices for Collaborative Research in Supply Chain Networks. The systematic approach ultimately provided valuable insights into the Influence of the Best Practices for Collaborative Research in Supply Chain Networks. Capacity building and knowledge exchange are also essential: joint training programs, secondments between universities and firms, and policy fellowships foster trust and cross‑sectoral fluency. Funding and sustainability mechanisms, blended finance, multi‑year grants, and cost‑sharing agreements, support longer‑term projects that move beyond one‑off pilots. Evaluation frameworks should measure both scholarly impact and practical outcomes, using mixed indicators such as model accuracy, implementation uptake, efficiency gains, and societal benefits (for example, reduced emissions, improved equity). Attention to ethics and inclusion ensures research does not reinforce power imbalances; inclusive governance structures give voice to small suppliers, communities, and developing‑country partners. The paper concludes with a pragmatic roadmap: initial stakeholder mapping and co‑creation workshops, pilot design with clear metrics, scalable data‑sharing architectures, and institutionalised pathways for policy translation. By adopting these practices, collaborative research in supply chains can generate robust, implementable solutions that align academic rigour with operational and regulatory realities.

detail.title: Indoor Air Quality, Sickness Absence and Academic Achievement in Primary School Children

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict or interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The field study collecting health data is registered in the database ClinicalTrials.gov with the reference number NCT02800616, and received medical ethical approval from the Medical Ethics Committee Zuyderland in Heerlen (Registration number: MEC 14-N-142). All participants were required to complete an informed consent form, signed by both parents or caregivers, and by the children in case they are 12 years or older. The second field study collected data on exam grades for each child and matched this data with continuous indoor environmental quality measures during the school year. This study received medical ethical approval from the Medical Ethical Committee azM/UM at Maastricht University Hospital, registered under the number METC 2018-0681.
declarations.funderStatement: Graduate School of Business and Economics

detail.abstract: Academic achievement in primary school is an important factor for human capital accumulation, productivity, and health outcomes in adulthood. A substantial share of public expenses is devoted to the renovation, refurbishment, and modernization of school buildings. Indoor air quality in school buildings has a profound influence on children's academic achievement and learning performance. Evidence confirms a negative impact of insufficient ventilation and poor indoor air quality on cognitive performance and learning outcomes in primary and secondary school children. However, no study has investigated the pathways that explain the effect of indoor air quality on learning outcomes. Understanding the underlying mechanisms is crucial for developing effective interventions that foster the academic performance of children. This study combines indoor air quality measurements in classrooms, daily absence data, and test scores from standardized exams in primary schools, to investigate if sickness absence explains the relationship of indoor air quality and academic achievement. The results confirm a negative effect of frequent exposure to poor indoor air quality, determined by elevated carbon dioxide concentrations, during the learning phase, on subsequent test scores. However, sickness absence was not affected by indoor air quality, neither did sickness absence influence test scores. Therefore, the empirical analysis could not confirm a mediating role of sickness absence between indoor air quality and academic achievement. The findings illustrate a direct impact of indoor air quality on academic achievement, independent of absenteeism of primary school children.

title: From Citizens to Consumers: The Commodification of the Indian Banking Sector

detail.title: From Citizens to Consumers: The Commodification of the Indian Banking Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. There are no relevant financial or non-financial relationships to disclose that could be perceived as having influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is based entirely on publicly available archival data, corporate documents, and historical statistical tables. It does not involve human participants, patients, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was conducted as an independent academic inquiry.

detail.abstract: The year 1991 was pivotal for the banking sector in India when the Narasimham Committee recommendations led to a structural transformation in the sector. For four decades, banks functioned as agents of the State for implementing the welfare-oriented policies of the government. Forty years of nationalization of banks—1969—ended the era of growth-oriented private banks and ushered in the phase of large-scale public financial institutions. The current phase of private sector entry since 1994 has, however, presented a contrast. The banking sector has, in a few years, moved from a totally welfare-oriented system of mass employment to expand its branch network to cover rural masses and to function with the trust of people to become hyper-commercialized entities offering a plethora of retail financial products, with a marketing-driven focus on expanding its retail financial services through a vast network of branches and customer service outlets and digital financial services. An exploratory working paper uses Institutional Logics and the Marketing Concept to study this structural change in the banking sector. A thematic analysis of the long-standing corporate values and current strategies, business models, and service delivery approach of public sector and private sector banks has been presented. The values and service approach of two large public sector banks—Canara Bank and Punjab National Bank—and two large private sector banks—HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank—have been contrasted and presented. Their long-standing servicescape of an extensive branch network and large employee base has been contrasted with current ATM-centric, digital financial services. The two largest public sector banks in India—Bank of Baroda and State Bank of India—have been studied in detail to understand how market logic has been spreading in these banks. By adopting market-oriented strategies and layering digital financial services on top of the vast network of their branches and business correspondents, the legacy public sector banks in India have changed their fundamental DNA and commoditised the country's financial services.

title: Who Bears the Cost? Automation and the Transmission of Monetary Policy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Who Bears the Cost? Automation and the Transmission of Monetary Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Automation makes disinflation cheaper in output terms, and it does so by shifting the cost towards the households least able to absorb it. We develop a Two-Agent New Keynesian model in which robotic capital is predetermined within the period of a monetary shock and enters a nested constant-elasticity technology as a close substitute for unskilled labour, with households partitioned separately by skill and by asset market participation. Predeterminacy leaves two margins free. The rental rate on a stock that cannot move must clear its market, and its weight in marginal cost rises with the robot cost share, which steepens the Phillips curve. Unskilled hours must absorb the whole movement in the composite input, in a proportion given in closed form by the same cost share, which concentrates the burden on constrained households. One parameter therefore governs both how much cheaper disinflation becomes and who pays for it. The aggregate result is a production-side one, surviving in an economy with no constrained households at all.

detail.abstract:
This book proposes and operationalizes the Skills Transition Readiness Index (STRI), a four-dimension framework — labor-market institutional flexibility, human capital stock and skill composition, AI adoption capacity, and transition/social protection mechanisms — for measuring institutional readiness for AI-driven labor-market transformation. Distinct from existing AI-readiness instruments, which rely on pooled cross-country regression, the book specifies a selection-corrected, heterogeneous-treatment-effect econometric strategy, in the applied microeconometric tradition of Heckman, Vytlacil, and Urzúa's work on selection models with heterogeneity, for estimating how the returns to cognitive and non-cognitive skills shift under AI exposure. The volume includes a full operationalization table, structural equations for the composite index, a comparative illustration across Latin America and Central-Eastern Europe using verified World Bank Human Capital Index data, and an executable specification for the companion empirical volume (worker-level estimation, robustness battery, and PCA-weight sensitivity checks). Part of "The Gap" institutional-readiness book series.

detail.abstract: Autonomous and generative artificial intelligence systems now author a growing share of brand-relevant output, from advertising copy and chatbot dialogue to entire synthetic brand personas, yet do so within governance architectures that were not designed with brand identity in mind. This paper presents an integrative review of three literatures that bear on this problem but have developed largely independently: artificial intelligence governance, brand identity theory, and cultural identity in artificial intelligence systems design. Drawing on a purposively selected corpus of 102 sources published between 2015 and 2026, the review finds that artificial intelligence governance scholarship treats cultural specificity as a repeatedly acknowledged but never operationalised concern; that brand identity scholarship treats artificial intelligence uniformly as a capability to be deployed rather than a risk to be governed; and that cultural identity scholarship, while empirically rich, virtually never engages brand as a category at all. No source in the corpus integrates artificial intelligence governance architecture, brand identity protection, and cultural specificity within a single framework. This confirmed, evidenced gap motivates the construct of Brand Drift and establishes the evidential foundation for the Brand Identity Governance Framework developed in the second paper of this portfolio.
